JANUARY. " Behold. now is the accedted time; now is the day of salva- ion."-2 Corinthians vi., 2. Just like an old friend whom we miss From bi. accustomed phace. Another year has passed away, And, we—WO miss his face. 'Tis true he was not always !right— At times he made us std; But then, by God's most loving will, More often we were glad. And, now the year has passed away. We think—but all in vain— How many good things we would do Had we the time again. We all have wasted precious hours We might have spent for God; We know we have not sought to tread Where Christ our Master trod; And, looking back through days and months. If we to self be true, We can but see that we have done The things wa should not do. What wonder then we grieve awhile Now the old year is dean! Wnat wonder that we all lament The time so quickly 81)31! And yet we should not weep or sigh: The past is past for aye! B it the new year is ours to use In better holier way. 0 'et us then delay no more, But use God's gift aright, Not trusting in our feeble strength, But in the Father's might! And then, it may be, when this year In turn his course bath run, The still small voice at last may say— " Well done, brave heart, well done !" GEORGE WEATHERLY.

HOW TO FM) CIIILDUEN ARIGHT.—Pray, mothers, do not forget that an interval of rest should ensue between the meils you give r our children, and do not ruin their young digestions by cramming them with cake or buns or sweets Of any kind. To do so is worse than cruel—it is a sin, and a sin which you are but little llizoly to commit if you truly love them, and vally wish to see them generate into strong and healthy men and women. Tarts, and sweets, and eon- feetiocery would be bad enough in all conscience for chit. den, even if they were always pure and wiadulterated. But they are too often positively poisonous. Feed on plain and wholesome food regularly from day to day, permitting no stuffing between meals, and not forgetting the benefits that accrue from frequent chan4es of diet, especially as re- gards d' . nner Do this, and your children will live to bless you; do otherwise, and expect to see them sickly, with veins and arteries possessing no resiliency, with mucous membrane pale and flabby, pines of lungs that the accident of a el!it cold is sufficient to close, muocles of limbs so •weik that exercise is a pGnanle instead of a pleasure, and flesh so unwhoiesome that a pin's, prick may cause a fester —and all this because the blood is impoverished through errors in diet.

TOOLS TO TRE BOYS 'WHO CAN USA: THEM.—To youths with a taste for mechanics an assortment of tools and a con- venient place in which to practise their use are valuable poseessiene, and provide the means of agreeable relaxation from study when oueof•door recreations are either imprac- ticable or undesirable. Working in wood or in metal is a fascinating occupation for those whose predilections lie in that direction, and ptrents would do well to encourage it. The lives of not a few of the greatest engineers and in- ventors the world has ever seen show that their peculiar genius was first roused to activity by their having access in boyhood to tools and workshops. Of course, it is necessary before entrusting hammers, hatchets, and chisels to boys to consider whether they are likely Li use them for purposes of construction or of destruction. If the former, let them have them by all means; but if the latter, withhold them. In the one case the youth will seek out nieces of wood, and endeavour to convert them to some useful purpose; in the other he will be found disfiguring the furniture, or driving nails into doers and windows everywhere.—Cassell's Book of Sports and Pastimes. BIFORE BREAKFAST ON THE ALPS.--it is 80 fanny, Bell, to get up about the time you are' going to bad. I was wakened from a dream, in which Tom and Mr. Mowbray were riding a steeplechase on the back of an avalanche, by a sand like thunder, which turned out on closer reflection to be the night porter knocking at my door. It was 1 30 a.na. I jumped out of bed, dressed, and had found my way through the dark passages to the Salle-Aernanger before I WAS well awake. Even at that dismal hour the house was astir. One party had just left for: Monte Rosa; another was leaving for the Breithorn ; two or three sleepy-looking mountaineers were seated round the table. Tom made me a callow a cup of steaming cafe au lait, eat a morsel of bread, and then we went out into the starlight. • It was terribly chilly for the first hidf-hotir, but we soon warmed . . • . A brilliant planet'still burned over to our work. Monte Rosa, and ;I thought of Coleridge's, " Hest thou a charm to stay the morning star ?" And then—then Bell— but what words can describe what we saw when the sun first touched the snow peaks? Then we came to the vast snow•fields that stretch away for miles, like an American prairie, in long, gentle undalations, to the foot of the Monte Rosa crags. . . . We were all tied to Klee rope by this time, and now came the tug of leer—they fairly dragged me up the steep slopes of the Ci'll& ..... We are more than a mile above the plain, and Italy lies at our feet. Out of its soft warm haze, beyond the purple mist that floats over Como and Maggiore, rise the peaks of the Tyrol. Macugnaga, in the Val Anzasca, is 7,000 feet below us, ite houses no bigger than beehives. On the other hand the mighty mass of Mont Blanc, standing fouLsivare to all the winds that blow, is clearly visible above the long ridge of lock that culminates in the Matterhorn. I went to bed the moment we got back, and didn't open my eyes till they were ringing the belljfer the table cl'hOte. De you know, Bell, I am coming to think that life is only worth living at 13,000 ft. above the sea.—" Alpine Resting Places; a Story above the Clouds," in "Good Words." The reason why so many are unable to take Cocoa is that the , varieties commonly sold are mixed with starch, under the plea I of rendering them soluble; while really making them thick, heavy, and indigestible. This may be easily detected, for if Cocoa thickens in the cup it proves the addition of starch. Cadbury's Cocoa Essence is genuine; It is therefore three times ! the strength of these Cocoas, and a refreshing :beverage like tea or coffee.—eldet.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

The French official journal publishes a report on oyster culture, which is in favour of the Portuguese oyster. It appears that 100 grammes of the flesh of this mollusc con- lain about 1-10th gramme cf iodine, bromine, and chlorine, I —just twice as much as the common oyster. A new and valuable use has been found for oyster shells, which until recently were only utilised in making lime. It has been discovered that the shells make a capital founda- tion for oyster beds, and within the past few years many thousands of bushels have been used for this purpose in the United States. THE ANTUROPOMETER —An ingenious invention, de- signed to measure large bodies of troops for their clothing, including caps and boots, has peen tried by an Italian mili- tary commission in Rome, under the presidency oi General di San Germano, commander-in-chief of the Roman Divi- sion.. It is called the anthropemeter, and is the invention of an Italian gentleman. Tne experiment is said to have proved its practical utility. Sixty infantrymen and thirty bersvlieri were measured with two of the new machines, and fitted with new clothing. They were then provided with arms, and reviewed by the General, the proceedings from beginning to end having occupied less than one hour. EDISON'S .ELEcTuic LIGHT METEL—It a current of elec- tricity be passed through a solution of sulphate of copper, contained in a copper jar, the sulphate solution is decom- posed and metallic copper is depositedepn the inside of the jar. Now it has been proved by experiment, that the amount of copper deposited is always directly proportional to the strength and duration of the electric current. Mr. Edison's meter consists of such an arningement, and he finds that by weighing the copper jar, so as to determine ixactly whet it has gained in weight through the metallic deposition of the solution it contains, he can accurately calculate in units the amount of electricity that has passed through the meter, By nims of this beautiful discovery elettricity can be supplied and paid for in a manner very similar to that em- ploved in the case of gas at the present time—Gee'] Words. OMP Ell,—The Times correspondent writes from Naples: —"A discovery has lately been made in Pompeii which le well worth noting. Not many data have passud since a quadri-valve speculum of great beauty and in a high state of preservation was turned up. By competent persons who have examined it, the mechanism of it is said to be very in- genious. In the National Museum of Naples there are now three Pompeian specula—one a bi-ealve, one a tri-valve, and the one just found, a quadri-valve. The last is said to be of a construetion so uniform and well proportioned, admitting the expansion of the valves, as to be superior to modern con- strectien. It is noted as a curious fact that in its various dimEn&ons it observes constantly the centimetric measure- ment. It will be found, in fact, on iesoeccing the National Museum of Naples, that many of the instruments ascribed as inveotions to moderns are clearly only exhumations of the pact."

THE t:Tes'a CoROSTa —Mr. truggitii real a paper on this last week before the Royal Seelety, in which he said It was generally known that our sea is surrounded by an immense atmosphere termed the corona, which is so over- powered by the scattered light of our own atmosphere that it is only daring total eclipses that it can be seen at all. Of this wonderful structure but little was certainly known; it was, however, certain that the corona mystery, like many another, contained truth of high importance; ant the only possible means of solution of the mystery was a method of ohserving the corona from day to day. Problems of the highest interest in the physics of our sun are connected doubtlees with the varying forms which the corona' light is known to assume; but these would seem to admit of solu- tion only on the condition of its being possible to study the corona continuously, and 80 to be able to confront its changes with the other variable phenomena which the sun presents. Unless some means be found of bringing out the structures round the sun which are hidden by the glare of our atmo- sphere, the progress of our knowledge must be very slow, for the corona is visible only about eight days in a century in the aggregate, and then only over narrow stripes on the earth's surface, and but from one to five minutes at a time by any ene observer. The coronal light existed, of course, behind the bright atmospheric glare which concealed it from our eyes. Consequently those parts of the glare which had the corona behind them must be in some degree brighter than where it was absent. The problem WAS to accen- tuate this minute difference, ordinarily insensible to us. This he had accomplished by combining two different principles. The first was to cat down the whole light which fell upon the earth to that portion of the spectrum alone, where, from the photograph of its spectrum taken during the eclipse of May last, the corona light was now known to be very strong. The seeond principle was the extreme s-neitiveness which photography possessed to minute differences of illumination which almost surpassed the eye's power of discerning them. One very strong rea- son for e riploying photography was that by this means alone a permanent and truthful record of so complicated a struc- ture as the corona could be obtained. Even at eclipses, when the atmospheric glare was absent and the corona shone out brilliantly, the differences between drawings done by observers sitting side by side had been so great as to de- prive them of any great scientific value. Consequently, even though the region of the spectrum was within the power of the eye, it was obviously useless to expect truth- ful drawings in sufficient detail to be obtained under cir- cemstances so much less favourable. There seemed no rea- son, however, why his method should not be need for eye obeereations of the corona under suitable atmospheric con- ditions. The results which he had obtained consisted of some 20 pates taken between Jane and September 28th. on all of which the corms might be seen with more or less dis- tinctness. Those showed not only an increase of photo- graphic action about the sun, but those rays and rifts which hal bosn observed in no other phenomenon of nature ex- cept the coroea. Many of these appeared to agree in gene. rat loon with similar appearances in the eclipse plates, and if this was so we might learn from them the stability, for some months, of the principal features of the May corona, netwithatanding that continuous miner changes must be taking place in it. Unfortunately, our climate and the cir- cumstance that his observatory was near the surface of the earth did not permit him to do much more than inaugurate a method of continuous observation of the corona, which, in more favourable climes, and especially at high elevations, most lead rapidly to an increase of our knowledge of the physics of the sun, which other wise might have been impos- sible to us for ages to come.

To young shorthorn bulls have recently been shipped to New Zealand by Mr. J. H. Shore from the herd of the Prince of Wales at Sandringham. No PROFIT IN BAD Cows.—A writer in the New York Times emphasises the fact that the profit of the dairyman comes wholly from his good cows, and that many a dairy might be reduced one-half in number of its cows and the dairyman make more profit tban he may have done from the whole original number, because one p,-)or cow will not onl "eat off its own head," but will eat off that of another and a better one, too, before it has equalised the profit and loss of the keep of the two.

UNREGISTERED MILK SELLERS—An Act of great impor- tance was enforced at Nantwich on Monday afternoon. Rupert Kirkham, farmer, Buerton, was summoned by the county police authorities for being an unregistered milk seller. Sergeant Fowler said the defendant MB in the habit of sending milk to Manchester, and it was necessary that he should be registered. The defendant, who sad he was entirely ignorant of the Act of Parliament compelling dairymen to register, was fined 203. and costs. A correspondent to the Cultivator and Country Gentleman (Albany, N.Y.) expresses his disgust at the value attached to fancy points by cattle breeders. He once showed Jerseys at the New York State Fair, a very small number, and won some premiums—a first on a heifer, a second on a bull—all In strong rings. The bull was from a cow that was one of twelve that averaged 400 pounds of butter a year. He was offered for sale at £3O, but purchasers were warned not to take him by the herdsmen of other breeders, and the reason given was that there were some white hairs at the end of his tail—his only fault. It is believed that the end of his horns were all ermine ilfaut. He was taken home, sold for beef, and the writer placed all his Jerseys in the market, to get out of a breed where so much value attached to the hairs on the end of the tail.

SOMEWHXT EXTENSIVH FEET.—Ex-Congressman Bill Slammon tells of a pair of feet that must have been objects of great regard in their day. One day a party of men, in- cluding Jackson, the man of big feet, were preparing to at- tend a politioal barbecue. It was soon discovered that there was no way of conveying Jackson, as all the vehicles were full. "Let me ride that mule over there?" asked Jackson. "There isn't a man in the world that can ride that animal. He'll work to a buggy or plough, but no man can stay on his back." "I'll try him, any way," and the determined man instructed several negroes to catch the mule and hold him. The animal plunged and kicked, but finally Jackson secured a seat in the saddle. Every one expected to see him dashed against the ground, but the mule looked around, saw the man's feet, and walked peacefully away. He thought he was betweqn a pair of shafts. ENSILADE.—Mr. T. Easdale writes to the Field from the neighbourhood of Northallerton, reporting a favourable trial with ensilage. Ordinary pasture grass was taken up at once behind the scythe, and was carted to a silo in the end ' of August and beginning of September. November 25 the pit was opened, and herbage found wholesome and palatable for cattle. This is an extreme case, because the wetness of the year and the nature of the herbage preserved—both are incidents which it has been assumed would be against so-- cess with a silo. Morsover, the grass was not "chaffed" bafore being pitted. but deposited in the silo as it tell from the scythe. Mr. Thorold Rogers, in Macmillan's Maya- z ' %ne has an article on the same subject; and both this and Mr. Easdale's letter are well deserving the attention of any of your subscribers who may desire information as to this very promising addition to the stores of a farm.—D. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 6, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 6, 1883.

meetings. in Saturday last one was held for the benefit of farmers only, and at which only farmers were to speak. The chairman was a farmer, and temperance melodies were sung as solos by farmers. Mr. D. B. Joyce, of Beckington, was the chairman, and he said that he had been a teetotaller for forty•six years, and though always in ill health, he had stack to his colours. He related the story of the sale of his stock some years since, which he insisted upon conducting on teetotal principles. He was Veld by all, even the auc- tioneer, that it would he a failure. At the finish of the sale the auctioneer said that it was one of the best sales he had ever conducted, and he believed more good had been done than by many teetotal lectures. He further gave his I experience of doing harvest work without ale, beer, or cider, giving extra wages instead. In one season, two teetotal mowers, who bad to walk 11 mile to their work, were pitted ag iinst two others who lived near his farm, and who were not abstainers, but who were admitted to be the best mowers for miles round. The former did a great deal more work than the others in addition to their long walks night and morning. Mr. C. Collins, of Orchardleigh, said that he had supplied his men with cold tea and coffee for harvest work, and found they did much better and were not so thirsty as when they drank ale. Others spoke in similar strains. Mr. Reines narrated some of the difficulties he had experienced as a lad in dealing with his father's men, when he vowed that if ever he became a farmer himself he would do with- out strong drink altogether. When he had a farm of nearly 300 acres he tried this plan, but daring the three summer months he gave his men 6d. per day extra instead of beer. Other speakers urged that a good example was set when the farmers acted in this manner, and it prevented oftentimes the labourers spending their evenings in a public-house. ARE WE TO LOSE OUR FUTURE HARVESTS ?—ln the last report of the Royal- Agricultural society there is the strange assertion that "all the competitors for the harvest- saving prize failed to make hay in wet weather." In the former report in the journal of that society the judges them- selves admitted that one competitor (Mr. Champion) did make it after four or five days' rain, and in spite of a heavy shower falling in the coarse of the process. They also stated that this required no farther making, and that it was dried at the rate of twenty loads a day, and at 6s. per ton for labour and fuel. Practical farmers pronounced this hay to be as good as if made in line weather; the auction price proved it 50 per cent. higher in value than the competing I stack; the consulting chemist of the society, Professor Voelcker, approves the System as scientifically perfect; his Grace the Duke of Northumberland, Mr. G. P. Faller, of I' Neston Park; Mr. C. J. Morris, of Wood Eaton Manor, have proved the machines do make splendid hay in ;wet weather, and repay theft entire C9gt in one, two, or three seasons re spectively ; and yet these droll lunges :Pe:n never tired of assuring us that we must continue to lose our millions. content with ignoring such facts, and despising such evi- dence, they have now forgotten their own facts and their own recorded evidence. This would be :simply absurd if it were not also so dlo3.strous. This reiterated official croak of "You will be drowned, and nobody shall save you," must unhappily ruin a vast number:of farmers who pin their faith to all croakers; but surely the noblemen and great landowners will not consent to lose their harvests, or meekly continua to make abatements of rent at the dictation of these gentlemen. Surely they will believe the positive re- sults obtained by men of their own "order," rather than oracular opinions, and dismal prophecies, based upon half a day's hurried and impatient trial. And, now that the second "oracle" flatly contradicts the first, the ridiculous ap- proaches the sublime. Whilst they are still reiterating "impossible" the thing has been done—" done" over and over again, and for season after season. It has been re. corded scores of times as an undisputed fact; recorded In every leading paper in the country—translated and pub- lished in Russia, Germany, Austria, Hungary, France, !eels', Belgium, Holland, and- is known to be a fact in new world as well as in the old. Rather a world-wi.ae delusion this—if these facts are not facts. Can three gentlemen have been living in the moon fur the last few years ? Wm. A. Gibbs.

well built in body, at times a little lanky, but more fre- quently inclined to be stumpy. The flesh feels firm when the rabbit is in healtb, and this gives the idea of a strong constitution. The legs are strong, and there is a compact- ness in the frame which cannot but be admired. The Him- alayan is one of the hardiest breeds extant, and it will thrive In almost any place under shelter and free from draughts It is on this account to be recommended to those who have not the opportunity of building rabbit courts or have not a warm shed at their disposal. It is by nature timid in it disposition, but can be tamed if kindness be used, and when it once gets to know its keeper, it loses all fear of him, and Is very affectionate. It must be kept clean and dry, and the hutch should be cleaned out daily. For food, it requires plenty of green stuff and roots, and with these oats and hay thbuld be given to keep it in perfect health. Cleanliness and ventilation, but no pampering should be the rule. div.head: HOUSEHOLD PETS.
div.p: HOUSEHOLD PETS.

Doets.—THE SE Yli TERRIER.—Skye terriers have of late years become, at least in the southern half of the island, such great favourites in the drawing-room, and as ladies' pets, for which purpose they have been very largely bred— though perhaps this involved the importation of foreign blood —that there has been great danger of the real and o-iginal character of the breed being lost. There can be no question that originally they were terriers in nature as well as in name, and a very determined effort was made a few years ago by old breeders in Scotland to save their favourites from being spoiled, and we are glad to say that this effort has been successful. Belonging to the Western Isles and Highlands of Scotland, they have been utilised in the de- struction of all kinds of vermin, which are to be found in such large numbers there. The chief difference between the real and the modern Skye terriers is that whilst the coat of the latter is of a silky texture, ranging from eight inches to a foot in length, that of the true breed is wiry, and rarely, if ever, exceeds in length four inches. We prefer in our description here to take the real standard, as the other is one that may be varied at will, and though some of our lady readers mey prefer the silky•coated animals, as these per- haps are nicer to fondle, there can be no question that the others are the better for ordinary purposes. The following is the description of this game and intelligent dog medium in size; muzzle, shortish and rather broad, not soipey ; jaws, strong and welt clad with muscle; leneth of head, about 7 inches; from end of nose to eyes, 21 inches; and from eyes to back of skull, 41 inches. Eyes dark hazel colour, very expressive and of moderate size, overhung by bushy eyebrows, but not BO long as to obstruct the sight. Ears—small, broad at the root, and tapering to ra ry)iut ; clad with soft hair, and slightly feathered. The drop-ear should not lie flat against the side of the head, but drop towards the front. In the prick-eared variety, the ears are carried erect. Length of ears from 21 to 3 inches, breadth at the root about 21- inches. Neck— strong and muscular, about 5 inches long, and about 9 to 1O inches in girth. Body—long in proportion to height of dog; chest and ribs deep, body neither flat sided nor yet round like a barrel; length from shoulder to root of tail, say from 15 to 17 inches, girth behind foreleg 15 to 161 inches Lags—short and strong, with plenty of muscle; they may be slightly bandy, but the less the better; hair on legs, softer in texture as well as lighter in colour than on back of the dog. Foreleg, :421- to 5 inches in length. Feet—small, .more or less hairy, and without dewclaws. Tail—short, and rather bu6hy, and the nearer straight it is the better. Height—from! 8 to 9 inches at the shoulder, and about the same behind. - Coat—on the body dense, and the outer or longer hairs of a decidedly wiry texture, that underneath being much finer in quality. Colour—dark gray, light gray, reddish yellow, or nearly black. Weight—males from 12 to 16 lbs., females about 3 ibs. lees.

PIGEONS.—THE KIND TO KEEP.—Fancv pigeons are very numerous as well as very beautiful, and there are almost in- definite varieties of form, as well as blending of feather. In , no one class of bird can be found the same variation of ' beauty, and hence tasted very opposite may be gratified. If the eye delights in colour, then some of the German toys can be selected. If gracefulness of form recommends itself to us, then that can be gratified by the dragoon or the carrier. If size is liked best, then we have the runt: if peculiarity of shape, then the stately pouter, or the welbbalanced fan. I tail ; or if email size is of itself an attraction, then the almond tumbler, the owl, or the torbit can be chosen. In fact, every taste can be gratified and every wish satisfied. The active man of business can find rest and repose in his comfortable pigeon loft, where in all weathers he can surround himself with his pets, and, at the same time, rest his body and refresh his mind. He Can select the higher. class birds, and spend as much money over his houses and birds as he thinks fit. Or the man who is cooped up all day and has nn opportunity for exercise in his ordinary avoca- tion, can, by keeping some of the flying varieties, such as homing, Antwerps, find an object which will be sufficient to take him out of doors, and he will get the long walks so necessary to him. The graceful young lady will find much pleasure in the beautiful fantail, which is the ladies' pigeon par excellence. The poor man can find much delight and pleasure in his flyers, the invalid can find that which will make him forget himself in the tame little tumblers, whilst those who are fond of curiosities can have trumpeters, or the Eastern toys. Modest persons may be attracted to the re- tiring Jacobin, with its fringed hood, not very unlike an old-fashioned bonnet, or those who are ecclesiastically in- clined may select the priest, the nun, the monk, or the car- melite. o far as the choice is concerned, therefore, there is no restriction' and it will be a strange and capricious Indi- vidual who, loving pets, cannot find one to meet his or her Ideas of beauty. CAGE BIRDS.—THE GOLDFINCH.—" Beauty of plumage," says Buffon, "softness of voice, remarkable cleverness, quickness of instinct, proved docility, tender affection are all united in this delightful little bird, and if it were rare, or if it came from a foreign country, it would then be valued as it deserves." It is five inches and three-quarters in length, of which the tail measures two. The beak, very pointed in shape and rather flattish at the sides, is white, with the point horn-coloured. The shanks are delicate and brownish in colour. The front of the head is a fine crimson, sometimes scarlet; a wide border of the same colour sur- rounds the upper base of the bcak'; the bridle, as it is called, is black; the top of the head also black, which colour extends downwards from the nape on each side, dividing the white on the cheeks from the white spot on the hinder part of the neck; the under part of the neck is white, the hinder part and the back are fine brown. The female is rather smaller, and has not so much red round the bill; the bridle IS brownish, the cheeks are mixed with light brown, the lesser coverts being of a similar colour, and the back rather darket. In a wild state goldfinches are found in woods and thickets, and are stationary, not leaving their summer haunts in the winter season. They merely as- semble in the autumn in families, or rather in little flocks of about a score, seeking places which abound in thistles When kept in confinement they need a square cage, if kept In a cage at all, but if at large in an aviary they should have a small artificial tree for a roost, as they like to perch on such a place, both when singing and at rest. RABBITS—THE HIMALA.YAN.—This is one of the most beautiful of all the rabbit tribe, and though some may fancy other breeds and naturally consider them the best, yet we think few will be prepared to deny the attractiveness of the Himalayan. It originally came from China, and hence in some places it is called the Ciiinese rabbit. It is not very large in size, but really good specimens often turn the scale at 7ilbs, and some nave been known to weigh over Bibs. They are pretty prolific, and the young ones are born per- fectly white, but, as the dowu beeins to grow, a tendency to darkness will be noticed about the ears, nose, feet, and tail, and gradually this deepens until the animal in time assumes its proper colour, which is brown or chocolate on the nose, tail, and ears, the feet grey, and the rePt of the body white. lithe markings can be obtained jet black. this I is preferred, but it is very seldom found. div.head: DEATH OF M. GAMBETTA.
div.p: DEATH OF M. GAMBETTA.

In the last moments of the old year M. Gambetta, Vic greatest figure ia currtnt French history, died at his resi- dence at Ville d'Avray. Only five weeks previously it was reported that while handling a revolver, M. Uambetta had accidentally inflicted upon °himself a trifling wound in the hand. His injury was minimised as much as possible, and the only feature of the cise that created alarm was the obvious endeavour to give a highly encouraging account of M. Gambatta's condition. Had French docters been as skilled in the treatment of gunshot wounds as were the medical practitioners who attended General Garfield, M. Gambetta's life might possibly have been spared. It may be that the complications which arose might have baffled the greatest skill, and not even have been prevented by amputation' but under efficient medical treatment a pistol shot in the hand or arm seems an inadequate cause of the death of a strong man who has only just completed his forty-fourth year.

Gambetta was born cf a Genoese family on October 30, 1838. Adoptiag the legal profession he became a mem- ber of the Paris bar in 1859, and soon acquired fame as a favourite orator. At the general election 1869 he stood for Paris and Marseilles as a representative of the "Irrecon- cilable opposition," and was returned for'both constituen- cies. fn j;iii:ltrY, 1870, he made a violent attack on the 011ivier ministry, declariro that the day would come when the majority of the people would, without appealing to force, succeed in establishing a RepubliC. On the fall of the Government, and the consequent formation of the National Defence in September, 1870, he was nominated Minister of the Interior, and soon showed that he possessed administrative powers of a high order. When a serious mis- understanding took place between the Delegate Government at Tours and the National Defeece Committee in Paria regarding the contemplated election of deputies, M. Qatnbetta was re-elected by his colleague e to proceed to the former city and explain the position of affairs in the capital. Accordingly h left Paris on October 7, 1870, in a balloon, and Pa.l;sed safely over the Prussian lines, and reachetLitenenin the evening. Proceeding without loss of tiine to Tours he there assumed the direction of affairs, and for some months was virtually dictator of all those pro- vinces of France which were free from the German invaders. His electior as deputy was annulled some time afterwards, and he proceeded to Spain, whence, after spending same time in quietness, he returned to Paris and obtained a seat in the Assembly, where he was regarded as chief of the Radical wing of the &publican party. On September 11, 1877, he was condemned to three months' imprisonment and to pay a fine of 2,000 francs for having said of Marshal MacMahon that after the next elections the President of the Republic must either submit or resign. M. Gambetta was also con- demned for issuing a circular to three months' imprisonment and to pay a fine of 4,000 francs. In the discussion in the Chamber respecting the election of M. de Fourtou, Gambetta called that statesman a liar. This led to a duel, but the encounter was a harmless one. The news of M. Gambetta's death has stunned France and been received with surprise and regret throughout this country, but it is scarcely an exaggeration to say that it has been received with jubilation in Germany. The Berlin newspapers openly rejoice at the death of this enemy of Germany and indefatigable though discreet preacher of the policy of revenge. It will be well if their indecent joy does not provoke 4 more bitter hostility in France than was enter- tained hitherto towards Germany even by the statesman whom France now mourns. The house in which M. Gambetta died was visited on Tuesday by large numbers of men distinguished in politics of art, and also by numbers of the rank and file of the Gambettist party. The Press in Paris, Vienna, Berlin, and St. Petersburg devotes much space to memoirs of the de- ceased statesman and examinations of the political changes which may follow his death. The Journal de St Petersburg affirms that M. Gambetta's greatness was on the wane. The deceased statesman's enemies among the Monarchists (says the Journal) will proclaim the Republic to have received a deadly blow through his death, while extreme Radicals will consider the Republic to have been rid of its most mortal enemy. "While France loses one of her most illustrious children, his loss does not jeopardise the interests of the nation." The Berlin jouroals believe that with the death of M. Gambetta "the party of war and revenge" is rendered harmless for a long time to come. On the other hand, the Deutsche Zeitung of Vienna thinks that the "revenge idea will survive until it, too, is interred upon some battlefield." It has been decided it a Cabinet Council that the obse- quies of M. Gambetta shall take place under similar condi- tions to those attending the funerals of MM. Thiers and Cremieux, as members of the Government of National De- fence. The Parisians have decided to close their shops on the day of the funeral, as a sign of general mourning.

div.head: CONVERTED CLOWN'S ADVENTURE
div.p: A CONVERTED CLOWN'S ADVENTURE

Some sensation has been caused in Leicester by the sud- den disappearance and subsequent attempted suicide of a converted clown named Fred Eugenie, who has taken a most prominent part in the Blue Ribbon Army movement all over the country, but especially in the mid- land and northern counties. The person in question had announced a free Christmas breakfast for 1,000 tramps and destitute persons at the Temperance Hall, LeiceSter, at his own expense. Considerable subscrip- tions were raised, but when, the morning announced arrived, the converted clown could not be found, neither could be be traced, and the local Blue Ribbon Army has been bur- dened with all the cost. Some time ago it was announced that a large fortune had been left by a gentleman in Newcastle to Eugenie to carry on temperance work, and large sums of money were paid to Eugenie to conduct missions in all the large towns in England. He was also announced to conduct a mission in Nottingham in a few days. Eugenie set up a very con- siderable establishment at Proi pect House, Castle Doning- ton, and seemed on the highway, if not to fame, at least to fortune. There are many rumours afloat, but it is now be- lieved that the story of a fortune is unfounded. It is stated that an arrangement had been entered into for a marriage, in connection with which there are some extraordinary dis- closures. A baronet is reputed to be a:-noung those who espoused the cause of the clown, and who have been duped. Every effort was made to trace Eugenie, but nothing was gleaned until Saturday, when information was received that he had been spending the week at the Half-moon Inn, Yeovil, spending money very freely, and had been dis- covered in the yard of the public-house with his throat cut, he baying attempted to commit suicide. He now lies in the hospital in a serious condition.

How Sam WAS COAXRD TO GIST MARBlED.—Justice- alley had hardly been opened to legal businesi when a sleigh, containing seven or eight persons from beyond the city limits, drove up to the door of a popular justice, and piled out with an air of business. His Honour Was poking up the fire, when an old man beckoned him into a corner and whispered, "Got a job of splicing here for ye. My darter Sarah is going to hitch to that chap there with the blue comforter, and then we're going out to have some oysters." "All right, all right," was the reply, and in two minutes the official was all ready. The man with the blue com- forter pealed his overcoat, laid aside his hat, and extended his hand to Sarah. "I won't do it; I'll die first !" she said, as she shrank away. "she'd a leetle timid—a leetle timid," exclaimed the old man; while the 'umber rebukingly ob- served, "Sarah, don't you make a fool of yourself here. William will make you a good husband." "And don't you forget is!" added William; "Come, Sarah." "I won't un- less we can go to New York on a bridal tower !" she snapped. "You'd look nice bridle towering around New York with no bettter duds than you've got ! said the mother; "Now, Sarah, you stand up and git married !" "Be keerful, mother—don't make 'er mad !" warned the old man. "Now, Sarah, if ye back out everybody will laff at us." "I don't keer. I want to travel." "Sarah, I'm yer father, hain tI ?" "Yes, dad." "And I've &Una bin tender of ye ?" "Yes." "Then be tender of me. I want to see ye married to Wil- liam. You can't have a tower (tour), nor a diamond ring, nor a set of furs, but I'll buy ye a pair of new gaiters. William will pay for the oysters, and I'll see that mother divides up the dishes and bedding with ye. Sarah, do you want to see my gray hairs bowed down ?" " N-o-o." " Then don't flunk out."—" Will they be two dollar gaiters?" ehe.asked. " Y-r."—" And all the oysters we can eat?" "Yes, all you 14.4 stuff."—" And a tower next fall, if wheat does well ?" div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

ST. HELENS V. WIDNEs.- -A team of players from each of the above towns met on New Year's Day, on Littler's Field, Denton's-green. The St. Helens " skipper " put his foot to the "oval ".at three o'clock, and, by quick following up, a return was prevented, a scrimmage ensuing. Con- nolly gett'ng hold made a good run, Gregson replying with a long kick. Edwards showed up with a dribble, but Connolly again replied with a run and kick. The play for a time was neutral, but after a fine dribble by the " Saints " a dead ball was registered. Foreman returned the drop out, and after some give and take play Finney handled the leather, and after a quick run passed to Cunliffe, who failed to proceed further. The "Chemicals," by good passing, now took the play near to the " Saints' " citadel. From the scrimmage which followed the play became neutral. The " Saints " now worked hard, and by a rush took the " oval " over the visitors' line; the result, however, was only a minor point. Finney replied to the drop out by a long kick, a (lead ball being the result. The drop out was next charged down, but by combined play the visitors kept it in front. Foreman getting hold was run in touch, and from a pass in the line out Cunliffe was given a good chance, but only ran across. From a line out Green broke away and cleverly grounded the leather behind the pests. Borthwick's attempt proved a failure. Both sides now showed up with dribbles and passes. Connolly having a chance essayed a run, but was brought down by Clegg. Ratcliffe now put in a shot and took the play into the home 25, soon after compelling Rogers to touch down. Gregson showed next with a run along touch, taking the play to neutral ground Penning- ton soon after gained a free kick, Morris trying for goal but failing. Ends being changed, Kiddie kicked off and soon scored a touchdown. Rogers dropped out, and loose play fallowing Parr cleverly ran in, Heaton, who took the plac, landing a goal. Widnes next scored two touchdowns, Harding replying to the drop out; and shordy after J. H. Smith for Widnes ran in, Morris kicking a fine goal. From the kick-off the home team gradually worked the leather on, and Martindale was forced to touch down. Connolly now shewed up with a run, but Finney smartly brought him down. From a line out Lyon broke away along touch to the visitors' 25. From the scrimmage following the visitors broke away with a dribliTrAnij registered a touch down, soon after scoring anot4,l" The result on the call of "no side" being St. Helens, one goal, one try, and five minor points, to Widnes one goal and six minor points, the home team being de- clared the victors. Although the weather was unfavourable, the game was witnessed by a *good number of spectators. Teams :—Widnes Martindale, back; Harding, Connolly, and Wilkinson, three-quarter backs; Morris arid Quinn, half-backs; Kiddie (Capt.), J. H. Smith, Ratcliffe, Woods, J. Smith, Davies, Waring, Spencer, Shaw, and PennimOon, forwards. St. Helens Rogers, back; Gregson, Cunliffa, and Foreman, three-quarter backs; Finney and Heaton, half-backs: Borthwick (cant.), Parr, Green, Arnold, Har- wood, Lyon, Jaq. Basnett, Chadwick, Edwards, and Clegg, forwards.

div.head: CHESHIRE VICAR AND HIS PAIZISHION[!RS.
div.p: A CHESHIRE VICAR AND HIS PAIZISHION[!RS.

A good deal of acrimonious feeling has been engendered in the village of Worleston by the action of the Rev. W. Yates, rector, in dismissing from the parish school the &and of John Humphreys, stationmaster, at Worleston. Humphreys alleges that he, being a Nonconformist, declined to admit his child to attend the parish school because it was a part of the school routine that the children should attend divine service at the parish church. He admits that in his letter to the schoolmistress requesting her not to take the child to church he said that he did not wish him to listen to " the tomfoolery next door," but he says that he and the Nonconformists were aggravated to make such remarks by reason of the circumstance that the rector described the Methodist chapel in the village as "a barn," and said that all those who attended it "would go to hell." Humphreys has received the following communications from the Educa- tion Department, which satisfactorily settles the matter as far as he is concerned :—"Education Department, White- hall, December 28th.—Sir,—I have the honour to acknow- ledge the receipt of your letter of the 12ch inst. I am to enclose you a copy of a letter ad- dressed on the 19th December, 1882, by the Educa- tion Department to the correspondent for Worleston national school It does not fall within the duties of this department to express any opinion on the tone of your correspondence with the Rev. W. Yates.—l have the honour to be, sir, you: obedient servant, F. T. Psiona.vs.—Mr. John Humphreys, stationmaster, Worleston, Cheshire."— (Copy.) "Education Department, Whitehall, December 19, 1882.—Rev. Sir,—Adverting to your letter of the let inst., and to the copy of the time-table enclosed, my lords understand that there is a rule at present in force in this school that a short service in church shall form part of the religious instruction which is given to the children.' lam directed to state that such an arrangement is not authorised in the time-table approved by Her Majesty's Inspector, nor by the Code. The rule should be rescinded, and in the event of this requirement not being complied with annual grants will be refused to this school. My lords are of opinion that the boy Robert Humphreys should at once be re-admitted to the school.—l have the honour to be, rev, sir, your obedient servant, (Signed) P. CIIMIN."—The contents of these letters have afforded the Nonconformists of Cheshire much grati- fication.
DEATH OF THE EARL OF STAMFORD.

George Harry Grey, seventh Earl of Stamford and Warrington, died at Bradgate Park, Leicestershire, on Tues- day morning, at half-past ten o'clock. His lordship's con- dition has been very critical for some time, but on Monday there was a slight improvement. A change occurred during the night, and his lordship gradually sank from exhaustion. The deceased nobleman iuherited three distinct titles, viz., Baron Grey of Groby, Earl of Stamford, and Earl of Warrington, and his family history includes some of the most stirring, as well as some of the most sad, episodes in English history. His ancestor, Sir John Giey, fought on the side of the Red Rose, and was slain at the battle of St. Alban's, 1461, and his widow, Eliz tbeth Woodville, became the wife of the Yorkist King, Edward IV. Her sons by King Edward were murdered by their uncle Richard; her eldest son of the first marriage was attainted as a traitor, and had to flee his country; her second 9921, Sir Thomas Grey, was beheaded; while she ended her days in a monas- tery. But there ate still sadder memories in the history of the house of Grey, and the fate of Lady Jane Grey—the ten days' queen—forms one of the most touching stories in English history. When the news came to Lady Jane she was at Bradgate Park, where the noble earl has just died, with her husbtnd, Lord Guilford Dudley. The tide turned in favour of the Greys in the reign of King James, and in 1603 Henry Grey was created Baron Grey of Grotty. His son by the daughter of Lord Burleigh was created Earl of Stamford in 1628, and more than a century later the then Earl of Stamford married the daughter and heiress of the Earl of Warrington, thus uniting the two titles. The seventh earl, just deceased, had all but attained the age of 56 years, he having been born on January 7th, 1827. Educated at Eton and Trinity College, Ctmbridge, he took his degree of M.A. in 1848. Inheriting an unen- cumbered estate of over 30,000 acres, with a princely in- come, the noble lord turned his attention mainly to field sports, and he was passionately fond of fishing, shooting, and hunting. As a follower of the chase he had few to equal him in his day, and partly from a love of fox-hunting and partly owing to the tender associations of his relative, Lady Jane Grey, with the spot, he, in 1856, erected ft splendid Elizabethan mansion at Bradgate Park, Leicester- shire, with extensive and elaborate stabling, the latter of which cost between £30,000 and £40,000 atone. The de- ceased peer was a magistrate for Lancashire, Worcestershire, and other counties, deputy-lieutentnt for Staffordshire and Leicestershire and honorary colonel of the!lth and 23rd Lancashire Rifle Volunteers. He was twice married, first in 1848 to Elizabeth, daughter of Mr. John Billige, who died in 1854, and second to Katherine, second daughter of the late Mr. Henry Cocks, who survives him. There is no issue by either marriage. He was patron of nine livings in Leicestershire, Lancashire, Cheshire, and Staffordshire. His seats ware Bradgate Park, Leicestershire ; Enville Hall, Staffordshire; and Dunham Massey Park, Altrincham. He is succeeded in the title by the Rev. Harry Grey, who was born in 1812 and educated at Sherbourne School and St. Edmund Hall, Oxford.

Tax Wantons or MsucifisTow.—Napier was supposed by the vulgar of his time to possess mysterious supernatural powers, and the marvels attributed to him, with the aid of a devilish familiar, in the shape of a jet-!..lack cock, are pre- served among the traditions of the neighbourhood to the present day. He impressed all his people that this terrible chanticleer could detect their most secret doings. Having missed some valuablee, he ordered his servants one by one into a dark room of the tower, where his favourite was con- fined, declaring that the cock would crow when stroked by the hand of the guilty, as each was required to do. The cock remained silent daring this ceremony; but the hands of one of the servants was found to be entirely free from the soot with which the feathers of the mysterious bird had been smeared. The story of how be bewitched certain pigeons is still remembered in the vicinity of Merchiston. Having been annoyed by some that ate up his grain, he threatened to poind them. "Do no, if you can catch them," said his neighbour; and next morning the fields were alive with reeling and fluttering pigeons, which were easily cap- tured, from the effect of an intoxicating feed of saturated peas. The place called the Doo Park, in front of Merchis- ton, took its name from this event. The warlock of the tower, as he was deemed, seems to have entertained a perfect faith in the possession of a power to discover hidden trea- sure. Thus, there is still preserved among the Merchiston papers a curious contract, dated July, 1594, between him ' and Sir Robert Logan of Restalrig—a Gowrie conspirator— which sets forth :—"Forasmuch as there were old reports and 'appearances that a sum of money was hid within Logan 's house of Fast Castle, John Napier should do his utmost dili- gence to work and seek out the same." For his reward he was to have the third of what was found—by the use of a divining rod, we presume. "This singular contract," says Wilson, "acquires a peculiar interest when we remember the reported discevery of hidden treasure with which the preliminary steps of the Gowrie conspiracy were effected." —" Cassell's Old and New Edinburgh," for January. div.head: FoREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FoREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

-- • --- An order has been issued by the Russian Minister of the Interior prohibiting the street sale of the Gobs. An amnesty for all political prisoners in Egypt, not already .dealt with, was promulgated at Cairo on Wednes- day.

A despatch from Rome states that according to private information from Berlin negotiations between Germany and the Vatican have been resumed on a basis which affords a prospect of a complete settlement. FATAL BOAT ACCIDENT IN AMERICA : • 18 PERSONS DROWNED.—lnteiligence received at New York announces that a barge containing 30 convicts has sunk while crossing a river in North Carolina. Eighteen of those on board were drowned.

A painful incident occurred at President Arthur's recep- tion on New Year's Day. It appears that the Diplomatic Corps had presented their congratulations, headed by their doyen, the Hawaiian Minister, Mr. Elisha Adams. They had then withdrawn; when Mr. Adams, while putting on his overcoat in the robbing-room, suddenly fell and expired soon afterwards of aneurism of the heart. The reception was immediately suspenled, the music stopped, and the guests all dismissed.

Cherif Pasha, in a letter to the Khedive accompanying the Budget, states that the Egyptian Government hag en- deavoured to keep the ordinary expenditure within the limits fixed by the law of liquidation. Recent experience showed that the revenue in normal years was much larger than was estimated by law, and left a sufficient surplus to be applied to the Extraordinary Budget for the following year. The recent crisis, however, caused a deficit in the Extraordinary Budget for 1882, so that the necessary resources for the Extraordinary Budget of 1883 are entirely. wanting. The Minister adds that the Government for some time to come will have to bind itself down to a system of exceptional economy.

PRINCE BISMARCK WANTING TO RETIRE.-At the Impetial reception at Berlin, on Monday, Prince Bismarck said that in the present position of politics in Germany, and now that Parliamentary institutions were working satisfactorily, it would cause no misfortune to his country if he gave place to other men. Taken in conjunction with the signs of ill- health he shows, this is sure to indicate his immediate retire- ment from political life. In military circles it is believed that there is still danger of war, though much diminished, and that Germany, however favourably situated, cannot permit herself to relax vigilance for a moment.

150 IlousEs BURNT Dow.—According to information received in Liverpool, it seems that by a tire which broke out at the village of Empire, Panama, no fewer than 150 houses were consumed, whilst the village itself was almost destroyed by the conflagration. Empire is on the line of the Panama railroad; and the houses are built almost entirely of bamboo, with thatched roofs. It is said that a single spark was the cause of the disaster, the material of the houses being very dry in consequence of the hot weather. Several stores were also included in the list, and in these the Chinese merchants of the place were said to be the chief sufferers. It was estimated that the loss would be at least £25,000. The flatly.; inhabitants were alsa great losers by the fire.

SUICIDE OF A COO-STT.—A very sensational incident occurred in Parts, on Saturday. Count Wimpffen, the Austrian ArfoaSsador, drew a revolver from his pocket in one of. the principal streets of the city and deliberately shot himself dead on the spot. The unfortunate gentleman left home in his carriage at ten o'clock in the morning, and before starting tenderly bade farewell to his children. The only explanation offered as to the suicide is the fact that the count had been subjected to a good deal of worry and annoyance during the removal of the Embassy to new quarters. It seems, however, highly improbable that such a slight matter should unhinge the mind of a diplomatist trained by long years of service to bear the heaviest responsibilities.

TIM EGYPTIAN ARMY- A telegram from Cairo states that the Government of the Khedive has accepted Sir Evelyn Wood's scheme for the reorganisation of the army. Four out of eight of the infantry regiments will be officered by Englishmen; the remaining four will have native officers. The artillery will have an English commander, and each battery will be under Englishmen. The cavalry will be commanded by an English officer. The infantry battalions officered by Englishmen will, as far as possible, be Stationed conjointly with equal forces under native com- mand. It is hoped that the inevitable emulation will pro- duce a good effect. The report is confirmed that the Ministry, intend to propose the prolongation of the International Tri- bunals for one year only.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

During an affray with firearms, on Tuesday, in the county of Tipperary, a man was shot dead. Three Emergency con- stables had been attacked by an armed party. The Dublin newspapers speak with approval of Mr. Trevelyan's visit to the distressed districts in,Donegal, and hope it will result in effectual reiief being given to the famine-stricken people. The election contest at Mallow has now fairly begun. Mr. Nish, the new Solicitor-General, is opposed by Mr. O'Brien, of the United Ireland., and also by Mr. Moriarty, a birrister and the son of a local solicitor. The grounds on which Mr. Moriarty appears are somewhat obscure. He claims to be an " Independent " Liberal.

At New Russ Mr. Edward Walsh, Mayor of Wexford, has been committed under the Crimes Act to 14 days' imprison- ment for having published inflammatory language in a paper owned by him. The article impuoged was admitted by a "Lady Land Leaguer" to be her writing. Leave was given to Mr. Walsh to appeal. One of the Dublin papers calls attention to what it. des- cribes as a studied insult to England on the inauguration of the Lord Mayor of Dublin. The City Hall, it says, was decorated with flags of other nations emblematic of Repub- lican and Democratic principles, whUe the flag of England was conspicuous by its absence. At the banquet the Queen's name was received with hisses, and many guests remained seated while the toast was being drunk. For his violent speech at the National Literary Club at Witt... Word last month, in which he denounced Lord Spencer as a bloodthirsty tyrant, and declared the conviction of Francis Hynes of murder illegal, Mr. Biggar, M.P., was on Tuesday formally proceeded against at the Sessions House, Waterford, on a charge of sedition. Evidence having been taken as to the language used by Mr. Biggar, the hon. mem- ber was formally committed for trial at the assizes, but was released on bail.

Th,t excessive zeal of certain Irish officials in the cause of loyalty has called forth a rebuke from the Lord Lieutenant. It appears that when His Excellency was passing through Monasterevan he received an unfriendly greeting from a few people, and the result was that several men were brought before the magistrates and remanded. Earl Spencer has asked the resizlent magistrate at Portarlington to withdraw the charges made, as he "does not wish that a prosecution should take place for an act which was quite unnoticed by him, and which does not, in his opinion, deserve any attention."

1 Christopher Quinn, an Irishman, was charged on his own confession at Guildhall Police Court, London, on Saturday, with being concerned in the Phenix Park murders. The prisoner was brought to the police by two men with whom he had been drinking in a public-house. It seemed that Quinn had said to his companions that "he was a good Irishman, that he was one of the four Who went to Phcenix Park, and that be should like to be on such a job again." The only suspicious feature of the case was that the men did not appear to be drunk; and the prisoner was remanded for inquiries to be made. INTENDED RESIGNATION OF MR. DILLON. Mr. John Dillon has definitely decided to resign his seat for Tipperary, but, in order that the constituency may have time to select a suitable candidate, his resignation will not be formally tendered until after the commencement of the session. In communicating these facts to the constituency, Mr. Dillon takes occasion to deny the statement that he is "disgusted" with Parliamentary agitation. He declares his firm convic- tion that an independent Irish party in the House of Com- mons is a necessity, and he is also in favour of nationalising the Dublin Corporation, Irish Town Councils, Boards of Guardians, and other bodies' and of organisation in all parts of the world where faithful Irishmen are to be found. By this policy, "the Castle and its infamous system " must, he thinks, shortly be swept away. Tim ARREARS ACT.—An encouraging view is taken by the Freeman's Journal of the working and the results of the Arrears Act. The time for taking advantage of the Act lapsed with the year, and the total number of applications under it is found to be nearly 140,000. Were all these granted it is estimated that the State would have to pay to the land- lords about £BOO,OOO, which is a very considerably smaller sum than presented itself to the fertile imaginations of the Tory critics of the Act, and does not reach the more moder- ate estimate of the Government. An immense number of cases, the Freeman remarks, have already been disposed of, and "there is no doubt that the operations of the Act will sweep away a very large weight of debt which had accumu- lated against the farming classes of Ireland." It is pointed , out, too, that not three per cent. of the applications that have been considered have been rejected. Stronger testimony of the necessity for and value of the Act need not be desired. THE ATTEMPTED MURDER OF JUDGE LAWSON.—The man Delaney, charged with attempting to murder Mr. Justice Lawson, was arraigned before Mr. Justice O'Brien, in Dublin, on Tuesday. At the outset his counsel (Dr. V' ebb) claimed that the indictment should be quashed, as disclos- ing no offence against the statute, and he said that the law officers, finding themselves in a dilemma and seeing that if they framed the indictment according to the statute the prisoner must be acquitted, had framed the indictment in direct opposition to the statute. The indictment, in fact, was made to fit the statute. After a long legal argument the Judge said that for the present he should decline to quash the indictment, and the trial was proceeded with; Out, after hearing the statement of the case made by the solicitor General, his Lord-ship said he thought the learned .gentleman could not prove the indictment, and he therefore suggested that a nolle prosecini should be entered. The Solicitor General accepted this suggestion, and said the prisoner would be tried next day on a second indictment charging him with conspiracy to murder.

BILLS OF SALE AND FAILL-lIES.—III the week ending December 30th, 1882, there were 247 bills of sale in Eng. land and Wales a decrease of 553 over those of the cores' ponding period last year; and the failures gazetted nitre' bered 111, a decrease of six. The totals for portion of Year to De2ember 30th, 1882, are bills of sale registered for Eng. land and Wales 41,632, a decaease of 10,573; the failureS gazetted number 10,553, a decrease of I,ol9.—Stubbs'S Mei'eantile Gazette.

THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—The market on Te,es; day was only a very quiet one, with very few inquir:e' stirring. Where buyers make offers they are at prices under current rates, which makers at present are not disposed to accept. Lancashire makers of pig iron who are easier liii their prices are now open to book orders on the basis O 47s 61, less 2, for both foandry and forge qualitiee delivered equal to Manchester. Buyers, however, are ne! tempted to place out orders at this figure. One or two transactions are reported in distinct brands at 6.1 to is Pe' ton under current rates; but makers generally are at Pre- sent holding for late prices, which, however, in the absenee of business are only nominal. In the finished iron trade there has been little or nothing stirring, and it is not likel/ there will be much business done until after the quartea Iwaymeeting. Buyers seem to anticipate a giving in priCaf but although makers are unable to secure orders on ril basis of the quoted rates of £6 103 for bars delivered ego to Manchester, they are not just now inclined to come mall lower to effect sales.
