MISCELLANEOUS.

By the death of the Earl of Wemyes and March, which occurred on New Year's day, Lord Elcho accedes to the Peerage, and a vacancy is thus created in the representation 04 Iladdingtonshire. A serious affray has taken place at Newry between soldiers of the Border Regiment and civilians, and two pickets had to be sent out to bring the former to the barracks. The cause assigned for the disturbance was that the soldiers attributed to foul play the recent death of Corporal Wil- liams, wko was found drowned. At Tavistock, on Monday, 12 navvies were charged with attacking two policemen and rescuing' a prisoner at Dart- moor, on Wednesday last. One was sentenced to six months' imprisonment, two to four months, one to three, and six to two months. The Order of the Garter has been conferred by the Queen OR the Duke of Grafton. The new Knight of the Garter is the sixth Duke of Grafton. The first of the name was a son of the Duchess of Cleveland, upon whom Charles 11. be Stowed large pensions. During service at Dr. Parker's City Temple, London, on aunday night, the electric light suddenly went out. The doctor at once said, " Don't be alarmed, there is no danger," and fortunately an attendant at once turned on the gas, Which had been left at a glimmer. There was an entire absence of panic. - Daring the year just ended 241 lives were lost by ex- plosions in coal mines throughout the United Kingdom, and With one or two exceptions they occurred where basting With powder was carried on or naked lights were used. The Illlmber of lives- lost were—ln January, 5; February, 85; a•Pril, 54 ; May, 42; June, 1; August, 4; and November, 47. Five persons have lost their lives by the upsetting of a beat in Barking Creek. They started for a journey of about two miles down the Rodisg River to Ilford. Owing to the 11,earY rains the river was much swollen, and the man in euarge of the boat lost all control, and it drifted down the iltrearn. On reaching the creek the boat was drawn under- neath a drawbridge, and the five passengers were thrown into the water and drowned. An extraordinaey riot has taken place at Hounslow, con- lektillent on the death of Dr. Edwards, who was in partner- Ship with Dr. Whitmarsh, at that place. The deceased gentleman died of poison under mysterious circumstances, and popular feeling has risen to a terrible pitch against Dr. Whitmarsh. A mob of three or four thousand people gathered round his house, and, in defiance of the police, re- Mained there for hours, and did not leave until all the win- adcws had been broken and the frost of the house much %%waged. A surgery belonging to the doctor, situate in another part of the town, was also wrecked, and so strong is the antipathy to Dr. Whitmarsh, that a subscription is on toot to. pay the costs of the defence of two lads who have been arrested for throwing stones. MRS. GLADSTONE ON THE TRAINING OF THE YOUNG.— M. Gladstone has contributed a preface to the new edition . "Early Influences," just published by Messrs. Riving- ;oils, in which. after bestowing warm praises on that well- 'mown little manual, she offers some observations on the training of the young. Mrs. Gladstone observes that it is "the step by step training—the learning of a child's dispo- aition by means of hourly watchfulness—which is too often aeglected ;" and she directs attention "to the way in which Children are often over-noticed and over-petted, and con- Ilidered in every conceivable way; and again, the dangers attending the very advantages of charming by interesting books. " All this, she adds, "unless regulated and c'eecked by proper home influence, may become an actual snare. So !Inch the more is it necessary that, from very early child- hood, the mother should guide and shape the child's mind and heart." SUDDEN DEATEs IN FOOTBALL FIELDS.—In the course Of a match on the Turton Club's ground, near Bolton, on Saturday, Mr. C. Duckworth, who was officiating as umpire, fell down, and on Drs. Cosgrave and Horrocke arriving they found that the gentleman was dead, the cause of death, it is er!lPPosed, being heart disease accelerated by excitement. During a football match at the grounds of the Greyhound Rotel, Dulwich, on Saturday, between the Old Blues of Dul- Wich and the Roslyn Park, Norwood, Mr. Sydney F. Welsh, the Captain of the Old Blues, whilst running after the ball, ,Wall Seen to stumble and fall to the ground. A medical sta- rlit at St. Bartholomew's Hospital, who was playing for the cloelyn Park Club, went to his assistance and recommended that a medical gentleman should be sent for. Dr. Rayn prOnlDtly attended, and declared that life was extinct. The deceased, who was only 23 years of age, was a muscular and ane young gentleman, standing upwards of six feet high. A NEW YEAR'S SURPRISE. Through heavy losses by „failures of customers in Canada Messrs. John and Edward rialaer, manufacturers and merchants of Golcar and Uuddersfield, and Montreal, were compelled to file a peti- !lon for the liquidation of their affairs in the Huddersfield ounty Court on the 15th of March, 1876, and at the meet- nlg of their creditors on the 10:la of April, 1876, the state- Inent of their affairs showed the unsecured liabilities to be £45,219 125. Si., and their assets £31,601 6e. 6d. Resolu- tltlas for the liquidation of Messrs. Fisher's affairs were Passed, but the creditors granted them their discharge forth- with. ThAr estate was disposed of in due course. and realised for the creditors lls, in the pound. Messrs. Fisher were enabled to commence business again, in the Canadian trade, and have since prospered • and on New Year's Day their creditors received from them cheques for the full balance of 9s. in the pound of their debts, accompanied by a circular of explanation. The total amount which this pay- ment involves is £20,349 165. 6d. T" PEERAGE.—The only minor peer who comes of age during 1883 is the Earl of Norbury. He attains his majority 00 the 2nd of July. The peers who are now minors, with the dates on which they come of age are as follow :-1884, Viscount Clifton; 1885, the Duke of Newcastle Lord Kenyon ; 1886, Rid Russell, Lord Athlumney, Lord Ten- terden ; 1883, Lord Southampton; 1889, Lord Ashtown ; 1,822, the Marquis of Downshire ; 1893, Marquis Camden, viscount Southwell, Viscount Mountmorres ; 1895, the Earl 01 Cottenham. The following eldest sons of peers come of •ge during 1883:—Lord Levinstone, son of the Earl of New- burg, January 1; Viscount Weymouth, son of the Marquis oi Bath, July 15; Viscount Vaughan, son of the Earl of Lisburne, July 30; the Marquis of Carmarthen, son of the eeeko of Leeds, September 18; Viscount Dunwieb, son of the Earl of Stradbrolie, November 17; the Hon. Hylton Jolliffe, son of Lord Hylton, November 19; The heirs pre- sumptive to the Marquis of Bristol and the Earl of Powis 41-10 attain their majority durirg the year; Mr. George Rerbert, nephew of the Earl of Powis, June 24, and Mr. Charles Henry Augustus Hervey, nephew of the Marquis of Bristol, June 30.—Court Journal. A PosTAL ANomA.Ly.—Attention is called by a corres- Pondent of the Times to the following postal inconsistency: • It has for a long while anpeared almost incredible that a letter may be sent to Pekin, or Tahiti, or Alaska, for ex- ample, for -21-d., when a struggling colonist in one of our his has to pay 6d. to send word to his parents of 3 welfare. and, indeed, the fact that a South American etnigrant should have greater facilities for describing to his relations and friends the conditions of fife in his new home than a settler in Victoria or New South Wales speaks bldly ellough for the large-mindedness of our statesmen. What, however, are we to think of a department that denies alto- gether the convenience, and privilege of the use of post- cards to the inhabitants of our own colonies, while it de- votes itself with a quite surprising diligence to a new issue ,of Post-cards of six varieties to such interesting and popular localities as Fernando Po, the islands of St. Toomas and Prince (in Africa), Antigua, Grand Bassam, Greenland, trann, Nicaragua, Celbes, Archipelagoes. of Bann arod f"otlw, New Guinea, ? It is almost touching to con- template the advantages of being able to send a reply post- card to one of the head hunters of Borneo or New Guinea, but Why may not the bank clerk of Melbourne or the as- sisted emigrant of Queensland enjoy a like privilege ?" Wolverhampton INVETERATE PAUPER.—There has just died in the his Workhouse a man who, for the whole of re lifetime, extending over 37 years, has been a source of Pthle and annoyance to not only the union officials in the urstrict, but also the central authorities in London. Picked „? originally by the roadside when an infant of a few days • his parents unknown, he was christened by a guardian Ilncl ier the name of Bytheway. He grew up in the work- es until old enough to be sent out as an apprentice. uring the next seven years he worried and tired out the tatience of his master as he had worried out and tired out the Patience of the officials of the union, and when his an- reuticeship was expired he came beck to the work- house as to his own home, to be again dependent on the Illten. Thus he remained up to the time of his death either an indoor or outdoor pauper, and he distinguished himself in no ordinary way. At various periods he wrote !IO many letters to the Local Government Board, complain- oft, almost every official connected with the house, that sue central authority at length ordered an inquiry into his foental state. This inquiry, however, did not establish 44scY, and Bytheway remained in and about Wolver- captor], and continued his troublesome proceedings, not %fining his attention to the workhouse and union officials ~!1(1• guardians, but also appearing from time to time with or imaginary grievances before the magistrates or 01°11nty Court judge. His death was the result of an attack aelrYsipelas. He was baptised in the Church of England, ▪ after professing various religious creeds during life, he :"Ped his chequered career by dying in the Roman Catholic salth. sa_l4e- FA.RINI AND THE MISSING LINE.—The latest reirnen of humanity obtained for exhibition at the Royal narium by Mr. Farini is a hairy child, whom he introduces Te public as a talking monkey, and the nearest approach a—tati the missing link" yet discovered. Anatomists and a, toPologists must decide whether Krao is in any degree ii7ll.cturally allied to the ape. The ordinary observer is not f.l!_°l3, to discover that she is. She is chiefly remarkable for Woe_ growth over her body of fine silky hair, which does not, tiow_ever,aconceal a very light brown skin, except about por- th,ll:7 of the face. The forehead is quite hidden beneath a ck growth of raven-black hair. Kra° is . also heavily c),;fikered. Her fingers have great flexibility. They can it7l:3ut far back without pain. Her cheeks are remarkably last"orld it is explained to visitors that she has been in the haul, f using them as pouches for her food. She is said to to some dental peculiarities, though it was not quite clear 4011`,Tle Who saw her on Saturday that what was held to be a Te row of teeth was not simply the second teeth of au.'uhood forcing out the earlier growth. The other charac- autakics of Krao are human enough to all appearance. She o,rellipi_ Very erect, her head,tvhich is large, being apparently ' cur...lY, poised on the supporting vertabrte, and the spinal Rita not striking the spectator as in any way exceptional. thi"o'cahhar.it ferward-jawed. Her face, indeed, in spite of the well for ir about it, is not at all unpleasing. Her feet are _ tned, and have high insteps. With the index finger ail;!_all. and does point freely. Her ready intelligence is atki" 1.11 nY the fact the she already speaks a little English, 8 quick to r ecogniseher friends amongher

On Tuesday the day schools at Accrington were re-opened, after having been closed thirteen weeks on account of the saarlet fever epidemic. By a Parliamentary return, issued on Tuesday, it is shown that the total amount raised in England in 1880-81 by local taxation, was £32,434,123, the Parliamentary grants in aid having been £2,088,807. Mr. Robertson Smith, formerly Hebrew professor in the Free Church of Scotland, has been offered and has accepted the professorship of Arabic in the University of Cambridge, vacant by the death of Professor Palmer. HALIFAX SCHOOL BOARD.—A new School Board for Hali- fax was elected on Tuesday without opposition. It consists of 13 members, of whom 7 are unsectarian and 6 denomina- thmal, including one Roman Catholic. Among the unsec- tarian members are two.working men. Six members of the late Board are re-elected. Several huge gaps having during the past few days shown themselves in the walls of the great central tower of Peter- borough Cathedral, Mr. J. L. Pearson was telegraphed for, and after inspecting the building, he pronounced the tower as unsafe. The Dean and Chapter have given orders for it to be removed immediately. The tower was erected in 1350. Louisa Taylor underwent the extreme penalty of the law on Tuesday morning within Maidstone gaol for the marder of Mrs. Tregellis by poisoning at Plumstead. Mar- wood was the executioner. Between her condemnation and the execution the culprit only saw one visitor, the solicitor who conducted her defence, and it is stated that she was absolutely without either relatives or friends. The Birkenhead stipendiary magistrate has fined a labourer, named Peter Doyle, £5 for assaulting a member of the Salvation Army. He was one of the mob who attacked the Salvation Army procession in Birkenhead, on Sunday, the 10th ult. Mr. Preston in imposing the fine, said if the riots continued he should adopt a different course, and send for trial any person against whom a charge of assault should be proved. A FORTUNATE CLERGYMAN. Lord Stamford's great wealth and family honours will go mainly to the heir pre- sumptive, his cousin, the Rev. Harry Grey, now Earl of Stamford and Warrington. The late earl was always thought to have at Bradgate the largest and finest collection of old English plate in the country. Some who have seen it speak of this collection as being extremely remarkable. THE ARMY RESERVE.—It is stated that arrangements are being carried out for the immediate discharge of the remain- der of the men of the Army Reserve who are at present serving with the colours of Guards. The men who are awaiting their discharge joined the Army Reserve after December 31, 1881, but were called out at the beginning of the Egyptian campaign. It is understood that the men will be provided with railway tickets to their homes in various parts of the country. BRUTAL WIFE ASSAULT.—At Sedgley, on Tuerlay, James Clarke, miner, was sentenced to six months' Imprisonment for committing a brutal assault on his wife. The com- plainant, who was one mass of bruises, stated that cn Sun- day prisoner came home drunk, and as his dinner was not in accordance with his wishes he assaulted her until she was rescued by neighbours. Complainant added that prisoner had systematically and brutally assaulted her since the first week of their married life. _ _

.• THE NEW TREASURY BOARD.—Tuesday night's Gazette announces that the Queen has been pleased to direct letters patent to be passed under the great seal appointing the Right Hon. Wm. Ewart Gladstone, the Right Hon. H. C. E. Childers Mr. Charles Cecil Cotes, Mr. Herbert John Glad- stone, and Mr. Robert William Duff to be Commissioners for the execution of the offices of Treasurer of the Ex- chequer of Great Britain and Lord High Treasurer of Ireland. he Gazette announces the appointment of the Right Hon. H. C. E. Childers to the office of Chancellor and Under Treasurer of Her Majesty's Exchequer. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND LOCAL TAXATION. Mr. Chamberlain, in a letter to a correspondent on the subject of the reform of local taxation, reiterates his well-known objections to the practice of making grants from the Con- solidated Fund, which he says is costly to the State and not economical to the ratepayers. A much better plan in his judgment would be the allocation of some of the taxes which at present are imperial taxes to local purposes, thus increasing the income of the local authorities while leaving to them the whole amount of and responsibility for their own expenditure.

ALARMING ACCIDENT ON THE MIDLAND RAILWAY: EXTRAORDINARY ESCAPE.—News reached Nottingham on Tuesday night of an accident on the Midland It tilway near Trent Junction. A goods train was standing on the main line when a passenger train from Leicester to Derby dashed into it and cut it clean in halves. Three wagons were smaslied to pieces and the contents strewed about the line, but not- withstanding the violence of the shock the passenger engine kept the rails, and the train passed safely into Trent Station. The passengers escaped with a severe shaking and all were able to continue their journey. Great damage was done to rolling stock. GREAT FIRE AT THE ISLE OF MlN.—The Bon Marche; belonging to Mr. Robert Clucas, and situated in the new street recently constructed in Douglas, Isle of Man, has been destroyed by fire. The fire broke out about nine o'clock on New Year's Night, and the premises had been locked up at seven o'clock. There was no one on the premises when the fire broke out. The building was one of the finest in Doug- las. The stock and premises were insured, but not to the value of the estimated damage—£ls,ooo to £20,000. All the family's and assistants' clothes were burnt. The books saved were in a Miler's safe.

THE NEW PRIMATE.—Bishop Benson, in a farewell .address to the clergy of the diocese of Truro, states that when the call to the Primacy came to him he consulted the chief layman of the county—the Earl of Mount Edgcumbe, lord lieutenant—and his judgment was that while it would have been wrong to exchange that for any other see, how- ever distinguished, he (Dr. Benson) had no right to decline a leadership full of labour and anxiety, and not wholly detaching him from the hone of working with and for them still. The right rev, prelate cannot take leave of Cornwall without acknowledging with love and gratitude that activity for Christ's sake, and that open-handedness, that kindness towards all good works, that fairour at beholding growing activities in the Church which have been shown by the Wesleyans, and by very many others, who, nevertheless, have and use energetically organisations of their own.

'THE LIFEBOAT SERVICE IN 1882.—A list of the services rendered by the lifeboats of the National Lifeboat Institu- tion during the year which has just closed, shows that a total of 731 lives had been saved by the boats, besides 23 vessels saved from destruction and brought safely into port. In addition to these services, the lifeboats were called out during the year, in replies to signals of distress, 98 times, when no positive results followed. On such occa- sions, however, lifeboatmen have no time for hesitation ; for the signal of distress always means urgency, and very often, in the absence of the lifeboats, death to those on board the distressed ship. During the year the institution also granted rewards for rescuing 143 lives by fishing and other boats, making 874 lives saved last year mainly, through its instrumentality. Altogether, since its forma- tion, the society has contribeted to the saving of 29,600 shipwrecked poisons. ENGLISH PATENTS. - The following patents amongst others published in the Commissioners of Patents' Journal were sealed during the week ending December 29th, 1882 : Robert Matthews, Elyde, for improvements in the construc- tion of dynamo-electric and electro-dynarnic machines, and in governing or regulating the same; George Varley and Walter Gregory, Over Darwen, for improvements in the construction of apparatus for lubricating steam engines; E. Foden, Sandbach, for improvements in thrashing machines; T. Hampton, Sheffield, for improvements in apparatus for re- moving ingots from moulds; Wm. Bell, Lancaster, iron mer- chant, for improvements in or connected with the furnaces of steam boilers; John Walter Bradley and Joseph Wood, Bradford, for improvements in machinery for combing wool, cotton, flax, and other fibrous substances; Charles Wigg, Liverpool, alkali manufacturer, for improvements in the manufacture of carbonate of soda, and apparatus employed therein; John Henry Topham, Manchester, for the filtration of water for domestic and other supply, by means of a new mechanical arrangement; John Shepherd Sawrey, Alfred Attwood and Henry Woodbourne, Ulverston, for improve- ments in pumps. List supplied by Mr. George Davies, C.E,, Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's Square, Manchester.

FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT: AN ENGINE GOING OVER A CLlFF.—Between six and seven o'clock on Monday evening a fearful accident occurred on the Cambrian line in Vriog cutting, within three miles of Barmouth. At Vriog the line runs along the face of a cliff between 50 and 60 feet above the sea, and the turnpike road runs along the cliff about the same distance above the railway. As the London evening train was passing a wall, which supported a portion of the turnpike road, loosmed by the rain, gave way. The debris threw the engine and tender over the cliff, and the driver and fireman were killed and frightfully mutilated. The carriage next to the engine, which fortu- nately contained no passengers, was suspended over the cliff by the couplings, while a carriage which contained Captain Price, vice-chairman of the Cambrian Railway Company, was thown on its side and half overhung the precipice. These and subsequent carriages, containing several passengers were kept from going over by a fall of debris, which meet have occurred immediately after the fall which threw the engine over. All the passengers made their way out of the debris with great difficulty, and walked over to Barmouth Junc- tion. The bodies of the two persons killed were removed to Barmouth Junction.

THE "BELT" CASE.—Long trials, like that of "Belt v. Lewes," which lasted 43 days, have not been in fashion a dozen years. " Saurin v. Starr," the "Convent case," tried in 1869, lasted only a fortnight, which was considered a long time in those days. "Tichborne v. Lushington," in 1872, lasted 103 days, and the practice of the parties paying jury- men a guinea a day was first introduced in lieu of their receiving the legal guinea per case. Then came "Regina v. Castro," in 1873 and 1874, which lasted 188 days, and since that case the floodgates have been opened. The £5,000 damages given by the jury, although approached in a case just decided in the Uuited states against the New ork Herald, which journal was cast in a verdict with 20,000 dollars damages as compensation for imputing the crime of arson, are probably unequalled in an action of libel in this country. in 1676, the case of "Lord Townsend v. Dr. Huglo.s." £4,000 damages were given for saying that the plains id was "an unworthy man, and acted against law and , reason ;" and the judges, of6whom Scroggs was one, declined to set the verdict aside on the ground of excessive damages. , The action, however, was brought under /tie obsolete statut aiins scandalum maynattint. There is an appro. priateness in the last of the causes at Westminster being tried by tke last of the lawyer-barons; but it is to be hoped that the Royal Courts of dnstice will not be inocu- lated with the modern disease of prolonged trials.—Law .Journal,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 6, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 6, 1883.

The Rosebery club will present 3n address to Mr. Glad- stone on January 18th, immediately before the Edinburgh banquet. Colonel Sir Owen Lanyon has arrived at Portsmouth to take over the duties of Assistant Adjutant and Quarter- master General of the Southern Division. The Dowager Lady Tredegar died on Thursday morning, at Tredegar Park, Newport, Monmouth. She was widow of the first Baron Tredegar, who died in 1875. Christopher Q lin% who said a few days ago that he was concerned in the Plicenix Park murders, was on Thursday sentenced to two months' imprisonment as a rogue and vagabond. THE VICAR'S RATE AT COVENTRY.—The amount paid into the bank in connection with the Mayor's voluntary fund for the extinction of the Trinity vicar's rate now amounts to 1;4,043 7s. dd. including a cheque for £250 given anonymously through the editor of one of the local newspapers. The bodies of John White, warehouseman, London, and Mr. James Smith, of Bo'ness, were washed ashore on Wednesday evening, at Crombie Point, near Dunfermline. They went out in a skiff in the morning with the intention of crossing to the south side of the Forth, and the cause of the accident is not known. _ _

At two mass meetings of colliers held on Thursday, at Rowley and Cradley, it was reported that at two of the largest collieries in the district the employers :were increas- ing the number of working hours, and also stopping the perquisites of dinner ale and fire coal. It was resolved to strike until the employers agreed to the eight .hours' system. At the Liverpool Police Court, on Thursday, John and Mary Latnbert, husband and 'wife, were committed to the assizes on the charge of the manslaughter of Bernard M`Guinness. In the course of a quarrel the prisoners, it is alleged, knocked M'Cruinness down, and both of them kicked him so savagely in the stomach that he died soon afterwards.

At the Kilrush Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, County Judge Kelly, referring to some evidence given in a civil bill case, said he would not sit there and tolerate obstruction of such kind as had been offered. He would not be browbeaten and dogged like the Government at the hands of Parnell, Sexton, Healy, and Co. His Worship's observation created considerable sensation.

During divine service in Auchnacloy Church on Sunday, the heating stoves which consume coke having been worn through, allowed an esca'pe of carbonic acid into the build- ing causing several of the congregation to faint. Immediately after the benediction both the officiating. clergymen, Rev. T. G. Stokes and Rev: W. Earl, were seriously afllcted, the latter gentleman being rendered unconscious for a short ann. _ _

On Thursday another alarming accident occurred on the Cabandar and Oban railway. While a goods train from Oban to Stirling was running through the dangerous pass of Glenagree between Killen and Lockearnhead, it came into collision with a mass of earth which had slipped from the mountain side. Nine waggons were thrown from the metals, the line was completely blocked, and much damage was done No one was injured. The Recorder of Birmingham, Mr. J. Stratford Dugdale, Q.C., in charging the Grand Jury at Birmingham, on Thursday, strongly advised all persons in business to carefully study the Married Women's Property Act, which came into force this week. Disputes would cer- tainly arise as to whether contracts were made with hus- bands or wives, and there would be considerable work for the lawyers.

A shocking murder took place, on Thursday morning, at Kearsley Moor, near Bolton. A butler, named Abraham Thomas, in the service of Captain Ansdell, of Kearsley Cottage, has been on unfriendly terms with Mrs. Leigh, the housekeeper, for some time. On Thursday morning a report of firearms was heard, and Thomas was seen coming from the direction of the photographic studio at the back of the house with a fowling-piece in his hand. The servant, on proceeding to the studio, found Mrs. Leigh on the floor with an ugly wound in the neck, and she expired imme- diately. The gun had been loaded with buckshot. No one had heard the two quarrelling, and the cause of the crime is a mystery. Thomas was arrested in the house, making no attempt to escipe. He is 30 years of age, and his victim was nearly 40. _ _

On Thursday morning a couple presented themselves at the Parish Churcb, Urmston, to be united in the holy bonds of matrimony, but the bridegroom found, to his annoyance, that he had forgotten the marriage licence. On the previous evening he had been staying at one of the city hotels, and when changing his trousers on Thursday morning he neglected to transfer the necessary order from one pocket to another. There was nothing left for him but to take the first train to town in order to obtain the missing document. In the meantime the bride and her friends had to take shel- ter for a couple of hours at a house adjoining the church, and the carriage and pair had to perambulate the village. Ultimately the pair were made man and wife. The affair caused much amusement in' the place. MARRIED WOMEN'S PROPERTY ACT AND THE POST-OFFICE SAVINGS BANK.—From the Ist instant the rules of the Pest- office Savings Bank affecting the deposits of married women in England and Ireland were, owing to the operation of the Married Women's Property Act, 1882, much simplified, and married women now enjoy many advantages as depositors in that bank, which they have not hitherto possessed. Hitherto it hai been necessary to draw distinctions between women married before and after the 9th of August, 1870, and between deposits made before and after that date. All these distinctions are now swept away, an the law is placed by the new Act on a simple and intelligible footing. The Married Women's Property Act, 1882, does not apply to women domiciled in Scotland, the Channel Islands, or the Isle of Man.

An excited crowd assembled on Thursday morning, out- side the Red Lion Hotel, at Hounslow, where the adjourned inquest was held on the body of Dr. Edwardes. At the opening of the proceedings a medical certificate was pro- duced stating that Dr. Whitmarsh was ill and unable to attend, and the Coroner stated that he did not propose to take the evidence of the doctor at the preient stage of the inquiry owing to the excited stnte of public feeling. Addi- tional evidence was given by Mrs. Edwardes, the widow of the deceased, and Mr. Garratt, the assistant to the medical men, was under examination when the inquest was ad- journed to Wednesday next. The solicitor who appeared for the relatives of the deceased stated that just before his death Dr. Edwardes had instructed his solicitor to take pro- ceedings against the woman Bignell, who made a charge against him and afterwards withdrew it, and also for pro- ceedings against Dr. Whitmarsh.

TILE MARRIED WOMEN'S PROPERTY ACT—The first criminal charge brought by virtue of the provisions of the Married Women's Property Act has collapsed in an almost ludicrous manner. It was heard at the Liverpool Police Court on Wednesday. The piece -of property alleged te have been stolen from the prosecutrix was,.oddly enough, a "freezer," and the accused person was her husband. The wife was possessed of some furniture before her marriage to the prisoner in 1877, and amongst this furniture was the "freezer." The husband does not appear to have coveted this "freezer " till Saturday last, when he left home and took it with him. In doing this he was, in the opinion of the stipendiary magistrate, acting within his legal rights," as the " freezer" became his property in 1877. The learned magistrate was at pains to add that if the article had been bought by the prosecutrix say on Tuesday last it would have come under the provisions of the new Act. On this view of the law, however, it is difficult to see how the prosecutrix could have been robbed last Saturday of pro- perty not vested in her till the following Tuesday, and the prosecution is altogether unintelligible. A desperate affray occurred, late on Wednesday night, between nine bailiffs of the Carmarthen Fishery Company. and about fifteen men and youths who, with spears and lights, were poaching salmon in the river Tave, near Llan- fyrlach, Pembrokeshire. The encounter took place in a narrow pathway between the river and the pathway, and two poachers with spears held the IDailiffs at bay for some time, whilst most of the other poachers escaped. Two of the bailiffs made a rush, but were itnromealatelv struck down with the spears, which the poachers used freely. Another rush resulted in the capture of these two men, and the bailiffs marked two others so severely that their detection will probably be an easy matter. The spears which were captured had seven or eight prongs each, and weighed 101bs. or 121bs. • One bailiff was very badly cut, on the forehead and back of his head with spear thrusts., and a prong was broken by the violence of some of the blows which he received. He is in, a very-serious condition. The whole gang belong to Llanfyrlach. Prisoners, who are miners, were taken before the magistrates at Cardigan, on Thurs- day, and remanded on bail. A terrible tragedy is reported from a farmhouse near Little Rideau, Ontario. Frederick Mann, who had recently arrived from England, and was employed there, showed himself to ha insane. Early on Tuesday morning last he attacked Emma Cook, the eldest daughter of the farmer, and strangled her with a rope. Then he seized the mother, who came to her daughter's assistance, and strangled her. He next went into the barnyard, and attacked the father with an axe, chopping his head all to pieces. Going up stairs he attacked the farmer's son George, who was in bed, and ' killed him with the axe. Then be fell upon the son Willie, inflicting a dangerous wound. Willie grappled with the maniac, and the noise alarmed two other sisters, who came to their brother's assistance. One captured the axe, but Mann struck the other with a lamp. Mann rushed down stairs, got the poker again, and attacked them. They snc- ceeded, however, in shutting the ,door upon him, and then ran shrieking outside, calling for assistance. Man upon this fled, having killed four persons and wounded two. The neighbours are hunting for him in great excitement. The house shows sad evidence of the desperate struggle.— Times.

On Thursday afternoon, at the Dublin Police Court, a gentleman named Keogh, son of the late Judge Keogh, was brought up charged with having been disorderly in the Queen's Theatre, and with being a dangerous lunatic likely to do harm. Defendant, who is known as an eccentric character, wont into the second circle of the theatre and caused a great disturbance by shouting remarks to the actors and actresses. Much commotion was caused, and the de- fendant, who persistently refused to desist, was forcibly ejected. At the police station he conducted himself in a violent manner, and said he was sure it was "Jemmy Grubb," meaning his brother-in-law, Mr. James Murphy, Q.C., the Crown Prosecutor, who was the cause of his being arrested, and threatened to murder him. The magistrate said the doctor refused to certify that defendant was insane, and, therefore, he would not commit him, but would bind him over to keep the peace for twelve months. The de- fendant, who said he did not mean harm to Mr. Murphy, , and would keep away from him, tendered the sureties and I left the court.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY AND • THE NATIONAL BANK OF LIVERPOOL.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY AND • THE NATIONAL BANK OF LIVERPOOL.

An important bank amalgamation has just been effected, by which Parr's Banking Company takes over the business and goodwill of the National Bank of Liverpool (Limited). The former com- pany, whose headquarters are at Warrington is one of the most successful banking establishments in the kingdom, and of recent years It has made immense progress in the business it has done. It has branch establishments at Wigan, Southport, and other places, and among those who have been associated with it for many years, is Sir R. A. Cross, the ex-Home Secretary and one of the county mem- bers. The National Bank of Liverpool has branches at Birkenhead, Bootle, Waterloo, and in Great Charlotte-street, Liverpool, and its shareholders are to be paid by Parr's Banking Company a sum estimated to yield £l7 per share. It was generally known on the Liverpool Stock Exchange on Wednesday that the purchase was about to take place, or actually taken place, and the consequence was that the shares of the National rose 30s. By the arrangement Parr's Company take over the whole of the stock and premises of the National, and Mr. Alfred Turner, Mr. H. W. Meade-King, and Mr. Christo- pher Atkinson, directors of the latter bank, will join the board of Parr's Bank. The following circular respecting the nroposed change has been issued to the shareholders of the National Bank of Liverpool (Limited) : Liverpool, 2nd January, 1883. . .

, Dear Sir,—We have the pleasure to inform you that Parr's Banking Company, Limited, of Warrington, have purchased and will take over, the business, goodwill, and premises of the National Bank of Liverpool, Limited, on terms which, we estimate, will approximately yield the shareholders of this company £l7 per share. The shareholders of the National Bank of Liverpool, Limited, will have the privilege of taking shares in Parr's Banking Company, Limited, in the proportion of one share for every twenty shares held in the National Bank of Liverpool, Limited, and at the price of £55 per share—viz., £2O per share to be paid up as capital, and £35 per share to be paid as premium. The present market price of the shares of Parr's Banking Com- pany, Limited, is equivalent to £62 ex div. The dividend paid by Parr's Banking Company, Limited, annually since 1874 has been 15 per cent., in addition to which a bonus of 21 per cent, has been paid annually since 1876. At this rate of distribution the shares purchased at £55 yield £6 7s. 3d. per cent. With the exception 3f Mr. Beckett, whose health necessitates his retirement, the staff, both at the head office and the branches, will be retained by the purchasers, and your chairman and managing directors, viz. Mr. Turner, Mr. Meade-King, and Mr. Atkinson, have agreed to join the board of Parr's Banking Company., Limited, and will (with your consent) become the liquida- tors of the National Bank of Liverpool, Limited. We enclose acircular, calling the necessary meeting for carry- ing out these arrangements. We expect at that meeting to name an early date for the return of your capital. A copy of the last balance sheet of Parr's Banking Company, Limited, is enclosed herewith.—We are, dear sir, your obedient servants, for self and co-directors, ALFRED TURNER, chairman.—P.S.--Should you be unable to attend the meeting, please sign and return, so as to be received here not later than the 13th instant, the enclosed form of proxy, your signature to which should be attested by that of a witness.

Notice is also given that an extraordindry general meet- ing of thd National Bank of Liverpool, Limited, will be held at the company's offices, on Thursday, the Bth inst., when resolutions will be submitted proposing the voluntary winding up of the bank and approval of the arrangements provisionally entered into with Parr's Banking Company. The Liverpool Daily Post in its "Notes for Investors," says :—The acquisition of the premises and business of the National Bank of Liverpool, Limited, by Parr's Banking Company, Limited, has at once advanced the market value of the National Bank's shares from 54 p, the closing price of Tuesday, to 6i p., at which business was done after three o'clock on Wednesday. It is announced that the pur- chase has been made on terms which will, it is expected, yield £l7 for each National Bank share. The National Bank shares are of the nominal value of £2O, with £lO paid; those of Parr's Banking Company are £lOO nominal, with £2O paid. The National Bank shareholders are to have the option of taking one share in Parr's Banking Com- pany for every twenty shares held i,n the National Bank, at the price of £55 per share—that is, at a premium of 35. The closing price of shares in Parr's Bank on Wednesday night was 431-4 i premium, and it is pointed out that on the basis of recent dividends the shares in Parr's Bank at 35 premium yield .E 6 7s. 3d. per cent.
MR. GLADSTONE AND THE DIPLO- MATIC RESIDENT AT ROME.

The following correspondence refating to the alleged pro- posal of the English Government to appoint a diplomatic resident at Rome is published "To the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone. M.P., First Lord of the Treasury. Protestant Education Institute, 38, Parlia- ment-street, December 27, 1882.—Sir,—I beg to draw your attention to the following paragraph, which appears in the Standard of this morning, from their correspondent at Rome, yesterday's date, viz. The English Government have pro- posed to the Vatican to appoint a diplomatic resident upon the same footing as the representative of Prussia, and that the acceptance of this proposal by the Vatican has just been dtepatched.' And lam respectfully to ask whether this statement is founded on fact.—l have the honour to be, sir, your most humble and obedient servant, G. R. BADENOUGH." "10, Downing-street, Whitehall, let January, 1883.—Sir, —I am directed by Mr. Gladstone to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 27th ult., and to say that he thinks your inquiry would be more regularly addressed to the Foreign Office. He is not aware, however, of any such intention on the part of Her Majesty's Government as that which you quote from the Standard newspaper.—l am, sir, your obe- dient servant, HORACE SEYMOITR.—The Rev. G. R. Bad- enough."

The Standard says that in view of this, and of some other more or less direct denials, it thinks it right to print tho following despatches "From Cardinal Maccabe to Cardinal Jacobini. Dublin, December 20, 1882.—Yesterday I had a long and confiden- tial colloquy with Mr. —, sent to me by the Viceroy of Ireland to treat upon divers questions. In the course of the conversation he said to me the following words:—ln conse- quence of the refusal of the Holy See to accept a Secretary of the Embassy accredited to the Italian Government, as being charged to treat with the Vatican, the English Gov- ernment, on the proposition ef the Viceroy, is not averse to send to the Holy See a Minister with the same attributes as the Minister of Prussia. Could the Holy Father accede to this proposal without having a representative of his own in London? I allow the hope that such an arrangement might be very possible (possibilissima), but I require a formal permission to speak in the name of the Holy See." .

"From Cardinal Jacobini to Cardinal Maccabe. Rome, December 24, 1882.—After having taken the necessary con- sultation with His Holiness, I believe I may amply author- ise your Eminence to reply affirmatively to the question made and contained in your letter of the 20th inst. In case of the English Government deciding, as appears likely (literally, as appeals, come pare), to nominate a Minister to the Holy See, the latter would only reserve to itself the power of indicating the modality of the attributes of the person to be nominated."

div.head: REV. J. G. ROGERS AND THE PRIMATE.
div.p: THE REV. J. G. ROGERS AND THE PRIMATE.

A Plymouth correspondent says a remarkable correspon- dence has taken place concerning the appointment of Dr. Benson to the Archbishopric of Canterbury. The Rev. J. G. Rogers, of Clapham, having written to the London press that the Bishop of Truro recently made a slanderous charge against the Liberation Society, and calling upon hist to re- tract it in the interest of Christian peace, the Rev. Paul Bush, rector of Duloe, Cornwall, forwarded a letter to Mr. Rogers, relating an incident, which took place some time since at Liskeard with the object of demonstrating that Dr. Benson had good ground for his expression. Mr. Bush stated that Mr. Fisher, agent of the Liberation Society, whilst lecturing at Liskeard, related an incident of a clergyman who was bribed to break the law of the Church. The statement was challenged, and Mr. Fisher was eventually obliged to confess that the story was one he had heard somewhere, and which he could not substantiate. Mr. Bush asked Mr. Rogers if this conduct on the part of one of the principal agents of the Liberation Society did not warrant Dr. Benson in charging the society with uttering forgeries, and whether Mr. Broadhurst's recent statements that the Church neglected to confer on the working classes the benedts of elementary education did not warrant the Bishop in employing the phase of falsity. Mr. Rogers, in reply, contended that Dr. Benson's utterances are far too sweeping to be covered by adducing some indiscre- tions on the part of individual speakers on the Liberation platform. The application of the word " forgery " was an example of recklessness in the use of words, and tke expres- sion of Mr. Broadhurst was an independent and honest opinion, which should not be branded as a falsity. Arch- bishop Tait, whilst disputing the Liberation Society's facts, never imputed moral wrong.

div.head: RETENUE IN 1882.
div.p: THE RETENUE IN 1882.

The Treasury issued, on Saturday night, an abstract of the gross produce of the revenue of the United Kingdom for the third quarter of the financial year. The total ree.eipts for the quarter just ended are £26,998,148, being £78,588 in excess of the revenue for the corresponding quarter of 1881, which was £20,919,560. The items of receipts for the quarter are—Customs, £5,340,000; excise, £8,155,000; stamps, £2,850,000; land tax, £5,000; house duty, £25,000; property and income tax, £815,000; Post-office, £1,830,000; telegraphs, £130,000; Crown lands, £130,000; interest on advances, £384,937; and miscellaneous, £1,033,211. For the nine months just completed, the total receipts are in excess of the revenue for the cor- responding period of • 1881 by £522,576, the principal increases being, in customs, £171,000; stamps £18,695; and Post-office £0,000; and the principal 'decrease in excise, £132,000. For the twelve months now ended the revenue was £86,344,858, showing a nett decrease of £337,321 on that of year ended December, 1581.

div.head: RIVER WEAVER TRUST.
div.p: THE RIVER WEAVER TRUST.

I A somewhat awkward blunder, writes a correspondent, I has been discovered in the management of the dues received by the Weaver Trustees. The Act of 1840 empowered the River Weaver Trustees to built three churches at different points on the river, for the spiritual benefit of the flatmen land labourers engaged in the salt trade. By the 19th sec- tion of the Act the trustees are empowered to provide schools, to be annexed to each church, at a cost of not more than £l5O for such schools, wherein instruction shall be given to the children of watermen and labourers on the river Weaver "by the representative ministers or curates in such manner and at such times as the bishop of the diocese shall decree." Instead of confining themselves to the amount stipulated in the Act, the trustees have discovered that for the past twenty years they had been paying £3OO per annum—in point of fact that they have spent quite £lO,OOO of the ratepayers' money, in addition to £l,OOO spent in building these schools, in supporting Church of England schools. The salaries of the masters and mistresses of the schools have been paid by the trustees, while children have been educated therein whom the Act was not intended to benefit. The matter has on several occasions been forcibly represented to the trustees, and, in order to ascertain the actual position of affairs, the trustees referred to their solicitors, who, in reply, wrote as follows :

div.head: WEAVER SCHOOLS
div.p: WEAVER SCHOOLS

Northwich, Cheshire. October 23, 1832. DEAR SlR,—Previous to the year 1854. the Weaver trustees, In addition to paying the masters of the Weaver Schools, made an additional donation to four of the national schools In the neighbourhood of the liver; but at the anneal meeting in 1858 a resolution was passed that such annual donations shotild be discontinued after June, 1855. • At the annual meeting in 1855, on a motion to rescind the resolution of the previous annual meeting, an amendment was moved and carried that before res •inding such resolutiod the opinion of counsel should be ta4en as to the legality of continuing such donations. A case was accordingly prepared and laid before Mr. Cowling and before Sir Frederick Thesiger, both of whom were of opinion that the donations to the four national schools could not be legally continued', and Sir F. Thesiger also adds—"lndeed I am bound to po'nt out to the trustees that they are not autho,ised to pay the masters of the different schools which were bLilt, it being expressly provided that 'lnstructions is to be given by the respective ministers or curates,' whose incomes are fixed at certain maximum and minimum amounts by the 6th sectiln."—Yours truly, J. L. TRAFFORD. The origin of the payment of the salaries was a resolution passed in 1843, when the trustees ordered that a building should be given up for the purpose of a school for the chil- dren of flatrnen and haulers on the river, the trustees not having any immediate occasion for the blinding. On the application of two clergymen, it was ordered that a school- master be provided for the school at a salary of £5O " for the present year." This arrangement was afterwards discon- tinued, and fixed salaries were paid to both masters and mis- tresses of all the schools, and, in addition this, all other expenses of maintenance and repairs, amounting altogether, on the average of the past four years to £452 per annum, with houses for the masters rent free. In board rates the trustees contribute to the Winsford, Weaverham, and other school boards £159 per annum, making a total payment for educational purposes of £6ll. It should not be forgotten that these schools are no longer Weaver schools for the use of the children of tlatmen and others employed in the navi- gation, but have for some years past become public elemen- tary schools, in order to obtain the Government's grants and inspection. The income of the trust is about £20,000, and, after paying all expenses, the balance is handed over to the county for the benefit of the rates. It will, therefore, be seen .that for the past twenty years the trustees have been applying large awns from county funds for the benefit of schools connected with the Church of England.
WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority ivas held at the Workhouse yesterday. Mr. W. Derbyshire presided, and there were also present the Rev. G: F. Roberts, Messrs. E. C. E. Cooper, R. Garnett, R. Owen, W. Gibson, R. Kil- shall, .L Houghton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. H. Gornall (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and G. Rawlings (inspector).

div.head: NEW YEAR'S GREETING.
div.p: NEW YEAR'S GREETING.
The CHAIRMAN wished the members a happy new year, and expressed a hope that the business of the Authority would be conducted amicably throughout the year.
NOXIOUS VAPOURS.

The ASSISTANT CLERK (Mr. S. Sutton) said he had received the following letter from Mr. Robert Holland, hon. sec. of the Association for Controlling the Escape of Noxious Vapours and Fluids from Manufactories (Lancashire and Cheshire);—"l _am much obliged to you for your letter. I feared from the first that you would get no assistance from the other sanitary authorities. I believe the inspector they have got at St. Helens is.only placed there temporarily by Dr. Angus Smith. He wrote to me sometime since to say he had asked Mr. Rolland to live there, for I think he said, three months. The authorities on the Liverpool side, how- ever, are joining with the Corporation of Liverpool in pay- ing the salary of an extra inspector, so something will be done. I will ascertain front the Liverpool Association what they have been able to do, and then call a meeting of our committee to see if we can suggest anything, but I fear it will be useless to try to avail ourselves of Clause 19 of the Act.—Mr. COOPER pointed out that instead of turning the gas up the chimney it could be utilized with advantage by the manufacturers. The orchards round Winwick had not for several years borne any fruit.—The CHAIRMAN stated that he had heard, but did not know how far it was correct, that when an inspector visited the works at Widnes a signal was given, and the method of consuming the vapour and smoke was at once put in operation, and as soon as he went away they went back to the old system.—The further con- sideration of the matter was deferred until the next meeting.
VITAL STATISTICS. •

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that during the month ending December 31st, 1882, the births were 14 males and 20 females; and the deaths 10 males and 10 feniales. The excess Qf births over deaths was 14, the death rate 192, and the proportionate mortality from preventable diseases 15 per cant. Mr. Gornall reported the extension of scarlet fever in the township of Penketh. One case of scarlet fever had been removed to the Fever Hospital from the Sankey district.

div.head: THREE BOATS' CREWS MASSACRED.
div.p: THREE BOATS' CREWS MASSACRED.

Latest advices received from Australia report that some further massacres have been committed. by the natives of the South Seas, and this time the victims are said to be rather more numerous than in most cases recently. It seems that the labour vessel Clara arrived lately at Tounsville from the South Seas. The vessel had on' board 146 islanders. She reported that at Laviona the natives had committed several outrages, and that the crews of no less than three boats had been murdered.

Another outrage was reported by the vessel City of Mel- bourne, which arrived from Noumea. In this instance the scene of the attack was Vanekoro, in the New Hebrides. A number of divers were engaged at the Beebe de Mer Station at Vanekoro, when a horde of islanders suddenly made a raid on their place. An Indian and two New Caledonians managed to escape, though the latter two were wounded, one of them:very seriously; but two others belonging to New Caledonia fell victims to the weapons of the assailants. The three men who escaped did so in a small boat, and put out to sea, subsequently reaching a friendly island. At latest accounts one of the men was in a dying state from his wounds.

At a meeting of the Executive of the Lancashire and Cheshire Amalgamated Association of Engine Minders, held at Bolton, on Thursday morning, it was decided to agitate throughout the district for an advance of wages equal to the last reduction.

DEATas iw . BREWER'S VAT.—An accident, resulting in the deaths of two persons, happened late on Tuesday night, at Corsley, a village near Frome. Mr. Randell, who keeps a public-house on the Heath, employed a man named Baines to clean a vat for brewtng. The latter on proceeding to commence his work, was overpowered by gases, and fell. Randell, on going to his assistance, was arso overpowered. A third man, named Mines, shared a similar fate, and when the three were taken out, Randell and Mines were found to be dead, while Baines is slowly recovering from his injuries. div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The Mayor (Councillor Crosfield) presided at the monthly meeting of the Council held on Tuesday evening. There were also present Aldermen Pickmere, Holmes, Burgess, W. Kean, Harrison, and Davies, Councillors Broadbent, Dakin, Greening, Brown, Wallington, Wright, W. Pierpoint, Wool- fall, Taylor, John Pierpoint, Mackie, Caldwell, Barker, Ashton, Sntton, Whittle, Francomb, Bolton, Monks, Burgess, Collin, Hutchinson ; and Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), T. Longdin (borough surveyor).

div.head: WATCH COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE WATCH COMMITTEE.
The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee. Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the motion, which was carried.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.
Alderman HOLMES moved that the minutes of the Finance Committee be passed. _ _
Councillor GREENING seconded.

In replying to a question Alderman HOLMES observed that the expenditure in connection with the gas department was that which was going on month by month. He did not know that anything had been paid for any new plant or machinery. The minutes were agreed to. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING. Councillor BROADBENT moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Street Improvement Committee, and Councillor BARKER seconded the motion, which was passed.

PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. Alderman KEAN, in moving the adoption of the minutes of this committee, obsetved that there was nothing of special interest contained therein. He had not the slightest doubt that the members of the Council residing in Latchford would be anxious to know something about the progress of the new drainage scheme. (Hear, hear.) That was going on as rapidly and as well as circumstances would permit— no time was being lost. And it would be worth their while if members of the Council went down to the gasworks and examined the air-pressers fixed there. He was sure they would be perfectly satisfied with the machinery. Councillor WooLFALL seconded the motion, which was carried.

Alderman BURGESS said he had one or two questions to ask the Chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. The first was as to whether the cost of the laying of the main from the) gasworks, over Warrington Bridge, and through Latchford, was included in the estimate for the sewerage of Latchford? His second question was whether in the con- struction of streets now in progress, and having been for for some time, had the resolution of the Council been rigidly adhered to? The MAYOR: Do you mean the foundations? Alderman BURGESS: I mean in every particular—whether that resolution is on the minute books of the Council—is rigidly adhered to, or whether, as it is hinted in some quar- ters, it is not being rigidly adhered to. If it is not—l don't know whether it is or not—the public at large are made to suffer in consequence of the laxity of the arrangealents. Councillor MONKS asked Alderman Burgess to repeat the question with respect to Latchford, as he did not exactly grasp it. Alderman BURGESS said he had asked if the cast of lay- ing down the main pipes from the gasworks, through Mersey-street, over Warrington Bridge, and through Latch- ford was included in the contract for Latchford sewerage. If it was not, where was it to be paid from? That was the question he had put, and he wanted an answer to it. Alderman KEAN said if any other member of that Coun- cil had asked so foolish a question—(hear, bear)—he would have been astonished. Alderman Burgess ought to have the working of that department at his finger ends, and especially with reference to Latchford, for he (the speaker) believed he had been present when every resolution had been passed with reference to that scheme. He might tell him and the members of the Council that everything had been strictly contraeted for, and all expenses had been in- eluded in those contracts—no future charges for laying of pipes. Alderman Burgess's second question was quite as , wild to him as the first. It was whether the committee were rigidly adhering to the resolution of the Council with reference to forming streets. There had not been the slightest deviation anywhere, and if Alderman Burgess was in possession of any information that would lead the Coun- cil to suppose that such a thing was being neglected by the committee, they would be very glad to have it before them. He thought it would be the most ridiculous thing in the world for the coaltnittee, who was constantly under the guidance of that Council, to attempt to deviate in any shape or form; and so long as be was at the head of affairs in that department he would take care whatever that Council sanctioned should be carried out to the very letter. (Hear, hear.)
The minutes were then passed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

Councillor WALLINGTON moved that the minutes of the School Attendance Committee be passed, observing that the Council would notice that their consent was required for the expenditure incurred in sending two boys to the reforma- tory schools. There was nothing more that demanded attention.
Councillor BOLTON, in a maiden speech, seconded the motion.
The minutes were passed. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS. The minutes of this committee were passed on the motion of UOIIIICiIIOt BURGESS, seconded by Councillor BRoAD- BENT .

div.head: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
div.p: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
Councillor BROWN moved that the Cemetery Committee's minutes be confirmed. Councillor J. PIERPOINT secoOed the motion, which was carried.
TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE.
Alderman PICKMERE : Ibe to move that the minutes of :his committee be confirmed. Councillor CALDWELL seconded.—Carried.
MAIIKETS COMMITTEE.
• Councillor GREENING, in the absence of the chairman, moved the confirmation of the minutes of this committee. Councillor TAYLOR seconded the motion, which was carried.
SANITARY.

Alderman BURGESS, in moving that the minutes of the Sanitary Committee be passed, said that the first resolution with reference to the nurses at the hospital, was simply carrying out the decision of the Council. The resolution with reference to the wells in Latchford would commead itself, he thought, to the members of the Council. If the wells were polluted so as to be injurious to health, it was quite time that they dealt with wells of that character. It would be in the recollection of the Council, he dared say, that a recommendation of a very similar character had already come before them—for dealing with wells in the entire borough—wherever they might b 3 formed. With reference to the grinding mill purchased for Longford he might say that it was not under- ' stood to be an introduction of any new description of ma- chinery that would not be necessary whatever system of manufacture was adopted there. Whatever system might be adopted—if that grand Birmingham scheme, which they had not heard anything about for some time, was adopted —still the mill would be required for the assisting of it. It did not matter if they had one system or another; and he thought they were not infringing .upon the rule laid down by the Council that no new machinery should be introduced until that great question had been settled. It was simply the introduction of machinery for the grinding of the material, so as to enable men to get at the markets sooner , than at the present moment. He thought the appointment ' of Mr. Dinwiddie as manager, at a salary of .£l5O per annum, would be exceedingly advantageous not only to the Council but to the town at large. Mr. Dinwiddie had had much experience, and he hoped the appointment would commend itself to the judgment of the Council. Councillor MONKS did not quite understand why the Birmingham system should have been brought in at that ' stage. He thought Mr. Burgess's modesty would have led him to say as little as possible about it, especially as it had , saved the Council £12,000. The grinding mill was to do a , lot of work that the machinery they now had was intended to do. He dared say it was very likely—he thought it was a pretty unanimous feeling of the committee—that the machinery they had would practically have to come out.. But that was a matter for future discussion. He most cordially supported the appointment of Mr. Diuwiddie, for he thought in Mr. Dinwiddie they would have a men who was capable of dealing with the question as it ought to be dealt with without interference from anybody. Alderman KEAN supposed the machinery at work at Longford had been very much weakened in its operations by long workings, and rather than dispense with it thocom- mittee would have a grinding machine to help it. He was astonished when he looked at the insight of the chairman , that he had not discovered it sooner. Alderman Burgess) said it would enable them o get tot ae markets with greater rapidity than hitherto, but he was surprised that Alderman Burgess did not discover it sooner. He had not told them one word about the probability of the machinery doing its work and they could not tell whether the grinding machine would be correct or not. He had been , wonderinff for a long time that they should have had a scheme :t Longford in operation so many years and now be told by the chairman that it was not capable of doing its work without the assistance of the grinding mill. Councillor FnANcOmB said he thought Alderman Burgess , would be satisfied that the machine they saw at work at I Rockdale was actually doing work that they required doing at the present time. the machine that they had at Longford would only reduce the material to lumps, which were sadly too large to sell to farmers. They could reduce it to the fineness of powder, but it took an erormous amount of time, so that it was the unanimous wish of the committee that the mill should be bought, and they believed by so doing they were spending the town's money in the best possible way. (Hear, hear.) So far as the Birmingham scheme was con- cerned, he thought the chairman of the cs, be very much adaoa tne committee. He might stiy It was more out of respect to him than out of respect te their own opinions that tthey had been so quiet of late. There were two sehemi s—Man- love, Alliott, and Co.'s, and the Birmingham scheme. They were not quarrelling about the mode of manufacture. He believed it was the unanimous opinion of every one present that the right thing to do was to manufacture it, for in its crude state it was impossible to get farmers to take it away, even if they gave it to them. But what they quibbled a little about in committee was the best mode of manufacturing it. The chairman believed, and conscitntouslv believed, that Manlove's scheme was the best, and the others believed the Birmingham scheme was the best, and just at this time the hot air process was brought out at Rochdale. They bad

been to Rochdale to see it, and he believed it was the b .st and the one that would eventually be adepted. He did not think it was the time even to give back-banded blows to any member of the committee, but he thought it was time that they should in a manly spirit meet this difficulty. (Hear, hear.) With what bad been going on at Longford for the last 18 months or two years, be did not think the ratepayers of the town at large were satisfied. (Hear, hear.) They did not understand the matter, and the committee could not go to every one of them and tell them that to manufacture was the best course. Bat eventually the committee must ask for more money, and whenever they asked for it he should certainly back up the chairman, because be be- lieved it the right thing to do, and he hoped the chairman and other members of the committee would stick together and meet the difficulty as they should do. As to the ap- pointment of a manager, he could only say he had known. Mr. Dinwiddie for a number of years, and he believed him to be a thoroughly pracieal steady man, and a man who would do his duty. This was flora new appointment. He believed before he was a member of the Council they had ainln at a salary of £2OO a year. But they had been put La this position. They must either take Norman from his duties as nuisance inspector, or appoint some one else at Longford; and it was, he believed, the unanimous opinion of the committee that the selection was a good one, and that the appointment ought to be made. (Hear, hear.) Councillor SUTTON, as a member of the Sanitary Commit- tee' merely wished to say that he should object to the ex- penditure of any large sum of money for machinery at j Longford until the Council had decided upon the machipery 1 that should be introduced. When Alderman Burgess got up be thought he was going to make an after dinner speech, but as people who made after dinner speeches were gener- ally very pleasant, he came to the conclusion that the alderman was on the wrong side of his dinner, and the sooner they ended the discussion in order that he might go and have it the better. Councillor BOLTON, referring to the minute relating to the closing of wells, said he thouebt the resolution passed at the last Council meeting was quite sufficient without passing another authorising the taking of necessary pro- ceedings to close all wells. He thought before the wells were closed the water ought to be thoroughly tested, and not pronounced injurious to health beio:e it was condemned. He held that the resolution passed at the last monthly meet- ing was quite sufficient as far as the town was concerned, that was to compel all property owners ta put in a proper supply of water. He moved that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of that minute relating to the closing of the wells.

Alderman Hor,NtEs confirmed the letter that came from Penketh school reqoecting the tent from the fever hospital. The children who had to go into it derived great advantage, and he believed .it thoroughly prevented the spread of fever in the school.

Alderman Bunar.->s, in reply, said in reference to the observations of Alderman Kean as to their not having dis- covered the machinery for grinding was wanted, he had nothing to say. If Alderman Kean had been on the com- mittee he had no doubt it would have been discovered. The proper time for the application of such machinery was when the necessity for it had been discovered. So far as Councillor Monks was concerned, he might tell him there was a wind bag to be pricked, and it would not be very long before it was; and he thought some people might be amused and other people might be astonished. As to the analysis that Councillor Bolton had spoken of as being taken in a iew minutes, he had no reason to believe the medical officer of health ran over his work in that superficial manner. Refer- ring to Councillor Franconib's remarks, he said the masters the Council had given him had determined upon the machine he should have.

The MAYOR did not think a matter:of £B3 for a grinding mill was worth discussing. The grinding mill was neces- sary, and therefore it must be got. The discussion that had taken place between Alderman Burgess and Councillors Monks and Francomb had been a little irregular, as there was nothing on the minutes to lead to it; but he did not like to interrupt them, because it was a pet subject with those gentlernen—(laugh(ke.)—and he liked men to have the op- portunity of ventilating their views. There was no decision yet as to which was the best method to adopt. The committee were a vaiting the result of experiments at Rochdale, and if they turned out satisfactorily, Alderman , Burgess, himself, and Councillor Milner on the one side, and Councillors Monks, Barher, and Francornb on the other would all be wrong, and they would adopt the system that would come in between the two. He hoped such would be , the case, and then those who had been fighting' and con- scientiously fighting, against each other such a length of time could lay down their arms and j,-)in together in Hewn- ! mending the adoption of the best scheme that had yet been invented. He trusted that in a very few weeks or months they would be able to go over to Rochdale, and see the matter settled. To his mind it was the most important iwatter connected with the borough of Warrington, because he confessed at present he was literally ashamed of the con- dition Longfoid was in, and it must be altered in one way or another. (Hear, bear.) The minutes were then confirmed. Councillor BARKER, with the permission of the Mayor, stated that if the Rochdale people were successful lie should be gratified, because it was the scheme he had advocated all along. He had never advocated time Birmingham system, but that they should have time to see what other people were doing, and judge for themselves. Alderman BURGESS asked if other members could make observations.
The MAYOR said they could not. He gave Councillor Barker a liberty which he knew he had no right to have, but he knew he felt rather strongly on the subject, and therefore he allowed it.

THE LIGHTING OF THE TOWN. Alderman HOLMES. in moving the anoption of the minutes of the Gas Committee, said the expenditure had been £2,060, and as the aggregate manufacturing expenses last year were nearly £19,000, he did not consider the amount unusual. Councillor MONKS' seconded. Alderman KEAN asked what number of gas stoves were now in use in the town. Alderman iiorzrEs : 200.

The MAYOR said he might tell the Gas Committee, for their consolation, that he had bcen over in DLblin once or twice lately, and the difference in the streets of that city and of Warrington as regarded lighting was the difference between the sun and the moon. Dublin was in a state of darkmss compared to Warrington, and he felt proud when he came back to Warrington to see the excellent lighting of the streets.

, Alderman BURGESS asked if it was, in consequence of the state of the Dublin streets that outrages took place. The N'AYOR replicql that he believed it.was. Councillor 13nolDBEITT : I think we ought to send Alder- man Holmes over to light them up. The minutes were agreed to.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE AND TIIF. SHIP CANAL. The MAYOR proposed, and the EX-MAYOR (Alderman Pickmere) seconded, the confirmation of the mikutes of the General Purposes Committee. Councillor Mac Kw. asked if any information could be vouchsafed to them as to ibel4teps that were being taken by the Town Council in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal. Enquiries were being made, and rumours, some false and some true, made the matter one to be looked into at once by the Council, and if the proper parties were pre- paring to put them in a legal position he had nothing more to say. He was very anxious, if there was any committee, whatever might be its name, or any gentlemen such as the Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor engaged in the work, that they should feel they had the Council at their back in any necessary expense they might incur in having the very best advice and taking the very best steps to put the town in a proper position. He referred to the changes that had been made in the scheme, which was nothing more nor less than one for a huge ditch from Runcorn, ald he urged that persons interested in the ancient rights of Warrington should take steps to secure the preservation of the Mersey so far as Warrington was concerned.

The Mayon said the committee had had the matter before them, and the town clerk was instructed to make an epi- tome of the Bill as it had gone before Parliament. The work took a long time to do, and the town clerk had not yet finished it, but at the next meeting of the General Purposes Committee no doubt it would be laid before them. There was a great deal of force in what Councillor Mackie had said; he agreed with a great deal of it himself. 'The com- mittee were fully alive to the interests of Warrington, and it would be their duty to protect the interests of the town. l(Hear, hoar.) When he went over to Manchester—he thought he should not be doing wrong in saying this—he had to speak for iVarrington, and he told them whilst they loved Manchester very much they loved Warrington more, and it would be the business of this Corporation to protect the in- terests of Warrington. (hear, hear.) The probability was —it was almost certain—that the committee would get the opinion of an eminent engineer, and they would be guided a great deal by his advice. He did not think it wise to have a discussion that night, because tht.y were not ripe for it. The probability was it would come up at the next Council meeting. • Alderman BURGESS remarked that in his humble judg- ment the question had not been referred to the committee which should have taken charge of it. They had a Rivers Committee, and it did appear to him one of its special duties would have been to have taken this matter in hand. He did not know why it should be delegated to the General Pur- poses Committee. At the same time he had not the least objection, but if the Rivers Committee was not the com- mittee to take it in hand, he thought the sooner it was die- solved the better.

The MAYOR said Alderman Burgess was out of it this time. The Rivers Committee pasea a minute that the town clerk and borough surveyor be instructed to point out the details of the scheme as it affected Warrington, and make a report to the committee. Alderman KEAN: No doubt Alderman Burgess was present. 'titre is nothing on the minutes re- ferring to the ship canal. Alderman BURGESS: I want to know why I had not an invitation to meet that committee as a member of it. The MAYOR said he had nothing to do with that. The minutes were confirmed. UPPER UERSEY NAVIGATION COMMISSION.
On the proposition of the 51AY0R, s2conded by Alderman BURGESS, Alderman Davies was re-elected to represent the Council m on the above Commission.
The Council then rose.
At Stratford-on-Avon, cn Wednes,lay, the Rev. George Arbuthnot, vicar, was fined LI 125., including costs, or one day's imprisoßment, for ariking one of his choir boys with an umbrella.

TESTIMONIAL FROM THE REV. R. H. DIGNUM. 176, Cleveland-street, Birkenhead, August 4th, 1882. Dear Sir,—From a feeling of deep gratitude to you, and a desire to benefit those who suffer, I beg to inform you of the great benefit I have derived from wearing your " Magnetaire " Appliances. When I came to consult you I was suffeiing much from indigestion and nervous action, so much so that I feared an attack of epilepsy or St. Vitus Dance. I was, indeed, distressed; now, thank God, the nervous action has greatly subsided. I attend to my duties with more ease and comfort, the digestive organs have con- siderably improved, and I look forward to a return of health and vigour. I would strongly reccommend your Appliances to all who suffer, as I am quite convinced of their efficacy in the treatment of all nervous complaints and of diseases in general. With very kind regards,—l remain, my dear sir, yours sincerely, Roßr. HAYDON DIGNUM. Mr. R. Lonsdale.

I have found them very effective for nervous debility and indigestion. 1 wish you to send me the " Magnetaire " Soles per return, and oblige, yours sincerely, Mr. R. Lonsdale, M.E. R. H. DIGNUM.

I was, at the time of visiting you, suffering with palpitation of the heart, pain in the side and general debility, with very poor appetite, but now am glad to say I am a great deal better, can sleep on my side with comfort, my appetite has much im- proved, and the palpitation seldom affects me. I can strongly recommend your applianses to sufferers like my self.—Yours sincerely, (Mrs.) M. J. RAWLINSON. Mr. R. Lonsdale, M.E.

I ndw am free from pain; my head is so much better that I can take my food with comfort, and sleep well. Seeing the benefit so many people in this town have derived from your treatment, I decided to try it, with the followingresult. After using your "Magnetaire Appliance only two hours I found relief, and may say with one week's use I am delighted with the c'Aange ; having entirely lost those terrible pains and stiffness I can now walk comfortably. 22, Ludlow-street, Lower Grangetown, Cardiff, Ist December, 1882. Dear Sir —I wish to express my great satisfaction, and to testify to the benefit I have derived from the " Magnetaire " Appliances I purchased of you a fortnight since. After a day's trial I felt a glow throughout my whole system, and commenced to lose the pain in my hip and knee, from which I had suffered acutely for three years, and had tried all sorts of remedies, and spent many pounds, without re- ceiving the least benefit; but I can safely say, after wearing the "Magnetaire " a few days, I have since been entirely free from pain.. I shall spare no trouble in recommending your Appliances to anyone I may know suffering.—l remain, yours very truly, DAVID WILLIAMS. Mr. R. Lonsdale.
