div.p: PARALYSIS.

Rodney Wharf, Newport. Dear Sir,--I have worn one of your " Magnetaire " Appliances with the following satisfactory results. For over four years I had been paralysed partly down one side. My arm and band I could scarcely raise, losing nearly all power, and the circulation throughout my system was very poor, my spirits were much depressed, and my nerves being completely prostrated, my life at times seemed a burden to me. I began to despair of ever getting better. I can scarcely express how thankful I am for the marvellous change your Appliances have effected in me. My arm and hand I can now use freely. My appetite is good, can sleep well and rise early in the morning to do my duties. I had tried other appliances with no beneficial results. Should any person inquire of me, I shall be happy to recommend your " Magnetaire."—Yours gratefully, Mr. R. Lonsdale. W. THOMAS.

have been favoured with a copy of the c44„,trafticii Reform i Almanack for 1883. It s I;,Y the most valuable publication of its that is printed, and to anyone who takes itri- ;interest in political matters it must be ec,—,4BPensable. Information on almost every W eeivable topic of Imperial significance is at.'pd before the reader in a most concise and,ill„telligible form, and the various tables the- 'l-pier data being carefully compiled from the-, verY best sources, they are of course DaD.-?lighly reliable. A few facts from the Nve—s the Almanack may be here cited, and gati?Oubt not they will prove interesting. We dep et.r,' then, that the cost of the civil Ivii."lllents for last year was £24,616,95, era 11 year it is £25;292,818, showing an stap—ase this year of £675,868. The active witi; cost in 1881-82 £r00,867, as compared 1•,4,103,982 this year, so that here is also inet;'re4se-23,115. There is likewise an Aavv-a-..e on the expenditure of the army and Nvasi's4.l-ast year the total of the army estimates show-7,16,589,500, this year it is £17,726,828, The "ig an increase of £1,137,328 this year. tr/ ,navy estimates this year amount to •Cro'4.-°n°'9o9, last year they reached only Yeii; '714:69, an increase of £503,44.0 this edit() ,vlth regard to the array estimates, the dep.„r, °f the Almanack rernars: " How the el,!; take crcJi :o ilif eithet fcir

an apparent decrease of £1,131,400 or a real decrease of £563,000, passes our comprehen- sion. Certain it is that both Tory and , Liberal Governments require much morel vigilant and stern watchfulness on the part of their constituents, both in and out of Parlia- ment, than they seem likely at present to get ;" and again under the navy estimates there is this note, "Mysterious figures of the depart- ment here also appear to show a saving of £62,018, with regard to which we can only say to the Heads of the Services, as the Irishman said to his host, that we will 'believe ye to obleege ye.'" Some interestinc, details are given as to the ownership of land. We find that in the "Three Kingdoms" there are no less than 1,173,724 owners of land holding 72,119,961 acres, the gross estimated • rental being £ 31470.360, exclusive of such parts of the counties of Kent, Middlesex, and Surrey as are included in the metr9polis. Of the 1,173,724 owners, 852.438 hold less than one acre each, 252,725 own between i and too acres each, 51,090 possess between /00 and 1.000 acres each, and 10,888 hold 1,000 and upwards each. It is rather remarkable, however, that while 852,438 owners have less than an acre each, and only 188,413 acres in the aggregate, their gross rental is estimated at £36 294,173, which is £14,936,517 more than 252,725 persons with 4,910,723 acres receive, £10,198,891m0re than 51,090 with 15,135,057 acres receive, and only £8,586,880 less than to,BBs holders of 51,885,118 acres receive. In addition to this there are 2,238 individuals holding 5,000 acres and upwards each, or 39 924,232 acres in all, the total rental of which is £26408,397. The 39,924.232 acres is 3,864,252 more than half the area ascribed to the 1.173.724 owners of land, and close Upon 16,000,000 of acres more .than a third part of the whole area of Gre- t Britain and Ireland. This shows the monopoly that exists. The Almanack contains two valuaLle tables relating to the Houses of Parliament. The first shows the House of Lords is com- posed of 516 members, of whom six are peers of the blood Royal, two aTe archbishops. 21 dukes, 19 marquesses, 116 earls, 26 viscounts, 24. bishops, 258 barons, t 6 Scotch repre- sentative peers, and 28 Irish representative peers. Of the 516 ten are minors, and one representative peer for Ireland is enumerated also as a peer of the United Kingdom, making the actual number of the House of Lords 505. Of these 4.38 are landholders, possessing amongst them 4,258,527 acres, with a rental of £11,886,308. Exclusive of generals, admirals, and other officers of the army and navy, also of some compensa- tionists, &c., the amount paid for annuities, pensions, salaries, &c, to members of the Upper House is £621,336, of which the pre- lates take £162,271, other peers the rest. The dispensers of Church patronage, including the prelates, are 289 in number, and they have 4,801 benefices at their disposal. There are in the House 36 members holding cffices under the present Administration, and 90 who were connected with preceding ones. Of army officers there are 46 in active service, and 61 (of whom 13 serve in Militia and Yeomanry) retired total 107 ; of naval officers there are 7 active and 3 retired—total ; of Militia officers 37 active, of Yeomanry officers 38—total (exclusive of Volunteer officers) 192 members who are interested directly or indirectly, or through the espiril de corps, in getting as much as possible for the services. There are also 6z peers repre- senting 14 railways as chairmen or directors. The second table has reference to the House of Commons, in which 639. members are accounted for, showing the House to be 13 short of the full number. The landed possessions of these 639 members represents 12,127,531 acres, the rental of which is Li 843,24.6. They own 273 Church livings. and they receive in salaries, pay, and pensions £102,940. If the acres and rentals of peers whose heirs or younger sons are in the Com- mons be added, then the total acreage owned by the Commons is 6,663,250, the rental being £5,022,739 The aristocratic interests in the Lower House is represented by 272 members, the fighting interests by 168, landed interests 267, law interests 122, the liquor interests 18, moneyed interests 25, literary, professional, and scientific interests 84, official interests 113, railway interests 'l3, trading, commercial, and manufacturing interests 155, and labour interests only 2. The sooner the labour interest is more exten- sively represented the belter. The details which the Almanack gives of the Pension List are somewhat startling. Twelve months' payments in connection with the Royal i Family amount to £898,302; but in addition to this the expenditure on the Royal parks and pleasure grounds reaches no less than £112,637. At the present time there is a total of over 150,250 persons drawing more than £7,000,000 yearly from the State funds of Great Britain and Ireland, and moo° persons receiving .£3,196,51 yearly being pensioners on the bounty of India. A list-is given of over 2,500 persons who receive pensions of Itso and upwards, and it is note- worthy that many of these favoured individuals pensioned on account of " ill-health " lived in some cases 4.0 years to enjoy the gift from the public exchequer, and that others again were rewarded with a pension after only about half-a-dozen -years service. It is rather remarkable, too, that one gentleman, according to the list, gets more for doing nothing than he got for working. A year's changes in the pension list unfolds a tale. Six hundred and eighty-one persons were re- moved from the list in 1881, 618 of them by death, with a decrease of £74,455 in the amount paid; on the other hand, the list was recruited by 84.9 additions to it, at a cost of L 76,168 ifs. 5d., being a nett addition of 1643 in the number of persons and one of £1,713 ss. sd. in the cost. The total amount of allowances remaining payable on the 3i st December, iBBl, including zo years' annui- ties to National Debt Commissioners, was £1,321,227 r6s. Bd. That a necessity exists for an inquiry into the pension list, as sug- gested by Mr. BRADLAIIGH, the above facts amply prove. Net the least instructive table in the Almanack is one giving a summary of the income and expenditure during the past ten years. From this we learn that the income during that period has been £799,465,353, and the expenditure £805,670,827, being in excess of the income by £6,205,474. The only years in which there was a surplus over expenditure was in 1873, when the excess was £6,205,573; in 1881, when it amounted to £1,129,267 ; and in. 1882, when it only reached £345,698; together, £7.4.95,538. It will be observed that in those three years a Liberal Govern- ment was in Power. In the Six years of Tory Government, which is included in the ten years referred to, there was 'always a deficit. the aggregate amounting td. £13,701,012. The net deficit of income over expenditure lin this period was ;C6,203,474. The publica- tion is on the whole a valuable one. Mr. Buudir says there is no other in this country

Ito be compared with it, and we hope it may 1 find its way into the hands more especially lof the working classes, so that they may be awakened to a keener knowledge o the heavy burdens under which they suffer.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 6, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 6, 1883.
LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.

Widnes School Board is doing a vaet amount of good among the population of Widnes, and the state- ment given at the last meeting by Mr. Robert Shaw showed that it was done in a very ecotomical way. The schools, it appeared, are almost self-supporting —that is, the school pence and the payments made to the Board by Government, are almost sufficient for the efficient working of the schools withont making any call from the rates. The attendance of the scholars' too, is highly satisfactory, but a walk through the streets during school hours reveals the fact that many " waifs and strays" still receive their education in the gutter. With hare heads, whose unkempt locks are seldom brought under the restrain- ing influences of a comb and brush; uncased feet and legs, brown with exposure to wind and wet; dressed in clothes "all tattered and torn," and lacking also the virtue of cleanliness, these children are one of the sights of Wisines, and a melancholy sight it is. Their number, it is true, has been much reduced since the formation of the Board, but although they have come under the vigilant e 3 es of the Board's officials, their attendance at school must be to a great extent un- willing and spasmodic. It is difficult to see, too, how the Board are to entirely remedy the evil. Prosecuting the parents before the magistrates, Mr. Wade Deacon recently stated, was of little avail—the fine imposed was paid, and in a many instances the old course pursued. The onerous and somewhat weighty labours now undertaken by the School Board tax its capacity, I doubt not, to the full, and a little outside help would be of great value. In Liver- pool the Council on Education, a body totally distinct from the School Boord, is doing good and successful work, and Mr. Wade Deacon some time ago stated he , was promoting the formation of a similar institution for Widnes. No information with regard to the , scheme, has however, since been volunteered ; but a knowledge of Mr. Deacon's thorough and painstaking character, which is highly valued on the School Board, will not permit me to think that the matter has been "shelved." I trust we shall soon see Borne outward sign that the project is progressing, and have the satisfaction, at no distant date, of knowing that the Council is at work, aiding in spreading the benefits of elementary education among the youth of Widnes. An instance of the loyalty to the Throne of Radical Birmingham is, I think, afforded by the fact that a statue of Her Majesty is just about to be erected in that hotbed of Republicanism. The municipality al- ready possesses a statue of the Prince Consort, which was generously subscribed for by the public, and as a considerable balance remained after its completion it was decided to expend it in the provision of a com- panion statue of the Queen. The death of the sculp- tor entrusted with the commission and other hind- rances delayed the execution of the work; but the statue is now, however, nearly finished, and the com- mittee who have had the matter in hand is arranging for the acceptance by the Council on behalf of the town of the piece of sculpture. The Council are co- operating with the committee with the view of get- ting the statue placed alongside that of the Prince, and very soon the work will be completed. After this it is absurd to assert that Birmingham ie not loyal. Mr. E. Clarke, the member for Plymouth, has die- tinguished himself on more than one occasion by his attacks on the leaders of the Conservative party, of which he is aby no means insignificant member. He addressed his constituents at Plymouth on Wednesday, and of course he roundly abused the Government, which was to be expected, but he also took occasion to have another kick a: his leaders. Mr. Clarke cannot understand the leader of a political party, who, out of the House of Commons had declared the Egyptian war to be unjust and unnecessary, refusing to bring those al- legations to a debate in the House. Like Mr. Clarke, I Could not understand this conduct, but I scarcely think it is becoming in Mr. Clarke to twit his leader with his shortcomings. Mr. Clarke deplores the dual eontrol, which, he says, will not do for any political party, and that the leader must be in the House of Commons. Again, Mr. Clarke says the stsvesman who hitherto led the Conservative party in theLowerHouse has broken down under tremendous responsibility and work. This is damning Sir Stafford Northcote with faint praise; and seeing that he has for some time been worried with unprovoked annoyance from his followers, it is not surprising that his health, as well as his leadership, should break down.

I am inclined to think that after all there is some- thing in the rumour that England is desirous of being diplomatically represented at the Vatican. The Standard this week published two letters furnished by a gentleman who vouches for their authenticity, and their contents seem to point to some arrange- ment being come to. The letters are from Cardinal M'Cabe to Cardinal Jacobini, and from the latter to the former. The Viceroy of Ireland is introduced as snding to Cardinal M'Cabe a Mr. but whether the gentleman, whose name is blank, is Mr. Errington, does not transpire. D Jubtless, when Parlia- ment meets, there will be some more light thrown upon this subject. The latest rumour, however, is that the letters were never written.
FLACCUS.
RCTIcea•RN DRUNICARDS.—At the Runcorn Police Court yesterday, before Mr. .Thomas, Kate Leighton and John George were each charged with drunkenrkess, and fined 59 and costs.

Itt,--Ncom BRIDGE.—A "slope" has just .been erected at the Runcorn end of this bridge, and will; we under- stand, h put into use in the course of a fn, days. The incline is not, perhtzps, so great as. the slope at the Widnes side, and it will, no doubt, ba hail,: as a great 'Loan to the inhabitants.

THE SECOND COELHO OF VIE LORD.—OiI each Tuesday during the present month, commencing ea ruesday evening -next, lectures will be delivered in Raucorn Public Hall., on the above subject, by an evangelist. The former lec- tures, we believe, have been attended with some success. CAMDEN MUTFAL IMPROVEMENP CLASS, RUNCORN.— The fourth annual meeting of this class was held in Camden schoolroom on Monday evening. The room had been taste- fully decorated. About 120' members sat down to the tea which had been ,provided. At the subsequent proceedings, Mr. H. Randle, the president, occupied the chair, and de- livered a short address. Mr. Thomas Page, the secretary, read the annual report, after which the election of officers took place. Mr.'Randle was re-elected president; Mr. W. J. Shore, vice-president; and Mr. T. Page and Mr. W. Col- lier were appointed joint secretaries. The proceedings con- cluded with a pleasing entertainment. LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIBNT SHEETIERDS. ASHTON UNITY, WARRINGTON 'DISTRICT. The quarterly meeting di he district was held at the Rams Head Inn, on Monday last, P.G.S. James Parr presiding. The usual business having been gone throv.gh, a very interesting ceremony took place in the reesentation of a splendidly framed emblem of merit by P.P.C.S. Wm. Stirrup to P.P.C.S. Lawrence Gilloolrfor services rendered as Pro. Chief Shepherd for the years ; 1881-2. The presentation ,wasampported by ?.CS. 'James Parr, D.P.C.S. Peter Edgar, P.P.C.S. James Delooze, P.P.C.S. Lawrenee Weir, Pro. Cur. See. Abel H. Mather, and others. After a suitable reply by Bro. Gillooly, the meeting was brought to a close. BETHESDA CONEEEGATIONAL CHAPiL, RIINCORIL—The annual tea meeting of the nembers of this church was held in Bethesda schoolroom on Wednesday evening. There was a good attendance, and the after proceedings were presided over by the Rev J.D.. Thomas, the pastor. A report onthe Progress of church work and St. Luke's Mission was read, and considered very satisfactory. Mr. John Wilson read an able paper entitled" How can we retain our elder scholars," end the discussion which ensued was taken part in by Messrs. Beck, F. 'Fairhurst, G. Lacey' and others. A unanimous vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Faulkner and Mr. Wilson for their services in connection with ft. Luke's Mission, and also to the superintendents and teachers for their work in the Sunday school. The choir received a hearty vote of thanks for their voluntary services during the past year. PROPOSED NEW BAPTIST CHAPEL FOR WIDNES.— Like the Welsh Wesleyans the Baptists of Widnes find their place of worship located in an undesirable part of the town in consequence of an unexpected diversion of traffic, and like them, too, are desirous of worahipping their God in a more suitable and pleasant situation. They have earnestly set to work to raise a fund to enable them to realise this desire. A few weeks ago they held a successful concert in Lacey-street schoolroom, and on New Year's day they held a sale of work in Nelson-street Chapel, both having this object. The sale was of an unpretentious character, the goods to be dipsosed of being arranged on one stall, which was in charge of Mrs. Hingley, Calland, Baker, Davies, and Priestnall. A museum of curiosities under the management of Mr. T. Smith, and a galvanic battery in charge of Mr. Streets, proved very attractive. There was no formal opening ceremony, but the sale was, nevertheless, patronised by a large number of people during the afternoon. In the evening a tea meeting was held, and the -followirig ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs. Carey, senr., Mrs. Hingley, Mrs. Baker, Mrs. Gallant!, Mrs. Davies, and Mrs. P: iestnall. Subsequently a miscellaneous entertain- ment was given, Mr. G. E. Young, of Liverpool, presiding. , Under the conductorship of Mr. David James, the choir rendered several anthems in good style, while i'diss Davie and Miss Rylands sang a duet, which was cordially ap- plauded. Songs were also given by Mr. Eustace Carey, Mr. Taylor, dm The sale realized the sum of £l5, fully I meeting the expectation of the promoters. I KAY'S C 31f POrND, frr e awl On4h9. The Rev. S. B. Handley, of Stafford, (brother of Mr. , William Handley, of Runcorn), has successfully passed the intermediate examination for the degree of Bachelor of Music at the London University. - RUNCORN SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.-Mr. Wright. school attendance officer for Runcorn Union, progecuted , Thomas Furfie, Mary Whitby, and Robert Musker, for neg- lecting to send their children regularly to school, and a fine of 53. was imposed in each case. YESTERDAY'S WIDNES POLICE NEWS.— James Carroll, Thomas Smith, and Thomas Campbell were each fined 53 and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the pre- vious night.—Michael Henry and John Wilkinson, tramp, were each committed to gaol for seven days' hard labour, in a charge of begging on the previous day. LECTURE AT RUNCORN.—A lecture, illustrated by experi- ments, was held in St. John's Presbyterian School, on Wednesday evening, by Mr. John Leich. The subject was "The air we breathe," and it was treated in an interesting manner by the lecturer, who at the conclusion was warmly thanked. A collection was made in .aid of the school funds.

FINAL NOTICE.—After a stay of three months, Mr. Richard Lonsdale, ME., aenounces Saturday, January 13th. as positively the last day of his attendance at the Public Hall, Rylands-street, Warrington. His magnetaire appliances have worked some wonderful cures, as many of our towns- people can testify; and as this is the last opportunity of consulting Mr. Lonsdale in Warrington, all intending purchasers should call on him while they have the opportunity. RUNCORN ANNUAL DIVIDEND STOIC AND FURIAL SOCIETY. —The balance sheet of this society, which has just been published, shows that the total income has been £72 15s. 61., and after payment of sick and funeral expenses there remains a sum of £29 13s. 4d. to be divided amongst the members. At a meeting of the committee, held on Tues- day, it was decided that the society should hold its gather- ings at the Cocoa House in High-street, instead of in a public-house, as formerly. TEMPERANCE LECTURE AT WIDNES. A crowded audi ence gathered in the Widnes Volunteer Hall on Thursday evening, to hear a lecture on "Happy homes and how to make them," by the Rev. J. T. Madden, of Christ Church, Everton. The lecture was under the auspices of the Church of England Temperance Society, and the presi- dent, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, presided. The Star of Temperance brass band, under the conductorship of Mr. W. Jennett, gave a selection of music. At the con- clusion of the lecture 32 persons signed the pledge. GOOD TEMPLARY AT WIDNES.—The members of the Star of Widnes Lodge 1.0.G.T. gave an entertainment on Wed- nesday evening. Brother Johnson presided and delivered an address, and a varied programme was gone through by Brothers Johnson and Inglefield, and Sisters 'l'urton and Birkhall. On Tuesday evening an entertainment was given by the members of the Sunbeam Juvenile Temple 1.0.G.T. Songs were given by Brother Kirkham and Sisters Wendt, Summerbell, and Gough. Brothers Pace, Langdon, Wendt. Broderick, Kirkham, and Galilee, and Sisters Wendt, Taylor, and iinsley gave recitations. Brother J. Broderick presided. At the conclusion of the entertainment the "coffee supper" was provided, and heartily enjoyed. ROBBERY AT WESTON.--At Runcorn Petty Sessions, On Monday, Charles Eyes, a youth, was brought up, in custody, charged with having, on the 17th December, at Weston, stolen one ounce of tea, half a pound of sugar, half a pound of soap, two spoons, one knife, and a shoe lift, the property of William Cawley, waterman of Northwich.— The prosecutor is the owner of a small cabin at Weston Point. On the 16th ultimo, he loked it up and went to Northwich. On his return next morning he missed the articles enumerated, and gave information to the police. On New Year's eve, the prisoner was received in custody at Barnton by P.S. Blair, of Great Budworth. He then admitted that he had eomtnitted the robbery, along with Rnotb er youth, named Nugent, who at present is suffering two months' imprisonment for another offence.—The priso- ner was committed for trial at the next Knutsford Sessions.

CARRYING A GUN WITHOUT LICENSE.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, a young fellow named Thomas Gayer, was charged with having, on the 24th December, carried a gun without being in possession of a license authorising him so:to do.—P.S. Mac Michael said he saw the defendant carrying a single-barrelled gun in High-street, and he asked him to produce his license. The defendant replied that he had a license at home, and that be would show it to him if be would accompany him there. The sergeant went with the defendant as far as the Linn Hotel in Greenway-road, when the latter stated he would not show the license until he was compelled, and in reply to the wit- ness gave a wrong name and address. He afterwards cor- rected this statement, and admitted that he had no license. —Mr. Heal, supervisor of Inland Revenue, who pros'auted, addressed the Bench, who•fined the defendant 205., includ- ing costs.

PoICHNG NT MIMIC Runcorn Petty &scions, on Monday. before Mr. Wm. Bankes and Mr. John Brundrit, Wm. Jolley was charged with having, on the 25th Decem- ber, at Halton, searched for game with two lurcher dogs, without having a license to kill game; and he was further charged with trespassing on land in the occupation of Jno. Finch in search of game without the license or consent of the owner.—George Rigby, assistant gamekeeper, said that about eight o'clock on the morning of the day named, he saw the defendant on John Finch's land at Astmoor. He had with him two lurcher dogs, which were" whipping the field over." There was no footpath across the field. He excused kis conduct by saying that the dogs were to run a race on the following Saturday, and he was exercising them. —The Bench tined the defendant 203. and costs us. 61 in each case.

MAINTENANCS Or Sons rs REFORMATORIES.—Peter Harrop was summoned to appear at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to show cause why he should not pay the arrears of an order made upon him to contribute is. 6d. per week towards the support of his son, who is an inmate of Stockport Reformatory School. Mr. Superintendent Williamson said the boy was committed on the 11th August, 1879, and the defendant promised to pay is. Oct. towards his maintenance. He, however, only paid a few shillings, and on the 28th November, in accordance with instructions from the Inspector of Reformtories, Mr. Williamson obtained an order for is. 61 per week. Since that time he had neglected his paymet ts, and was £6 in arrear. The defendant, al though in full work, refused to pay. The Bench made an order of 155 per week upon the defendant, who did not appear.—Mr. I Superintendent Williamson applied for an order of is. per I week upon Soseph Wilson, whose son was sent to a 'reforma- tory on the sth February, 1681. The Bench made the

RUNCeRN FREE LIBRARY LECTURES.—The ruird Of the -series wts held in Bethesda school-room, on Thursday even- lug, but the audience which was present to listen to a dis- quisitien on the "Folklore of natural history," by Mr. Robert Holland, of Frodsharn, was oi so limited dimensions' that it could not fail to be discouraging to the promoters. Whether the. spares attendance was owing to impede.: advertising. or to the attraction of a ball which was held in another place, we are not in a position to determine, but-a gathering of 20 persons would scarcely be satisfactory to the lecturer, and would seem to show that the townspeot.le have no taste for literary lectures. There are yet several ether lectures arranged for, and it is to be hoped that some means may be taken that they may ettract the " mu- Aar ear." Dr. Steele, the.chairrnan of the Commissioners, occupied the chair on Thursday evening, and introduced Mr. Holism!, who delivered R most 'interesting lecture, in 'which he described the traditions and -superstitions attwehed to certain plants and animals of a century or two ago, men- tioning some which existed at the present time. He also related numerous superstitions believed in in Cheshire. A, vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Holland for his enter- taining lecture, on the motion of Mr. J. R Frith, seconded by Mr. William Handley, and a similar compliment haying been paid to the chairman, the meeting concluded. A STREET RIOT AT WIDNES. At Widnes Tolice Court, cn Monday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. John Brock, Wrn. Connor was charged with being drunk, and also with assaulting P.C.. Doodson whilst in the execution of his duty.—Patrick Knockton was charged with recisting P.C.'s Doodson and Snowdon at the same time and place.— From the evidence of the constables, it appeared that Con- nor, who was drunk, was acting in a disorderly manner in Dickson-street, on Saturday night. In consatiaence a large crowd of people assembled in the neighbourhood, and, when the constables took the offender into custody, a riot took place. Connor struggled to release himself, and he was aided in his efforts by a number of men, of whom the pri- soner Knockton seemed to be the moving spirit. Theetreet was in a perfect uproar for half an hour, at the end of which time the police succeeded in secnring their prisoners. —The prisoners met the charges by a blank denial, and a witness named Elizabeth Keogh -stated Knockton took no , part in the struggle.—lnspector Ilirnett observed that he re- garded an attempted rescue of this kind as worse than an ' ordinary assault, and pressed the charge against Knockton. —Connor, who had been several times previously convicted, was fined 10s. and costs, with the alternative of 14 days' imprisonment, and Knockton, was ordered to pay a fine of 20s. and costs, or go to gaol for a month.

, WESLEYAN METHODIST HAW-YEARLY MISSIONARY MEETING AT EARLESTOWN. - The half-yearly juvenile missionary meeting, in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Home and Foreign Missions, was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Cross-lane, on Sunday afternoon last. On account of this meeting the usual school lessons were dispensed with. After the meeting had been opened with singing and prayer, the Rev. J. M. Wamsley, of St. Helens (who presided), gave a brief though appropriate address. Mr. T. Newman afterwards addressed the meeting and spoke of the condition of England before Christianity was introduced into it, afterwards adverting to that event. He contrasted its condition then with what it was now, and alluding to a mottos on the wall of the school, "The Bible is the secret of England's greatness," pointed out how, since the Bible was brought into England, she had greatly risen and prospered. It was that Bible and it. truths they were sending to the heathens abroad, whom, he said, were in a similar condition to that of the inhabitants of our, own eluntry before we received the Bible. If it had done such great things for .us as a nation we had every reason to expect that it would do the same for every nation. Another hymn was then sung, and Mr. Pearson, of Prescot, gave an address. He alluded to the importance of unity amongst the children engaged in working and collecting for the society, and by several illustrations showed what mieit be accomplished thereby. He expressed his sympathy with the mission Cause, and encouraged the children in their lv renting numerous anecdotes. The meetier; thee Cem riLh ing aed the Bundle:ion.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending December 30th.—The mean temperature was 43.6 Fahrenheit, and therefore 4 9 degrees warmer than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 55 F. was recorded on the 29th inst. and the minimum temperature 23F. on the 24th inst. The rainfall measured 174 inches. The general direction of the wind was south. During the week, which was the 52nd of the current year, 33 births and 23 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was cqual to 28 per 1,000, against 18.2 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 33.4 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from whooping cough, 1 from premature birth, 5 from pulmonary consumption.—Eight cases of scarlet fever and two cases of entesic fever were reported under the require- ments of the Act of Parliament. JOHN H. GORNALL, medical officer of health. A -11.EGLECTFUL HUSBAND AT WARRINGTON. James Sykes was charged, on a warrant, at the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, before Captain Reynolds, and Messrs. John White and Ziba Armitage, with having, since the 30th March last, neglected to maintain his wife.—Mr. Rar- bourne, relieving officer, said the woman lived in Naylor- street, and endeavoured to earn her living by sewing. She was a very industrious woman, but suffered.from bronchitis, and the prisoner had left her without a bed to lie upon. The case was such a bad one, and the prisoner had been away so long, that the Guardiaas had had to offer a special reward for his apprehension.—The prisoner said that when he was in work he supported his wife, but unfortunately of late he had had very little work, and had scarcely been able to support himself, but if he got work he would pay the Guardians.—Mr. Harbourne said that he had not time to look through ale books before the case came on, but he thought the owing amount was £5O. The wife was re- ceiving ss. per week.—An order for 10s. a fortnight was made, the prisoner to pay 10a. down.

AN ELBLESTONIAN IN CUSTODY FOR DESSERTING HIS FAMILY.—At the Occasional Court House, Warrington, on Monday last, before S. Thewlis, Esq., Patrick Callaghan, a brickmaker, of Earlestown, was brought up on a charge of neglecting to maintain his wife and three children, who were then, and had been since the 23rd December, charge- able to the common fund of the Warrington Union. He now promised to pay the amount expended on his family at the rate of ss. per week, and he was thereupon discharged. PENERTH WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT AssoCIA- TION.—The members of the above association wet on Wed- nesday evening last, when a most interesting and instructive essay was read by the secretary, Mr. C. Parker, on "Charles Kingsley." The essayist dwelt at great length on Kingsley's life and character from infancy to the period of his death. The following members took part in the debate which fol- lowed :—Messrs. A. White, W. Craven, B. Hobson, It. E. Garnett, D. Garnett, Colin Cooke, and R. Garnett. After the essayist had replied, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to him as well as to the chairman. CHOIR ENTERTAINMENT AT CROFT.—The members of the choir of Christ Church, Croft, to the nunfoer of 27, were entertained by the Rev. T. P. and Mrs. Kirkman, at tEe Rectory, on Monday afternoo-. About five o 'clock the party sat down to tea, after which various games were in- dulged in. Several songs, glees, dm., were given during the evening in a most creditable m inner. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH- CONGREGATIONAL TEA PARTY.

I The annual Parish Church tea party was held in the i' National Schools, on Wednesday evening. There was a very large attendance. The donors of the trays were Mrs. Barclay, Mrs. C. Hazlekurst, Mrs. Brundrit, Mr. Lloyd Wigg, Mr. S. B. Chadwick, Mr. Briscoe, Mrs. Whittaker, Mrs. Lello, Mrs. Pownall, Mrs. Savage, Mrs. Imison, Mrs. Gorst, Mrs. Hampson, Mrs. Tonics, Miss Mack, Mrs. Barker, !Mrs. Crosby, and Miss Booth. Subsequently an entertain- tainment was held in the large school-room, which was well filled. The Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., vicar, occupied the chair, and amonst those present there were the Revs. J. J. Bryant, M.A., T. M. Ammon, R. Edwards, E. D. Garven (vicar of Bollington), Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., Mr. P. Briscoe, Mrs. John Brundrit, Mrs. Barclay, Miss Barclay, Mrs. Bryant, Misses Edwards, Mr. and Mrs. Lello, Mr. and Mrs. Whittaker, Misses Hazlehurst. During the evening a programme of vocal and instrumental music was performed with great credit. The performances by the band were greatly enjoyed, and the singing of the choir was met with much favour. Miss Pierpoint gave a pleasing rendering of the song "Come to me 0 la 7 children," and she was encored. Miss Jukes gave a. pianoforte solo in a manner 1 which showed delicacy of touch. and fine taste, while Mr. 1 R. W.Pierpoint received a merited encore for his perfor- mance on the cornet. Mr. Johnson presided at the pianoforte. The CHAIIIMIN, in opening the proceedings, expressed the hope that the year which had just begun would prove to everyone of them a prosperous one both in mind, body, and soul. He thanked the audience for their attendance, and also for many acts of personal kindness he had re- ceived during the past year, as well as parochial exertions, especially for those exertions made by all classes, and he might say all denominations in connection with the bazaar which was held in summer. It was a matter of which the Parish Church congregation might congratulate themselves on achieving such a magnificent result. (Applause.) He trusted that their exertions in the past would not be dis- continued, but if ever there happened to be occasion for it, he should experience from them the same good feeling and hearty co-operation which he had received for 37 years, which had seen wonderful changes in the cengregation and in the parish. He expressed the great obligations he and the congregation were under to the churchwardens and , sidesmen for the regular and efficient services they had per- formed, and he asked the audience to show their apprecia- tion by giviug a hearty round of applause, which was ' accorded with enthusiasm.

The Rev. J. J. BRYANT moved that a vote of thanks be given to the lay readers of Newtown and the Parish Church, to the district visitors, to the Sunday school teachers, and all who had engaged ie any spiritual work during the past year. Some of them might know that Macaulay, in one of his striking essays, put very clearly before his readers a charge which had been again and again repeated against the English Church. He showed that the English Church, like the Romish Church, was unable to employ the enthusiasm of laymen. The general lay opinion now-a-days was that there was no active interest for them in the Church, but the en- thusiasm, if it could b 3 called enthusiasm, which desired publicity was of the lowest kind, and certainly much lower than the enthusiasm of the individual who could work quietly and effectively on lines that were far from public. Since Macaulay's time the Church had aroused from ha legarth, ; she had provided means for the enthusiasm of lay- men, wherever he.was disposed to do the work of the Church. (Applause.) The moticn was carried with acclamation. The E. D. GARVEN proposed, in a humourousspeech, a vote of thanh,..) Mr. W. John Brundrit, the treasurer of the Additional Carat., Fund, the Penny Bank, and New- town Mission School, and sir. Whitaker, the treasurer of the National School.
The vote was cordially carried, an,. Mr. JOHN BRUNDILIT, in reply, advent,. ,o the work of the Penny Bank, which he said was doing ...,%lculable work in the town.

• The Rev. T. ARDISON, in appropriate terms, moved a voti. of thanks to the organist (Mr. Johnson), to the choir, to the bellringers, and to the vocalists and instrumentalists who had contributed to the evening's entertainment; and it was heartily accorded. The Rev. E. D. GARVIN then rose, and offered to Canon Barclay and his family, on behalf of the audience, every wish and every blessing during the coming year. He was sure there was no parish that had been presided over for 37 years, with such attention, diligence, and skill as Runcorn had been. Runcorn had grown beyond, perhaps, the reach of one man, and far beyond Canon Barclay's idea of what it would grow when he first acaepted the charge, and he thought it spoke volumes in his favour, as regarded his ministry amongst them that he had, notwithstanding the divers elements thrown in his midst, kept the grand old church and her service in that state, dignity, and glory, which was, he believed, the pride of the whole people of Runcorn. (Loud applause.) The Rev. Canon BARCLAY, in reply, said it was true—he did not say it in a boastful spirit, but he thought Runcorn bad something to boast of—that Runcorn Parish Church was the first church in the deanery, if not in the diocese, which was then much larger than it was now, to have a solemn dignified musical service. He believed they were , the first to set the example of decorating for Christmas in a decent and comely manner, and not as it used to be, a kind of sprie,•,7,-spriggy, but with some attention to taste and decorum. He congratulated the people of Runcorn on the harmony which had for so many years existed between pastor and people. He could only say that any good which had been done could not have been done by one man, but it required the efforts of a good, willing, energetic, staff to bring the services to the pitch of perfection at which they had arrived; and therefore he felt thankful to the audience not only for receiving the proposition so kindly, but for the valuable help they had always afforded in anything to pro- mote the welfare and prosperity of the parish. The proceedings then terminated.

TIIE REF. W. PRESTON ON TURKEY'S DOWNFALL. . The Rev. W. Preston, M.A., delivered the fifth of his series, of Sunday evening sermons on Prophecy, in Holy Trinity Church, on New Year's Eve. He said he desired to set. before the congregation one more visible token that the end draweth nigh. They would remember how the angel told Daniel that after the Roman Beast, or empire had passed away, two separate powers represented by little horns should arise—these being the Western or Papal, and Eastern or Mahomedan Powers. The former was to hold sway for 1,260 years. Its temporal dominion had passed away, and so the period which marked the times of the Gentiles was rapidly ending. The duration of the second or Mahomedan power was equally foretold, and to that he directed atten- tion. In the apocalypse the rise of the Ottoman power was likened to the overflow of the river Euphrates and from the banks of the Euphrates did come those terrible horsemen who carried woe and death over Eastern Christendom. In the language of the angel this power had "destroyed wonderfully," and had kept in check "the holy people." Rome overthrew Jerusalem, but Turkey kept her foot on her neck. Rome destroyed the temple, and Turkey had there erected now the Mosque of Omar, where no Jew dare go.. Rome cast the people down to the (Net, but Turkey kept them in the mire; and the fruitful land was cursed by his presence. Pagan Rome which did the first had disappeared, ond Papal Romei which followed had lost her temporal power, ,as it was foretold should happen and Turkey, the Eastern little horn, has its day too, and likewise must disappear. The question was How long is this afflicting power to last? They got the reply "Unto 2,300 days ;" that was 2,300 years. They must remember that the question and answer of the text took place at a time when the daily sacrifice had ceased, for the Jews were in captivity; hence the prediction implied a national restoration, during which the predicted 2,300 years took their starting point. The earliest starting point was the decree of Artaxerxes, which permitted the Jews to restore or rebuild Jerusalem. This was in 457 8.C., and 2,300 years counted from that date brought them to 1844, when, for the first time since the days of Mahommed, the Sultan of Turkey was compelled by Europe to grant religious tolera- tion in his dominions. From that time there had been going on quietly a restoration of the Jews to Palestine. Turkey was fast losing power, and every diminution of it was a sten towards the complete cleansing of the Sanctuary, and full restoration of the Jews. Mr. Preston referred to two other periods which might be taken, and said the period that had so far elapsed since the middle of the 18th century, which closed the 2,520 years. the time determined by God for the existence of the Gentile supremacy over Israel had been most conspicuously marked by the de- cline of the two little horns, the Mahometan and the papal, the last forms of supremacy over Israel. literal and spiritual, and it yeas noticeable that years of crises to the one bad been marked by years of trouble to the other. Since the complete fall of David's throne 2,520 years had, and not as yet, fully run out. They were swiftly doing so, and events around proved this. The great event which terminated " the times of the Gentiles" was the personal coming of Christ, who would restore the throne of David and reign thereon during a period of millennial blessedness, after which the great white throne should be set, the books opened, mankind judged, and "they who have done evil shall go into the resurrection of damnation;. but they who have done good into life everlasting."

ALLEGED ROBBERY BY • WORE:NUN AT ST. HELENS. —On Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, Michael Norton was charged on remand with having broken into the office of the Globe Alkali Works, and stolen therefrom some time books.—lt appeared that on the evening of Saturday, the 23rd Deeengber, an officer, who is specially, retained by the Alkali Company, was on duty near the office window, from which he saw a man jump out. He recognised the man as being the prisoner, who was a boilerman employed at the works. Prisoner, on seeing the officer, ran, but dropped the'books, and although the officer shouted a him by name to stop and said that he knew him, continued to run across some waste lead. The officer thereupon went to where the prisoner worked, and concealed himself. On Norton coming in he apprehended him, and brought him to the police office.—Mr. Riley, who prosecuted on behalf of the Globe Alkali Company, asked the Bench to commit the prisoner to the sessions, which, alter Mr. Swift; who defended, had spoken fur the defence, was done, bail being refused, as prisoner had been previouslY convicted for similar offences.

TREATS TO THE POOR. Sir,—lt is a pleasure to notice the success which always attends the annual treat for aged men and women, but it does appear to me that the excellent committee which mana- ges this undertaking might very properly extend its benefi- cent work by providing an annual treat for poor children. We must have hundreds of children in Warrington who know nothing of the joy and gladness which Christmas brings to the majority of homes, and to whom a treat would afford intense delight. Why not incorporate with the old people's treat one for these poor children? I have had conversa- tions with many who would willingly contribute to a fund for such a purpose, and I would respectfully suggest to the committee to give the matter their consideration. The expense for providing a tea for 1,000 children need not exceed twenty pounds, including hall expenses. How small an amount for so great a boon! I suppose it will be considered too late this season to commence such an undertaking; still lam convinced that should the committee prefer not to mews in this direction that there are many others in War- rington who another year will gladly assist in carrying out so deserving an object.—l am, sir, yours respectfully, WM. ROBERTS. 7, Suez-street, Warrington, January 4th, 1883.

COUNTY MAGISTRATES: WHO APPOINTS THEM? Sir,—l read with considerable surprise the intimation which appeared in your issue of Saturday last with reference to the above. At the outset permit tie to say that I have not the slightest personal objection to either of the aentle- men whose names were mentioned—my objections being entirely on public grounds. Of Mr. Armitage, I can speak with nothing but respect ; his conduct and judgement as a borough magestrate is above criticism; and I have only to say that he is comparitively a young man, and could well have afforded to have taken his turn after some men who have been in the public service for a much longer period had received due recognition. In reference, however, to the second gentleman (Mr. Marson) I cannot for the life of me understand what were the reasons which recommended ""i to those who sent in his nomination. It has been ecedent for many years past to confer these positie-' upon .men who i have been more or less remarkahl or their ability and r..-aess, and I, up to the pre- sent, am entirely ignoran' assiduous attention to public the. services which entitle Mr. Matson to such „r•stin.ction—in addition to which he ' is and has been some time a magistrate for Cheshire. On reflect • . when one considers the names of some of the ,- •-auential and devoted of our public men, who, up to 4 present time have been ccmpletely ignored, one cannot help thinking that some sinister motive, equally contemp- tible and injudicious, has actuated some, at least, of those in whose hands the nominations originally rest. If this be the case the sooner those who led themselves to such , practices are brought to the bar of public opinion and thoroughly exposed, the better it will be for society generally. That such a thing should be possible as that two or three local magistrates should, of their own sweet will, be able to ignore completely the claims of men of high social pAition and integrity, and instead, to substitute their personal friends, is an outrage upon the rights of the public. I earnestly hope that the people of Warrington will not allow these men who have served them well and faithfully for years past to be completely thrust aside in order that family and private interest may be gratified.—Yours truly, PROMOTION BY MERIT.

div.head: "NEWTONIAN" AND " ANGLO-SCOTUS."
div.p: "NEWTONIAN" AND " ANGLO-SCOTUS."

Sir,—"A gnid New Year I wish thee l—and Anglo- Scotus,' " and all your gentle readers, and may you have many happy returns of this day and festive season, which many, both Scotch and English, are keeping with the ardour of Frenchmen, to whom it is also a peculiar day. Far be the thought from U 9 to seek to draw " Anglo- Scotus " over sea after us, or to tempt him into any of those devious ways which he has devised for us in his latest letter to you. Let him only look upon the reverse or obverse side of a coin of this realm, struck in the reign of one of the Georges, and he may read the significant words, " Honi Boit qui maly pence," and remember the word of Scotia's bard, with some of which we began this epistle. "Then gently scan your brother man, and gentler still your sister woman." Tile piquant example he gives of quaint signboards is quite sufficient to satisfy us that his knowledge of this kind of pictorial art and literature is con- siderable, if not quite perfect. Will he believe it, after see- ing the "Lapin qui fume," we came home by way of Calais and passed the fort called "Lapin," the smoke of the guns of which may have suggested the sign to some retired warrior, and Lapin may have suggested the name of the fort to the authorities at the War Office, for there is a rabbit warren along that shore. But what " Lap " means no man yet knoweth or showeth, being like a "lap" stone, a hard nut to crack. Yes, he may say, this may be all very true, but I am free to doubt its accuracy, so we maybe permitted to doubt the accuracy of the derivation of "pig and whistle" frern "pige-washail," although we have seen it in print before. For, while it is quite true that " pig,e " is the present Danish word for girl, maid, or lass, the word pig in the same language means, among other things, a quill of the hedge-hog, so . the idea of " pig " or " hog " remains. Moreover, the Danish word piher, if we must have it to be Danish, means a pipe or whistle, so the piping-pig might be made out of the first word alone. But this won't de, for " Anglo-Scotus " says he thinks it is "Our Lady's" salutation because of the (Anglo) Saxon word washail, and prefers to take the religious view rather than the secular, which we should prefer, with what he calls our usual inconsistency, if there were no other view of the matter, than those he points out; for while we find "Hail" in his lerte,hail we fail to find. " Mary " in his pige, for of course he is talking of Roman Catholic Englana when pe talks of Our Lady's Salutation. By a slight twist we conld of course find "Peggy," the diminutive of Margaret, i.e., "a pearl" in pigs, but that would reduce the matter to an absurdity. The common version of the Bible has it thus: "And the angel cetne in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women." At this time of the year, when there is so much indiscriminate drinking going on, it would be odd if we did not think when writing on this subject of the pipes of wine drunk in England in the olden time, and being a lineal descendant of one of the original Staffordshire potters we are reminded of the fact while eating our New Year's Day dinner off a platter with some of the initials in our own name, a hundred years old at least, and lead to think of the pipkins our ancestors made; but neither will this derivation do, for while a pipe was a barrel, a pipkin was a pot, and there must be a clear line of descent or the reasoning will fail altogether. Bat we turn, as we often can do, to our in- variable and trustworthy authority, Bishop Wilkins, 1638, who says pipe means a barrel, and that " piggin " is the diminutive of tub, while pipkin means an earthenware vessel in the diminutive, and that wasseil means a country banquet, and that the word was in common English use in his day (1688), at the time of the Restoration. Now, if we are not egregiously mistaken, the two common English words " pig- gin-wassail " gave rise to the three English words "pig and whistle," for all this time the conjunctive word "and" has been deftly left out of the account, and it remains to be ac- counted for. " Anglo-Scotus," while in Newton, may have rambled so far as Croft Well. There is the sign of the word "noggin," a word remarkably like " piggin," and still in use in Scotland, if not in England, and a wooden vessel withal. Moreover, public-houses, as we understand them, were only instituted and legalised in the time of King James I. of England, so Bishop Wilkins, writing within the century in which King James died, would be likely to know that the Dano-Saxen language had given way to a language not very far removed from that used in the common version of the Bible, which became our standard of English. At any rate, we prefer to think that the early publicans, like proper licensed victuallers, exhibited a foaming tankard with an invitation to partake of their good cheer, rather than any far-fetched symboliere. As for the unfortunate word wassail, it is gradually but surely _giving way before the word " wesley," for on Christmas Dal, we head a carter tingin a refrain of " A weeleSsin' we wilt g ll go," "A weSle we will go." " A nglo-Scotns " bewails our degenerarellanguage, And will not have a "free fight," although it .appeared in the Daily Yews a few days after we used it of -bine' and were rebuked, we might have said "in the thick of the fight," because somebody had used it before our time, and somebody else had gone and put it into a dictionary, so it bad a respectable appearance, and had been seen in good society—and now befalls foul of us for saving that a bridge " sits," which, he says, he never heard' of before. Bridgee "span," " cross " are ." thrown acrose," " ath wart" over, but never "sit." This is rather hard on us, for we were trying to be precise and particular, and imagined we were rather poetic when we personified a neuter verb, but all to no purpose. The thing hadn't been done before, so far as he knew, so he thinks it peculiar, and so it is if we cannot Use a living language to express living thoughts. The new coroner may next be told that he must not" sit" On any case; but there is precedent for that, but not for this, it seems. Seven of the nine arches of the Viaduct seem to stride over the land, while two vault over the canal and brook. To make " plim " is part of the businese of a

" plumb "line, but as it is not put into dictionaries any more than the declensions of the four thousand three hun- dred and odd verbs of the English language, it won't do for him. Apropos narrowly escaped censure, because it was placed after a full point, but should have been written at twice. Landscape should have been like the bridge, a land " strip," all of which and every new blunder of ouns he will perhaps kindly class in future under the head of synchysis, the beautiful rule of grammar, which embraces every blunder in thought or speech which cannot be reduced to rule by grammarians, but is under- standable by the common intelligence. This synchysis literary means confusion or conmixtion ; and, in grammar, is significant only .of some poetical jumble of words, some verbal kink or snarl, which cannot be gram- matically resolved or disentangled ; as, in Butler's poems, p. 161: "An ass with his long ears fray The tiles that tickle him away; But man delights to have his ears Blown maggots in by flatterers."

" Anglo-Scotus " may say this is another "Tale of a tub." Now with regard to the grammatical part of this .same "'its." The two verbs to sit and to set are in general quite different in their meaning; but the passive verb, to be set, sometimes comes pretty near to the sense of the former, which is for the most part neuter. Hence, we not only find the Latin word sedes—to set—used in the sense of being set, as, Ingens ecena sedct, a huge supper is set (Jno. 2, 119), but with reference to the personal posture of' sitting, for Dr. Bishop Lowth following Dr. Bishop Wilkins at a distance of a hundred years, contends that there is no such thing in English, nor indeed in any language, as a sort of verbs, which are really impersonal, which ought to be sufficient, as being the opinion of one of the first Royal Academicians, and one of our greatest grammarians—to be candid, it is a little fatiguing to have to descend to quibble so often.— Tours, Arc., January 1, 1333. div.p: LY.1131 LOCAL BOARD.

A monthly meeting of this Board WAS held in the Board- room, en Thursday evening. Present : Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Dewhurst, Rogers, Bayley, Forste, Gibbon, Dr. Fox (medical officer), Ridgway (clerk), and Mullard (assistant clerk).

div.head: ILLNESS OF THE SURVEYOR.
div.p: ILLNESS OF THE SURVEYOR.

The CHAIRMAN stated that there would be no surveyor's or nuisance inspector's report owing to the illness of the surveyor.—Mr. GIBBON said the Highway Committee had been round, and they found all the men working according to the surveyor's orders. A sewer had broken in at Top- lane, and some of the men had been ordered to repair it. FOWLER'S PATENT SELF-ACTING CLOSET TAP.

The CHAIRMAN said Dr. Fox, Mr. Appleton, and he bad visted Longton in order to inspect the system of Fowler's patent self-acting closet tap, and they had had the advan- tage of the guidance of the borough surveyor, who had gone round with them and shown them everything. As far as he could judge the success of the system mentioned depended upon the water supply. If adopted at 1 ymm, the alterations that would have to be made would, roughly speaking, cost about £2 per closet. It was a question as to whether they had a sufficient water supply.— Dr, Fox said that in the new system they would have a larger supply of water than in the case of the ordinary water closet, as all the water used in the house would go to flush the soil pipe, whilelin the other case only about two gallons were used. Referring to the visit, he said that they went to the Town Hall, and were very court eously intro- duced to the Mayor, who placed the Borough Surveyor at their service. He came away very fav,aurablv impressed with the new ?ystem, and he thought it would in a decided advantsge if introduced into Lvmm.—Mr. DEWHURST suggested the system be first attached to one block of houses, as an experiment; and the subject was then allowed to drop with the understanding that an experiment be tried. This was all the business of public interest.
