great deal to be thankful for to the Mayor and Corporation, and the corporate officials. They could spend their money admirably, they could collect their taxes—(hear, bear)--- and they could do everything they thought necessary. Although they were a very mixed Council, he verily be- lieved that every one of them did his very best for the town, and therefore they ought to be very thankful to the Corporation. He had pleasure in proposing the toast. (Applause.) Councillor MONIES, who responded, said he was sorry the Mayor was not present that night. He was sure if his Worship had been present he would have done full justice to the toast. However, he could assure Major Cartwright it gave the Council very great pleasure to collect all they could from him, and spend it as freely as he wished. But he thought he would find' if he looked at the accounts, the money was well spent, and while he did not claim that the Council made no mistakes nor spent money rather foolishly —because he believed they did—he thought, on the whole, they would admit the work of the Corporation was very well done. If the burgesses of Warrington would continue to send to the Council a body of men equal to the present members, he was quite sure they would have no cause to regret it. (Hear, hear.) It was always gratifying to those who were in office to feel that their efforts were somewhat appreciated. They did not always get the thanks of their fellow towns- men, and in this instance he could only say that they had a just appreciation of their work, and if they had been able to carry on the work of the town satisfactorily in the past he thought they would have no cause of complaint in the future. (Applause.) Mr. W. PORTER gave The trustees of the Blue Coat School." He said the trustees were a body of gentlemen of whem they as Old Blues and inhabitants of the town bad every cause to be proud. They administered a trust by which some hundreds of the poor of the town had been fed, clothed, and educated, and as one of the recipients of the benefits of that trust he felt it no mean honour to be allowed to stand there and thank the trustees for the benefits received at their hands whilst an inmate of the institution ; and he was sure he expressed the sentiments of every Old Blue, whether boy or girl, when he said their debt to the trustees they could never repay. (Applause.) He concluded by expressing his regret at the death of one of their trustees, and also of the head- master, Dr. Bowes, whose memory they cherished. Mr. W. S. BURGESS, in supplementing Mr. Porter's remarks, hoped the trustees would be able to extend the charity, and that others might be able to share in the benefits and blessings they had received from the charity. He trusted they might ba long spared to manage the school and administer the trust as they had done. He coupled with the toast the name of the chairman.

The PRESIDENT, in replying, observed that there were not so many trustees present, but he thought they would be satisfied that the best-looking of them were there that night. (Laughter.) There was no doubt the trustees had a very serious trust in their care. (Hear, hear.) For many years the trust had been carried on well by the trustees, and there was no doubt the present trustees were quite prepared to fulfil their duties. He trusted that Mr. Rose would fulfil the duties he was called upon to fill as well as that man who went before him. He assured them that dear John Bowes, who was so long the master of the Blue Coat School, not only did his work well, but with a loving regard and affection that seemed to command the sympathy, respect, and he might say the entire love of the children under his care. About 28 years ago lie well recollected Mr. Bowes came to him at Bank Quay and told him what good the Liverpool Brotherly Society was doing, and suggested the desirability of establishing a similar society. The result was the formation of that society, which he was proud to say uas still living. He did not know that they could expect the society to increase in numbers, because they had not the same number of scholars as formerly; but he was quite satisfied the young men he had seen, although fewer in number, would well sustain the Blue Coat Bretherly;Society. (Applause.) Mr. W. Routrisox also responded, remarking that the trustees commenced the work, and it remained for that society to finish it, and Like care of those who had left the school. '

"The town and trade of Warrington" was the next toast, proposed by Mr. T. Moanes. Mr. H. B. WIRTH then gave "The Warrington Blue Coat Brotherly Society." It was impossible, he said, in dealing with the toast, to avoid glaneeg at the great loss the society had sustained by the death of its late president. Twelve months ago they assembled together, and were all sad with the knowledge that the president was lying on a bed of sickness. They had a hope that he might be spared to pre- side at other meetings, but that hope was gone, and they could only deal with his memory. He was quite satisfied the society was a most valuable supplement to the institu- tion itself, and he thought the success of young men who had been trained in the school was in every way as mush dependent upon the operations of that society as it was in their school days. lea Mr. W. J. Fonsnaw (the hon. sec.), in acknowledging the toast, said beyond the benefits given by the school itself it was very necessary that some Blues should have further assistance after leaving the institution, and that further assistance was afferded by the Warrington Blue Coat Society, the 23th birthday of which they commemorated that night. It must be a source of satisfaction to know that the society was still prospering. If it was not for the society they would find that the majority of old Blues would want the means to put to good account the education they had received at the insti- tution. Just consider for a moment the position of a boy who, at the early age of 14, was thrown upon the world— without father, without mother, and almost without a friend. They knew it was impossible at so early an age for a lad to earn a livelihood for himself, and it was then the society was of most use to him, not only by its pecuniary aid, but by the parental aivice and kind sympathy given by those who had experienced the same difficulties. (Hear, bear.) It might be, too, that some, after a few years' steady performance of the duties devolving upon them, in their various station's in lif4, would have opportunities of rising to positions of fortune and honour, but lacked the means, and the society at this stage lent it to enable them to obtain such positions. The society was ever willing to give all Old Blues who required it and who were deserving of it, all the assistance in their power, and counsel and support in their difficulties. So far as the society was concerned, he thought they had during the past year thoroughly per- formed their duties, and had endeavoured to carry out their benevolent objects, and they earnestly hoped all Old Blues and everybody interested in the welfare of the society, would continue to give them that approbation and support which was so richly deserved. (Applause.) The other toasts were " Kindred societies," proposed by Mr. ROSE, and responded to by Mr. CROSIER; "Our old friends, the Sisterly Blues," proposed by Mr. J. ALLEN ; " The Press," proposed by Dr. WHITE, responded to by Councillor MacKIE ; and "The Chairman," proposed by Mr. PERCIVAL.
The proceedings concluded with the singing of :the National Anthem. BLUE COAT SCHOOL.

The annual tea and entertainment in connection with these schools was held on Tuesday, when about 120 persons partook of an excellent tea. Many Old Blues, both male and female, were present, and Mr. Rose, the master, enter- tained his guests admirably. The evening was spent in a very enjoyable manner. Dancing and games were freely indulged in, while songs and recitations were given by the scholars, and the band performed several selections of music. Amongst the gentlemen who were present and took part in the entertainment, might be mentioned Mr. Ankland, Mr. J. Whittaker, Mr. N. B. Percival, Mr. Vernon, Mr. W. J. Forshaw (hon. sec:), Mr. William Porter, and Mr. Charles Bowes.

div.head: NEW YEAR CELEBRATIONS.
div.p: NEW YEAR CELEBRATIONS.

In dull damp weather similar to that of Christmas Eve, the New Year was ushered in at Warrington by the merry ringing of bells in the several church towers in town, and the interchange of greetings between those who had attended the Watch Night services held in both churches and chapels. As the last day of the old year fell on Sunday the midnight services were largely attended, there being crowded congregations at most of the places of worship, where appropriate sermons were preached. New Year's Day was observed as a holiday by the workpeople, large numbers of whom paraded the prin- cipal streets in holiday attire. Many proceeded by train to the neighbouring cities to witness the performances of the panto- mimes, and those who remained in town bestowed their patronage on the local places of amusement, or found en- joyment at the congregational gatherings held in the even- ing. Most of the tradespeople opened their establishments, but business was so slack that many had put up their shut- ters by noon, and the remainder followed their example soon afterwards. Rain fell at biter- vals during the day, and the strong wind that pre- vailed made the weather anything but pleasant for the plea- sure seekers. An account of the celebrations, which have been continued during the week, will be found below.
WARRINGTON BLUE COAT BROTHERLY SOCIETY. ANNIVERSARY DINNER.

The members of the Warrington Blue Coat Brotherly Society celebrated the 28th anni,:ersary of the society by a dinner, which was held at the Lion Hotel, on New Year's Day. There was a very good attendance of members and friends. Alderman Joseph Davies presided, and he was supported by Mr. W. Robinson, Dr. White, Alderman Webster, Major Cartwright, Councillor Monks, Mr. P. Davies, Councillor Mackie, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. E. St. A. Duke, Mr. H. B. White, Councillor Sutton, and Mr. T. Morris. There were also present Messrs. N. B. Percival E. Aukland, E. Rose, W. Porter, W. J. Forshaw (hon. sec:), G. Shaw, Emmerson, Rnncorn, Gleave, Barnes, Wilcock, Rathbone, J. Smith, G. Roughlev, P. Morris, T. Clare, J. Podmore, W. Porter, J. Whittle, T. Whittaker, G. Vernon, W. S. Burgess, G. Crosier, John Burgess, T. S. Burgess, W. Perkins, J. Short, J. Povey, R. Hewitt, J. Toft, Dainteth, A. Deeley, J. Allen, and I'. Lane. After dinner, The Hon. SECRETARY said he had received letters from several gentlemen expressing their regret at not being able to be present, and wishing the gathering every success. Amongst them were letters from Lord Winmarleigh, the Mayor (Councillor Crostield), Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., Sir G. Greensll, and Alderman Pickmere. The Hon. SECRETARY then read the following report:—

The committee have to express the great pleasure they feel in meeting the pstrons, friends, and members of the society, and in presenting them with the twenty-eighth annual reporf. The objects for which the society was originally eor.- stituted have been steadLy kept in view during the past years, n d timely and friendly help has been rendered to many, who thus encouraged have been spurred to renewed exertions in the arduous struggle of life. Its operations during the past year are marked by no new feature, hut have been of the same useful character as hitherto. The society continues to assist those younger members who need assistance. It has done its duty in counselling and supervising those who have lately left the school, and in every way possible promoting the welfare of those under i s care, and the committee believe and trust that their efforts have been generally appre- ciated. The e anmitlee lament that the soc ety has, during the past year, lost its late president and one of its bests friends. Tne mere mention of the name of John Bowes will arouse in the hearts of every member of the Warrington Blue Coat Brotherly Society, sentiments of the warmest sympathy and affection for departed worth. In silence they recall his name and cherish his memory. It is also with the deepest regret that they have to record the death of Mr. George Artingstall, one cf its patrons and a trustee of the institution. The com- mittee are pleased to announce that they have prevailed upon Mr. Aiderman Davies to act as their future president, and they feel assured that under his supervlsi n they will be enabled to carry on the society as successfully in the future as they have done in the past. The treasurer's statement of accounts is of a satisfactory character, there being a balance in the savings Bank of £6O after satisfying all claims. The balance sheet will be distributed amongst the subscribers in a few weeks. The committee again repeat that great en- couragement would be afforded them by a more general co- operation of those who are indebted for their education and training either as day scholars or Batse to the institution, and who as yet have not bee >me members of the society. In con- Nusion, the committee beg to offer in the name of the society their warmest thanks to the t, ustees of the Blue Coat isch,ol for the r constant and valuable support, and they take this op- portunity of wishing all present a happy and pr,sperous new year. (Applause.) The PRESIDENT announced that he also had received let- tars of apology for non-attendance from Captain Nicholson and Captain Ridgway. The PREmIDENT then gave the toasts "Ties Queen whom God preserve," and "The Prince and Princess of Wales, and the rest of the Royal family," which were duly honoured.

Alderman WEBSTER said he had been entrusted with a toast, which he should proceed to submit for their accept- ance, and he was quite certain they would receive it with all the honour with which it was possible they could do. At- tachment to the Church of England had always been a cha- racteristic of the Warrington Blue Coat School—(hear, hear) —and the aim and object of all the masters and teachers he had known in connection with it had been to further the principles and doctrines of that church. Under these cir- cumstances they would not at all wonder that Lie should submit to them the toast of -" The Church," and he coupled with it also the Bishop and clergy of the diocese. In War- rington they were, he thought, singularly happy in the clergymen that they had amongst them—(hear, hear)—and if he might do so, he would also couple with the toast the other ministers of religion. (Hear, hear.) There seem:d to h m to be harmony amongst them which, if anything could further the progress of religious feeling, be thought was eminently calculated to do that. They saw in many other places heart-burnings of various of sorts which were very lamentable, but in Warrington, fortunately, they were free from that. The clergymen, he thought, almost without exception, were earnest in their endeavours to further the good cause of religion, and coupled with it also that of edu- cation ; and he thought there was no question they were eminently successful. They had, as he said before, none of those heart burnings, all seemed to be working together for good ; they were putting their shoulders to the wheel, and using their very best endeavours to produce the very best effects. (Applause.) The toast having been drunk, .

_ The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON responded. He said he looked upon the Blue Coat School as certainly a monument to the Church's interest in the matter of education. These institutions carried their minds back to a very early period in our history when education was generally promoted upon a system somewhat different to that upon which it was pro- moted at the present day. In the good old days he thought there was very often little talk about education, but those responsible for the welfare of their country looked upon it very much as a duty to take the work of education in hand. They said little about it, but what they did was none the less effectual. (hear, hear.) Under the shadow of their old church grew up their universities with their colleges and endowed schools, public schools, grammar schools, and such schools as that they were doing_honour to that even- i ing. He felt sure that those institutions were after all the 1 backbone of the best education that was being given throughout the length and breadth of the land—(hear hear); and he thought churchmen could look with a feeling of pride upon those monuments of the generosity and piety of their ancestors. There was very little talking and fighting about education. Men quietly put their hands in their pockets and established endowments and various other funds, and in that way the work was done. During the last 50 years education had been promoted on a somewhat dif- ferent system ; at least, fresh interest had been aroused in the question, and it was necessary fresh interest should be aroused. Of course in this new movement the church had not been behindhand, but he wished to draw attention to the different mode in which they tried to promote educa- tion. Whereas wider one system men put their hands in their pockets as a matter of duty to make the provision neces- sary for the wants of the people, on the other hand our modern educationists, who were very enthusiastic and gained a great deal of eclat, thought they had fully dis- charged all claims upon their liberality and their public spirit if they carefully levied a rate .upon the district and I took care that that rate was judiciously expended in leducation. He thought it was well, in fairness to the old Churcl!., which was always first to move in the matter of e(bleation, that they should bear this in mind. He did not A wish to disparage what had been done of late years, be- cause possibly it was a necessity', but he thought it was well to compare the two systems ; and when people came to look upon what he might call the church system and no church system they would come to the conclusion that the church system did not come very badly out of the ordeal. He thought there was a bright future for the Church. He felt sure it was growing more and more in strength, and he thought all chuechmen during the last few days would have been animated with hope by the excellent appointment that bad been made in the translation of Bishop Benson to the archbishopric of Canterbury. It was a great thing for them to have a man who commanded the confidence of all sections of the Church, and he looked to his rule with great expectation knowing it would be car- ried on for a number of years, as he was not far advanced in life. (Applause.) Councillor MACKIE, in proposing "The army, navy, and reserve forces," remarked that the English constitution was supported, there was no doubt, by the strength of the ariny, navy, and reserve forces, and it was gratifying to know that during the late little war, which, if it was a war at all, re- dounded much to the credit of both men and o'fficers, the great men associpted with the town were all in favour of giving that support to the Government, without which the Government would have found it a heartless task indeed. There had been such noble traits shown in connection with war, that they should never slavishly bow down to that doctrine so often taught by unthinking men, making it in all cases sinful and wrong._ _ _ 1

Major CARTWRIGHT replied, and stated that be believed iii war when trespassed upon but not beyond that. He felt gratified in being called upon to respond to the toast for the reason that it was always a pleasure to an Englishman to respond to the toast because he knew there was not the like of it in the world. (Applause.) Major CARTWRIGHT then proposed "The Mayor and Cor- poration of Warrington." He remarked that he never was called upon to propose that toast before in the whole course of his life, and he hardly knew what to say because they had the automaton of the Council in the chair. (Laughter.) lie (the Major) was a very keen observer,—(laughter)- -and he asked Alderman Davies sometimes "Who are You going to make Mayor ?" " Oh," he said, " you'll see when the time comes. I think you will be perfectly satisfied." (Laughter.) So be was. He was always satisied when a good man was put in the position. He thought they had a

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S MISSION.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S MISSION.

The annual tea meeting of the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay, was held in the schoolroom on New Year's Day. There was a good gathering, about 200 persons par- taking of an excellent tea. An entertainment was after- wards given in the chapel under the presidency of the Mayor (Councillor Crosfield), who was supported by Mr. Williamson, Mr. Naylor, Mr. G. Dale '(Crewe), ani other gentlemen. The Secretary, Mr. F. Williams, read the re- port, which showed that during the past year the society had made considerable progress. Two new vestries had been built, but the number of scholars incre..sed so rapidly that they were now as straitened for room as ever they were. A young men's mutual improvement class had recently been opened, and it was progressing very satis- factorily. The report alluded in very touching terms to the death of Mrs. John Crosfield. The number of teachers were 17 male and 19 female; the number of scherars, 194 male and HO female. The income had been £32 14s, 71, and the expenditure £3B Os. 4d., so that there was a balance due to the treasurer of £5 11. s. 9d.—The Mayor. in addressing the meeting, congratulated the teachers on the success of the past year, and said he thought the society was in a better position than it had ever been in before. He was glad to see that disputes had been settled, and that they were settling down into a happy family. Dis- agreements often arose from people thinking too much of themselves, which was both contemptible and pitiable. He was certain that the chapel had done a world of good in Bank Quay; it had been like a light in the midst of darkness. He urged the parents to see that their chil- dren attended the Sunday school regularly, because that was the principal part of the battle. The greatest difficulties that teachers had to contend with was irregularity of atten- dance.—The Mayor left at a subsequent part of the proceed- ings, and Mr. Naylor took the chair. The choir rendered the anthem, "He maketh me to lie down in green pastures," and Mr. A. Crosfield gave two pianoforte solos. Recitations were given by Miss Willi.sms, Miss Whittaker, Miss John- son, Mr. D. Monks, and Mr. H. Holborne ; and songs by Mr. F. Williams, Mr. .G. Tanner, Miss Monks, and Miss Martha Monks, the latter of whom appeared to be only about four years of age. Miss Dickson and Miss Crosfield gave a pi inoferte duet in a 'very pleasing manner. Mr. Naylor and Mr. G. Dale addressed the meeting; and the proceedings were brought to a close with the usual votes of thanks.—CM Tuesday evening the scholars and teachers, numbering over 500, attended the annual tea, kindly given by Mr. Crosfield. After tea the scholars and parents assembled in the chapel, when an excellent programme, consisting of songs, recita- tions, Sic., was contributed by the following :—Mary and E. Tilling, F. Ashton, L. Williamson, M. Monks, R. Long, D. Monks, A. T. Lawton, P. E. Wynne, N. Collins, H. Kay, Jas. Mills, and a song in character entitled "King Christmas," which provoked much amusement, by F. Williams. The Sunday school choir, under the leadership of Mr. Williams, gave several pieces in a very pleasing manner. The meeting was presided over by Mr. J. Naylor, of Grappenhall. During the evening the Mayor attended, and was greeted with much enthusiasm by the scholars.

Mr. Naylor vacated the chair in favour of His Worship, and at the close of the programme the Mayor briefly addressed the meeting. A vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Mr. Monks, and seconded by Mr. Hough, was most heartily given, and terminated the proceedings. An apple was given to each scholar on leaving.
BUTTE RMARKET-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOLS.

Probably the most successful annual tea meeting held in connection with the above Sunday school took place on New Year's Day, in the Public Hall, Warrington. The teachers and elder scholars had adorned the hall with ever- greens and artificial flowers, and the motto " Success to our new Sunday schools," stood out conspicuously from the gallery. About 400 persons partook of tea, and the attendance was considerably augmented afterwards when the meeting was held. The superintendent minister (Rey. J. Eglinton) pre- sided, and he was supported by the Rev. J. Agar Beet, Thomas Rippen, and Rev. J. Young : Messrs. J. B. Isaac, Guest, Barlow, M. Bowden, and others. Trays were given by the following ladies :—Mrs. Eglinton, Mrs. Beet, Mrs. Rippon, Mrs. Starkey Smith, Mrs. Guest, Mrs. Gornall, Mrs. Barlow, Mrs. T. Carter, Mrs. Dutton, Miss B. Dutton, Miss Stelfox, Miss Blackhurst, Mrs. Garnett, Mrs. R. Garnett, Mrs. D. Garnett, Mrs. Mackie, Mrs. Lamplugh, Mrs. Bowden, Mrs. John Bennett, Mrs. Benson, Mrs. Collin, Mrs. Moss, Mrs. Fairhurst, Mrs. Pendle- bury, Mrs. Laverock, Mrs. Greening, Mrs. Hen- shall, Mrs. Josiah Carter, Mrs. W. Bennett, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. T. Jones, Mrs. S. Jones, Mrs. Craik, Mrs. J. J. Sanderson, Mrs. E. Richardson, Mrs. T. Grime, Mrs. Muir, Mrs. Hartley, Mrs. John Laverock, Mrs. R. Silcock, Mrs. Isaac, Mrs. John Taylor, Mrs. Prince, Mrs. Lilly, Mrs. Bur- ton, Mrs. Lunt, Mrs. Sobey, Mrs. Nicholson, Mrs. Alleneand Mrs. Heyward.—The CHAI fitMAN wished them all a happy new year, and said they ought to feel it a great mercy they were spared, and that they were beginning the year under such favourble circumstances. He rejoiced very much that their feeling about the matter that had brought them together was so very earnest, and he believed that the project would turn out successful, so as to give them great joy in the remem- brance of it as they realised in the prospect.—Mr. HENSHALL read the annual report, which stated that the high spiritual tone which had been vouchsafed to the school had been fully maintained, and the best proof of the genuineness and reality of the glorious work of two years ago was found in the fact that the great majority of those who then consecrated them- selves to Christ's service had hitherto proved faithful sol- diers of the cross, had thrown themselves into the work of carrying the good tidings of the Gospel to perishing sinners around, and were that day, he believed, more than ever determined to follow on to know the Lord and to offer all their works to Him.— The committee reported a continued satisfactory progress, both in the number of scholars on the books and in the attendance each Sunday. The number en the class books was 452, compared with 400 two years ago. Of these 230 were males and 222 females, and there was an average afternoon attendance of 307. Of teachers the school had a staff of 40-17 males and 23 females—with two superin- tendent', two school secretaries, one librarian, and one visitor, in whose praise the committee felt they could not speak too highly. The great question of the new schools had been the subject of earnest discussion and deliberation at every one of the committee's meetings, and after much anxious thought they had prepared a scheme which they trusted they would ba enabled to carry to a successful termination. The committee had come to a satisfactory arrangement with Mr. Samuel Broadhurst, of Sankey, for the purchaso of about 700 square yards of land, situated on the northerly side of Bold- street Chapel, upon which they felt perfectly satisfied a building adequate in every respect to their requirements could be erected. The great advantages which would accrue to Methodism, both in Warrington and the circuit, from the possession of such a building adjoin- ing the principal chapel, were too obvious to need enlarg- ing upon. One of the most important would follow from the wise course their worthy superintendent intended to adopt with regard to the purchase of land, that it should be bought by the new Board of Trustees now being appointed for Bold-street Chapel, so that the new school, when erected, and Bold-street Chapel would be practically one trust pro- , perty, managed by one Board of Trustees, thus for ever putting an end to the feeling which had at times cropped up that chapel and schools were two distinct institutions. i They could not speak definitely as to the expenditure necessary, bat they felt confident that their friends would , all agree with them that after waiting so many years the work, when undertaken, should be well done, whether the cost be £2,000 or £3,000. Its the opinion of the committee the time had now come when this work should be vigorously ' taken in hand, and they trusted their friends that night would give them such support and testify such approval of their scheme as should strengthen their hands, and encourage them resolutely to enter upon this important enterprise. —The Rey. J. A. BEET, in addressing the meeting, said the circuit had suffered immensely from having no Sunday school worthy of the name. The Wesleyan Church was ex- ceedingly strong ha Warrington ; they had grand congrega- tions at Bold-street and at Bewsey-road, and if they had only proper premises the increase in the attendance at Sun- day school would be enormous. He cculd understand people not sending their children to Buttermarket-street or .:3ilver- street. They had to pass scenes which i: was not desirable children should witness, and if they had noble and proper premises the school would be immensely increased from the children of their own families. They were glad to save the outcasts, but their first care must be their own children. They wanted to have noble and splendid schools, and they could have them for a smaller sum than £3,000. He urged them to have a fine school, remarking that if they went in for a large scheme they would call forth people's sympathy. He hoped the matter would be taken up in a proper spirit and carried to a successful conclusion.— Mr. Isaecs said they had begun with a debt due to the treasurer of £34. The expenses for the year, which had been cut as fine as possible consistent with efficiency, amounted to £35. The collection at their schools realised £l5, and after the proceedings of that meeting they hoped very soon to clear the debt due to the treasurer. Time school was never in a better state of feeling than it was at present, and from fourteen officials of the school he bad got the promise of £l4O towards the new schools.—The CHAIRMA.N said the trustees of Bold-street Chapel had voted £5OO to- ward the same object.—Slips of paper were then distributed amoegst the audience for promises of donations, with the following result :—Mr. Barlow, £100; Dr. Starkey Smith, £100; R. J. H., £5O; Mr. E. Guest, £5O; Mr. Carter, £53; Mr. Matthew Bowden, £25; Dr. Mackie, £2O; Mr. and Mrs. Buckley, £25; Mr. J. Bennett, £25; and others amounting to nearly £6oo.—The Rev. J. Ywecee briefly addressed the meeting, and wished the scheme success.—Mr. BOWDEN proposed a vote of thanks to all the ladies who had done so much to secure the success of the gathering—Mrs. Dutton and her assistants who had prepared the tea, the vocalists, and the decorators.—Mr. GUEST seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried.—lnstrumental and vocal music was given at intervals during the evening.

div.head: WATCH NIGHT SERVICES.
div.p: WATCH NIGHT SERVICES.

HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.— On New Year's eve, a watch night service was held in Holy Trinity Church, Sankey- street. There was a good attendance. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton read the prayers, after which the Rev. Alfred H. Jones, 8.A., delivered a short discourse, based on the words, "Even' good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness neither shadows of turning," James 1, xvii. After remarking upon the solemnity-and seriousness of the occasion, the rev, gentleman said they had come there to give back to their Heavenly Father with gratitude and thanks the year 1882. It was given them to live holy, faith- ful, true and loyal lives, and to let their light so shine among men that they might see their good works and glorify their Father in heaven, so that men might join in the universal hymn of creation, and send up praise in one glorious anthem to Him who was Lord of all. And every Sunday from the beginning of the year to the present time the voice of the Crucified One had been heard in His Sanc- tuary. Had they listened to that voice? Did they plead guilty or not guilty? If they never used the prayer of the publican before let them use it that night and say "Lord be merciful unto me a sinner." Let them go down on their knees and receive the gift of their great and living God, their Heavenly Father.—At the conclusion of the sermon the congregation engaged in silent prayer until the church clock announced the advent of another year, when a hymn was sung and tkie service closed. WESLEYAN CHAPEL, SAIIKEX BRIDGES, WATCH NIGHT AERYICE.—At the appointed time, 10-30 p tn., a large n um- ber of people had assembled, the chapel almost full. The service was both selomn and interesting. Among those who addressed the meeting were Mr. Clement George, Mr. W. Summerfield, Mr. J. Corocline. Several appropriate hymns were snag, and prayers offered. At the hour of 12 o'clock, the congregation rose and joined in singing the well-known Methodist hymn, commencing ‘• Come let us anew our journey pursue." As the p'eople dispersed it was with many good wishes to one another for a happy and prosperous year. BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—The watch night service held in this chapel, on Sunday night, was well attended. The service was conducted by the Rev. J. Agar Beet, who, in addressing the congregation, remarked that during the past year each of them had been building up his or her character. They had been moulding themselves, and were that night what they had made themselves during the past 365 days. What a multitude of events had happened during the past year, and how many persons they could call to mind who never dreamt at the beginning of the year that they would now be what they were. To some it had been a year of unexpected gain, to others of unexpected sorrow, but this he saw—that whatever would come to them in the next year would come from God. Whatever would - be held back from them would be held back by God, and, therefore, would he held back well. If God disappointed them, and it was no fault of theirs, if a thing was inevitable and there was no sin about it, they might rejoice, because they could say "God kept it from me, and I am better without it."—The Rev. J. Eglinton conducted the latter part of the service. At the solemn moment, as they bowed before the mercy seat, he prayed those who had come to the service, perhaps under the influence of cariosity, by covenant engagement to give themselves to Him, and He would speak peace to their sonls —Silent prayer was then engaged in, and the advent of the new year having been proclaimed, the hymn com- mencing "Come let us anew our journey pursue," was sung, the Benediction wus tben pronounced, and the Rev. J. Eglinton wished all Kivery happy new year, WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHCRCH..—A large con- gregation attended the NOateh night service held .at this Church. The pastor, the Rev. J. Yon,ge, after reading ap- propriate portions of scripture peached from the worth,

"I thought on my ways and turned *my feet unto Thy testimonies," Psalms, caix., 59. In the course of his dis- course the rev, gentleman said there was a necessity for those who were making more or less a profession of religion to pass themselves in scrutiny. It was possible for a man to think that he was in the pail] when he was not, to make a considerable profession of religion and not have it; and it was possible for sincerely godly men to be betrayed and decoyed into walking in paths which were not good, and ways which were not Christian, and right, and true. It was a solemn fact that professing Christian people were some- times to be found walking in very questionable paths, Lct them remembtr that God's testimonies spoken of in the text were the only safe charts by which any of them could steer their course to heaven. What was a Christian? A man who professed to follow, imitate, and obey Jesus Christ—a man who had pledged himself by the most solemn pledge a man could take in this life, to try and live an honest, Christian life, to seek to love others better than he loved himself, and to follow in the marvellous footsteps of the marvellous Son of God. That was what it was to be a Christian. If they professed to be religious, and did not submit themselves to the proof of God's book, they were imperilling their situation, and might hear the Master say "I never knew ye—ye that work iniquity—depart from ;ne." It was, therefore, incumbent upon them to take the text and make it their own. If they had hitherto been walk- ing in their own ways let them leave them and turn to God's way; young people should walk in God's ways, and forsake their own; and let them all seek mercy for the past and grace for the future.

COGIEHEDGE MissroN.—The watch night service at this place was attended by a large congregation. Suitable hymns were sung from Moody and Sankey's hymn book, and ap- propriate passages of scripture were read by Mr. Farrar, who conducted the service. Short addresses were given by Messrs, John Plinston, Wm. Willett, John Willett, and Mr. Farrar; each asking the congregation to think seriously of the solemnity of the occasion to give their hearts to God, and to take warning from the dreadful calamities that are continually taking place. Mr. Farrar made reference to the death of Mrs. Murray, of Belfast, whose husband; as well as herself, were great friends of the mission when in Warring- ton; and said Mr. Murray would be comforted to know that he had a large number of friends in Warrington who deeply sympathised with him in his great bereavement, amongst them being the people at Cockhedge Mission. The last moments of the old and the first moments of the New Year were spent in silent praper; then Mr. Farrar asked the con- gregation to join in the old familiar hymn "Come let us anew our journey pursue," Jrc., which was heartily rendered. He afterwards wished all a very happy New Year. The meeting closed in the usual way. This was the beginning of a week of special services. Rev. John Youge preached on Monday and Tuesday; Rev. E. Moores, on Wednesday ; and Mr. Farrar, on Thursday, to very fair congregations.

div.head: OLD MEN'S DINNER.
div.p: THE OLD MEN'S DINNER.

The annual dinner to the; old men of Warrington was given in the Public Hall, on Thursday. About 250 men, all above three score. years, sat down to the excellent things provided for them, consisting of beef, legs:of mutton, pork, rabbit and veal pies, cheese, and beer. An abundance of tobacco was also provided. The rule that no man under 60 years of age be allowed to partake of the dinner was rigidly adhered to, and several individuals who were under the qualifying age were asked to leave, so that the donors will have no cause to complain that their generosity has been indiscriminately disposed of. The carvers were selected from the tradesmen of the town with the addition of a few other gentlemen. After dinner the Rev. S. Wilkin- son took the opportunity of wishing them all a happy new year, remarking that he missed not a few of the old faces which were present at the dinner given last year. An old man named Campbell thanked the donors on behalf of those present, for their kindness in providing them the dinner. Subsequently Mr. Petty, of Liverpoool, sang two songs, entitled "Could I live my time over again" and "Simon the cellarer," by the accompaniment of Mr. George Riley. Mr. W. S. Woods presided at the organ dnring the dinner. The patrisrchs left the ball much pleased with the treat they had received. The committee consisted of the following gentlemen :—Messrs. John Pierpoint (president), Thomas Jones (vice-president), Thomas Morris (hon. treasurer), Thomas Sutton (hon. secretary), William Woods, W. J. Horton, S. Jones, Peter Crimes, Charles Skinner, Noah Legge, W. Dowlev, James Smethurst, Councillors J. E. Wright and Caldwell.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

The time-honoured custom for welcoming the New Year seemed to be extensively observed in Runcorn. For several hours before midnight on Sunday the streets presented an animated scene, as men and youths in groups of four or five passed along in an almost continual stream, apparently with aimless feet. Companies of the latter were in possession of a variety of instruments, from which they extracted sounds more noisy than melodious; while others amused them- selves by yelling the refrain of some song, and, to the utter disquiet of those within, by raising the knocker of each door they passed. As midnight drew nearer these "young sparks," drawn home, perhaps, by fear of the fatherly "rod of corruption," seemed to leave the streets, and their places were taken by the wait singers, who filled the night's air with melodious melodies. Watch-night services were held at almost all the places of worship, and they were invariably well attended. On New Year's Day, the weather, like on the previous night, was wet and dull; but there were, never- theless, many people to be seen in the streets, although a considerable number left by train for Liverpool and Man- chester, to indulge in the various amusements which those plaees afforded. Most of the large manufactories were at work, but the tradesmen closed their shops about noon. The various brass bands of ivhich the town can boast performed selections at the houses of their various supporters during the day, and never failed to attract a considerable following in:, their wake. The day passed off 'quietly.

div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

Although the atmosphere was laden with suffocating gases, through which the rain penetrated at intervals, pedestrians were numerous in Widnes on New Year's Eve, and the town, like its sister across the Mersey, was not quite free from rowdyism. Great numbers of the inhabi- tants, however, took leave of the old and welcomed the new year, with all due solemnity, in the various places cf wor- ship, the Parish Church bell telling the surrounding inhabitants, with its merriest peal, that 1883 bad com- menced its record. New Year's Day exhibited no improve- ment in the weather, and with the exception that the tradesmen's shops were closed, the town wore its ordinary appearance. The important operations at the minuf actories were in full swing, and the greater portion of the male inhabitants consequently at work. The day was notable in the adjoining parish of Farnworth, from the fact that the temperance and total abstinence society of the Parish Church held a demonstration, but the success of the out- door proceedings were militated against by the extremely unfavourable weather.
DI TRICT NEWS,
ALTRINC HAM.

It is announced that a poll of the ratepayers of Altrin- sham, in respect to the proposed triennial election of guar- dians will take place. Voting papers will be delivered on the 22nd instant, and collected on the following day.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCII.—Tho annual parochial concert in aid of the Frodsham parish churchwardens' fund was held on Thursday night, at the Town Hall, Frodshain. In former years it has been the custom to have a public tea in connection with the concert, and which has always, with the exception of last year, been well attended, and been most thoroughly enjoyed by a very large portion of parishioners and other friends. As the tea last year was rather a failure on account of the inclemency of the weather, it was decided at a meeting of the ladies' committee not to have the tea this year, which is very much to be regretted, as the weather on Thursday was most favourable, and a large amount would have been taken, which would have materially assisted the churchwardens' fund. The doors of the concert hall were announced to be open at seven, and the concert to commence at half-past, and long before the time for commencement, the hall was well filled in every part. The well-known piartette company from Hope Hall, Liverpool, consisting of Messrs. Josef Cantor, N. P. Bust, E. Edwards and S. Kirkham had been engaged, and in addition the following local ladies and gentlemen, viz: Misses Emily M. Riley, K. S. Rigby, and Edith E. Riley, the Vicar, and Mr. B. A. Rigby. At half-past seven the Rev. A. P. Reynolds announced from the platform that the train by which the quartette company would come by was very late, and that Miss K. S. Rigby had promised to fill up the interval by playing a pianoforte solo. This was taken in good part, and Miss Rigby received well- merited applause for her performance. Of the Quartett Company it is needless to say anything in their praise as they are so well known and have gained such a widespread reputation, we will only notice that they received well- deserved encores for all their quartetts to which they very good humouredly responded, with the exception of the first. The first solo was given by Miss Edith E. Riley, and was rendered so well that an encore was the result, to which she responded. This is the first appearance of Miss E. E. Riley, and she has made a very favourable impres- sion. She possesses a very good contralto voice, and she gave "The lost chord" with a crispness and decision that showed she knew what she was about; and we hope that it will not be the last time she favours the Frodsbam audience. Mr. Burt's rendering of the deecriptive scene, " Rage thou angry storm," was very good, but it is a peculiar song, and requires to be well- known before it can be appreciated. He was very success- ful in "Simon the cellarer," and:got an encore, for which.he gave "Where are the boys of the old brigade." Mr. Edwards got encores for both of his songs, and for the second he sang "When the bloom is on the rye." He i possesses a very sweet tenor voice, and it s not often that the Frodsham people have such a treat as to hear a tenor singer of his equal. Mr. Kirkham has a falsetto voice, and gave his "True till death " in his usual style. The duet between the Misses. Rigby awl Riley was redemanded, and was, if anything, better rendered the second time. Mr. Cantor is a host in himself and fairly brought down the house„ He gave as encores "Two spoons "and "The cork leg." Mr. Rigby's "Will o' the Wisp" was well received, but as he possesses a deep bass voice, we think the song is not quite suited to his style of singing. Miss Emily M. Riley's song, "The chil- dren's queen," got an encore, for which she gave "Only speak kindly to me." It is only fair to say that the vicar was suffering from a very severe cold, and it was with great difficulty that he gave "The lark now rises from her watery nest." Miss Kate S. Rigby got an encore for her spirited rendering of "A summer shower," to which she responded. The evening's entertainment was brought to a °lose by the artiste giving the National Anthem, and thus the pleasantest

evening and the best concert that has been heard in -fired' sham for along time ended. -RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board-room on Wednesday. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present Dr. MacDougall, T. Norman, J. Dobson, W. Fisher, J. Williams, W. Whittaker, F. Speakman, J. Meadowcroft, Timmins, Lake, Pritchard, R. Shaw, P. Bris- ooe, W. Rhodes, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), W. Barker (surveyor).
