div.head: GOOD WISHES.
div.p: GOOD WISHES.
The CHAIRMAN said as this was the first meeting of the year, he wished them all a very happy and prosperous new year, a wish which was heartily reciprocated by the as- iembled Commissioners.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The MEDICAL OMCER (Dr. Mou-ritz-.) reported that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 44, including 3 at Halton within Run- corn. Of the above deaths 11 were due to pulmonary diseases, 9 to measles, 7to brain affections, 5 to scarlatina, 3 to dropsy; abdominal disease, cardiac affection, premature birth, rheumatism, marasimus, natural decay, diptheria, diarrhcea, hcemorrhage, and phthisis account, for one each ; representing a death-rate of 35 per 1,000 per annum. Twenty-seven deaths occurred among children five years old and under, and 17 under. one year.
PROPOSAL TO FOUND AN ACCIDENT HOSPITAL.

The Chairman read a letter from Mr. Clarke Aspinall as follows :—The Coroner's Court, Liverpool, December 9th, 1882.—Dear Dr. Steele,—At an inquest held by me to-day upon the body of a poor man injured recently on the rail- way at Runcorn, and brought to the Liverpool 'Royal Infirmary, I mentioned the subject of hospital accommoda- tion in Runcorn, rather in view of finding out its extent. The opinion seemed to be that no institution of the kind existed. Upon this being stated, I observed that I felt sure the authorities would take kindly any suggestion on the subject, and in returning their verdict the jury approved of my writing to you asking your attention to the matter. The accident in question was to a workman on the line, so that the question of an under or over ground crossing did not arise. lam sure you will quite understand that I write simply in the interests of injured pe.ple, and with a full knowledge that the good people of Runcorn will gladly do all that is required if they have not done so."—Dr. STEELE said he hardly need tell them that there was no provision made for an accident hospital, for although the Board could lay a rate of Id in the pound for a library, they could do nothing for a hospital. He had always thought it was not very creditable that a town of 15,000 inhabitants should have no hospital. He believed that one might be easily maintained if the clergy of all denomina- tions were to hold a "hospital Sunday." as was done in other towns, and thus get a subscription up. He had issued post- cards to the clergy and tradespeople in the neighbonrhood asking them to discuss the matter at a meeting next Wednes- day, and see if they could not form n a hospital. Fortunately there were not many accidents in Runcorn, but it was a cruel thins to send a man down to Liverpool by train when suffering, perhaps, excruciating pain. If lsy establishing a hospital one life could be saved in one or two years they Would be amply repaid.—Mr. R. Sne.w suggested that the employers should receive invitations, and Dr. Steele was understood to say he would do so.
Alf 0FF)312.
The Lsw CLERIC announced that Mr. Thomas D. Timmins had made an offer of £3OO for the town's yard, and on the motion of Mr. NORMAN it was referred to the committee.
TINE LIBRARY AND. RRADING-ROOM QUESTION.

The following resolution from the Free Library Com- mittee was now considered :—" The committee having con- sidered the resolution passed at the ratepayers' meeting, on the iitla instant, respectfully request the Commissioners to grant, for the use of the library and reading-room, the breakfast, dining, and drawing-rooms of Waterloo House ; and also to empower this committee to make and carry oat the necessary arrangements."- 31r. P. SPHAKMAN said before any steps were taken, it would be well if the Board knew its legal position with re- gard to charging the Library Committee a rent for the premises.—Mr. SHAW observed that the Law Clerk had clearly stated that they could not charge a rent, so that it was a question which did not require discussion. He sug- gested that a committee of three members be appointed to consider and report on the best way of providing accommo- dation at Waterloo House for the library, the reading room, and the Commissioners offices. He did not see how they could carry out the suggestion as it now stood, because the Library Committee wished to take all the bottom rooms of Waterloo House, and it was questionable whether this was a wise proceeding. The Board should have a decided plan before they moved one single step, and he proposed that a committee be appointed. He should not ask any member en the Library Committee to serve on the committee, because he thought it was advisable that the question should be considered from a comprehensive point of view.—Mr. Nort- MAN seconded.—Mr. RHODES thought the Library Commit- tee should be represented by at least one member.—Mr. NORMAN : I don't think the Library Committee had any right to be.—Dr. MACDOUGALL was of opinion the Library Committee ought to be represented; and the CHAIRMAN, in stating an opposite opinion, observed that the committee to be appointed would be only too glad to meet the Library Committee at Waterloo House, and hear their views.—The resolution was carried.—Mr. SHAW then proposed that Mr. Fisher, Mr. Meadowcroft, and himself form the committee. —Mr. RHODES moved the addition of the name of Mr. Lake. —The amendment received no seconder, and the original esolution having been seconded, was carried.

div.head: MR. HA.ZLEHURST'S RESIGNATION.
div.p: MR. HA.ZLEHURST'S RESIGNATION.

Mr. NORMAN moved that Mr. Pritchard be appointed a member of the General Purposes Committee in place of Mr. Haziehurst. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion, which was carried. Dr. MACDOUGALL proposed that Mr. Pritchard be a member of the Free Library Committee in succession to Mr. Hazleburst. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN seconded.—Mr. NORMAN thought .other members quite equal to the position, and with all due respect to Mr. Pritchard, moved an amendment that Mr. Meadowcroft till the vacancy. —Mr. DOBSON seconded. Dr. 111.1cDouGALL pointed out that it was the custom for the new member to fill the positions held by his predecessor, and said no one would more willingly support Mr. Meadowcroft's nomination than he, but he (Mr. Meadowcroft) some time ago declined to act.—Mr. NORMAN remarked that this Was an extraordinary committee, and Mr. SHAW said it would only be an act of courtesy to elect an old commissioner.-Mr. MEADowcnorr said if his proposer and seconder would withdraw the proposition he sLoald be extremely pleased to give way for Mr. Pritchard. --The matter, however, went to the vote, and there being 7 Commissioners in favour:of each candidate, the Chairman gave his casting vote for Mr. Meadowcroft, who was declared elected.

div.head: UPPER MERSEY NAVIGATION.
div.p: UPPER MERSEY NAVIGATION.

The next business was to appoint a Commissioner under the Upper Mersey Navigation Acts, in place of Mr. Charles Wigg, who was eligible for re-election.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded, the re-appointment of Mr. Wigg.—Dr. MACDOUGALL remarked that the Commis- sioners had had no report of the proceedings of this Board, which was constituted some six years ago,for certain specific purposes, by Act of Parliament, although they had a repre- sentative upon it. They would be glad to know how the monies that were -collected were disposed of, because the Commissioners did not know whether the Board was injuri- ous or otherwise to the trade of the district or the prosperity of Runcorn. In the next place it would be a very good thing if they had some information.—A conference took place between the Chairman and the Law Clerk, whereupon the latter said it was perfectly clear that the Board could not re-appoint Mr. Wigg until he ceased to be a member, which event would not occur until February.—Dr. MACDOUGALL ObberVed that nobody was more willing to support the nomi- nation, but he thought it desirable that the Commissioners should have some information. The Board would be glad to have Mr. Wigg's views on the ship canal scheme, in which Runcorn was interested greatly. The appointment was not made. A SCANDALOUS PIECE OF BUSINESS.

The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee stated that a claim had been received from Messrs. Greenell, Whitley, and Co., of £lO for damage to a mare, alleged to have been caused by the road in Fryer-street giving way. It was resolved that Messrs. Norman and Timmins be deputed to wait on them with the view to arrange the best terms on which the claim can be settled.—Letter was read from the Ratepayers' Association drawing attention to the bad state of the roadway over Waterloo Bridge, and the danger to pedestrians, owing to the want of a footpath. Its considera- tion was deferred until next month; in the meantime Mr. Barker to look up the correspondence with the Bridgewater Trustees on the subject of the road and the bridge, confer with the Law-Clerk, and report thereon.—Resolution in- structing the Law-Clerk to write to those owners of property in Ashridge-street, giving them notice that unless they pay their street making accounts before January Ist, legal pro- ceedings will be taken.—Resolution that a letter be sent to the directors of the Runcorn Gas Company with reference to the price charged for gas to general consumers, and drawing their attention to the price charged at Liverpool.— Recommendation that 2s. per week be added to the wages of thainarket superintendent's assistant, and that he attend such tunes as required by the superintendent.-Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. WILLIAMS seconded, the confirmation of the minutes.—Dr. lascDoriGALL inquired what was the state of the street prior to this accident.—Mr. BARKER (surveyor) replied that the street was all right on the aarface.—Dr. MacDorma.u. Had- you any information that there was a hole underneath t—Mr. BARKER: 0 dear! no, sir.—Dr. 31AcDotTGALr. said i It seemed very singular that they should admit their liability, f there had been no prior information with respect to anything of a serious nature in the street. He compared the circumstances of the accident with those connected with the falling. of two houses owned by Mrs. Scott, where the Board declined any liability, remarking that the surveyor was responsible for the state of the street, and the Board were responsible to him. The surveyor, however, stated there was no defect, and he took it that the claimants must prove that there was a defect before they could hold the Board liable for any damage. It seemed to him that when they had a powerful claimant the Board had no objection to admit liability and offer him a £5 note, but when a widow lost her all they could say "There is no claim upon this Board; we will fight you, and we will do our best to beat you." He took exception to the recommendation, because by paying claims of this kind without ascertaining that the Board was liable, they might land themselves into a serious mess. —The LAW CLERK said the facts in this instance were different from the facts in the case cited by Dr. MacDougall, and the latter knew they were different.— ..■.Dr. MACDOUGALL said he had stated the facts as they

occurred. He was in7ormed that the deputation had been to Warrington, and had settled the claim without giving the I ratepayers' representatives an opportunity of expressing their opinion on the matter. It was a most improper course to pursue ; in fact, he never knew a more scandalous piece of business in connection with public life. There was no use now in proposing an amendment, but he would never- theless move that the minute referring to the claim be struck out.—The CHAIRMAN said a similar course had been pursued in regard to purchasing books for the library, when Dr. MacDougall said he would pay the cheque, but didn't do so. This was just a similar case.—Dr. MACDOUGALL : Oh dear no; nothing of the sort.— Mr. NORMAN said he should like to say that Dr.MacDougalit was a member of the committee, but, instead of attending he went to the Board to throw his spleen upon the members and say this is wrong and the other is wrong. (Interrup- tion from Dr. MacDougall.) Mr. Norman : lam talking to the chairman and not to you; don't interrupt me. Dr. MacDougall comes here to throw his spleen, because he wants to show that he is the economist of the Board. (Inter- ruption.) It's me that's talking, Dr. MacDougall.—Dr. MACDOUGALL : You are addressing me personally.—Mr. NORMAN: I am addressing you, but I shall have my say. He meant to say that Dr. MacDougall, not being present at the committee meeting, had no right to talk in the way he had done about the matter, and unless he knew more abaut what he was talking. Mill-street was not adopted, and Tyrer-street was, and besides this they had the opinion of the Law Clerk that:the Board was responsible for the damage. The matter had been settled.—Mr. P. SPEAK- MAN asked whether the deputation had any right to settle the claim before the minutes were confirmed.—The CHAIR- MAN said they had no right to do so, but they had done the best they could in the interests of the ratepayers, and had paid the money on their own reponsibility, It rested with the Board whether they should receive the money back again.—Mr. NORMAN : It won't break us.—Mr. MEanow- CROFT said he opposed the matter in committee, as there was a very important principle involved, and it was only after the very decided opinion expressed by the Law Clerk, that he gave way.—E'r. MACDOUGALL, replying to Mr. Norman, said he would not descend into any personal attack on anybody. If any gentleman liked to bespatter another individual with dirt the responsibility must rest with the person pursuing such a course. [Mr. NORMAN: Hear, hear. Go on, Doctor.]
TIIE -PRICE OF GAS: APPLICATION FOR A REDUCTION.

Dr. MecDouGALL then asked for information with regard to the minute referring to the price of gas, and the CHAIR- MAN said he saw it stated that Liverpool charged a shilling per thousand feet less than was paid in Runcorn, and he thought it the duty of the Board to get a redaction in price for the consumers if they could. He therefore brought the matter before the Highway and Sanitary Committee, who decided to send a note to the company' asking them to reduce the price.—Mr.Suaw : We ought to have it cheaper than Liverpool.—The CHAIRMAN: I should like to know where the harm is, and what opposi- tion can be taken to such a resolution as this. I think it is due to the Board that Dr. MacDougall should give some ex- planation.—Dr. MACDOUGALL said he would do so. He was not there as the apologist of any public company, bat the duties of that Board were limited by Act of Parliament, and the Board had no right to make any inquiry as regarded the price of gas to consumers, but simply as re- garded the lighting of the lamps in the street. If the Board wished to be informed what the income of the company was they could apply to the Court of Quarter Sessions for an order to examine the accounts of the Gas Company, and see what they can do to enforce a reduction. That was what they could do! The Board had made an application for a reduction in the price of gas supplied to the lamps twice within the past twelve months, and it seemed to him an extraordinary proceeding, after the replies they had from the Gas Company. Liverpool supplied its gas at a cheaper rates but it must be borne in mind that a city of a quarter of a million could produce gas much cheaper than a smaller town could. He quoted the prices charged in surrounding towns to show that Runcorn was not overcharged, but Mr. SHAW inter- rupted and said the figures quoted were worth nothing.— Dr. MACDOUGALL said he could not see that the Board had any right whatever in the course they had taken, but it was their doing, and they must take the consequence. (Laugh- ter.)—The CHAIRMAN did not think it was worth while hav- ing any discussion on the point raised by Dr. MacDougall. He thought the Board was only doinc, its duty to the rate- payers in asking for a reduction. He shonld have been sorry to have demanded an order without first asking the Company to reduce the price. He was sorry that Dr. MacDougall bad raised the question he had. It would raise between the Gas Company and the Board. He thought it was most ill-advised.—ln reply to a qaestion from Mr. P. Speakman as to the powers of the Board in the matter, the LAW-CLERK said if the Board felt aggrived they could go to arbitration on the question of the price under the company's clauses.— The CHAIRMAN said any one consumer could do so.—The minutes were then passed; and, on thc motion of Mr. SHAW, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMS, a cheque for £6, the amount of stttlement, was ordered to be signed.

div.head: CANAL 140A.TS AND HOSPITAL.
div.p: CANAL 140A.TS AND HOSPITAL.

The minutes contained a resolution that a letter be sent to Mr. Statham with reference to the slow progress of the hospital works, and giving him notice that the conditions of the contract will be enforced. Recommendation that the services of Mr. John Wilson, as clerk of the hospital w%rks, be dispensed with at the expiration of one week, from Jan. 3rd. A letter had been received from the clerk to the Runcorn Union with reference to :lledical attendance on pauper patients in the Commissioners' infectious hospital, and it was recommended that the secretary reply stating that in the opinion of the Commissioners, it would be better for the Guardians to make arrangements themselves for medical attendance.—Mr. FISIIER moved the confirmation of the minutes, and Mr. BRISCOE seconded.—ln reply to Dr. MacDougall, Mr. FISHER said it was the unanimous opinion of the committee that Mr. Wilson's services would no longer be required, as all the practical work had been done. Mr. Barker would be able to superintend the work.— The minutes were adopted.

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE,
div.p: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE,

At a meeting on the 27th ultimo, the secretary was instructed to write to Sir R. Brooke's agent, stating that no allowance can be made from the account for fire brigade expenses, in connection with the recent fire at Norton Manor farm ; also to write to Mr. J. A. Ford threatening legal proceedings if the amount due from him is not paid at once. —Minutes passed.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee reporred that the receipts for the past month amounted to £307 2s. Bd., and the accounts amounting to £193 Os. 7d. were recommended for payment. It was recommended that legal proceedings be taken against the owners of property in Percival-lane if their accounts for street making were not paid by January 11th next.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

The CHAIRMAN, reWying to Dr. MacDougall, said the Ship Canal Committee hact held a meeting, and appointed Mr. Shaw chairman, in place of Mr. Dobson, whose state of health would not permit him to take the duties. No business had been transacted.—The Board then rose.

div.head: A, COLM.TEUR SENT TO GAOL
div.p: A, COLM.TEUR SENT TO GAOL

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, before Mr. J. C. Gamble, Aldermen Cook and Harrison, a young man named Northcote Willy, was charged with having caused an obstruction, by means of a cart, in St. Mary's-street, on the 23rd ult.—Superintendent Johnson said the defendant, with a cart containing a number of bibles, pamphlets, etc., came to him during the week to ask if he could put up in St. Mary's-street. He told him that wherever he put.up he must not cause any obstruction, but on one occasion as he (Superintendent Johnson) was going to the letter box at the post office he found the cart on one side of the road close to the parish church; and defendant at the other ad- dressing a crowd of people. After be had cautioned de- fendant that he could not stand there he went and put his letter in the box, but defendant still eontinued to stand where he was, and some time after that a constable still found him there.—P.C. Bremner said that about 20 minutes to two o'clock, on the afternoon of Saturday, the 23rd December, he saw the defendant and his cart in St. Mary's. street. He spoke to him about standing thc•e, telling him he must shift. Defendant asked by whose orders must be shift, and witness said by his own, and he would give defendant 15 minutes to shift, and if he did not shift by that time he would report him. Defendant replied that he had seen Superintendent Johngon on the previous night, and he told him he could stand there. Witness replied that the superintendent would never tell him such a thine, and even if he had he would still report him if he continued there. Defendant said he would not shift, and also said he had been a superintendent himself, and knew what the law was as well as witness or his superintendent. He followed witness up the street, stopped him two or three times, and said be would report his conduct to Superintendent Johnson. Witness went back to St. Mary's-street about half-past two o'clock and saw defendant still there.. On speaking to him he used the same sort of language as before. He continued to stand till twenty minutes to four o'clock, and then went into the market. There had been a crowd of people aiound defen- dant, wko prevented persons from getting to the letta• box. —Defendant said that what the last witness had said about his telling him that he had been a superintendent of police himself, was not correct. He was, he said, connected with the Liverpool Bible carriage, which was sent out and sup- ported by the British and Foreign Bible Society, awl was entering into an account of the work of the society when the Chairman, interrupting, said they did not want to hear about that.—Defendant: I have come here to spread the Gospel—to spread the word of God.—The Chairman: Well, but what have you to say about this obstruction P—Defen- dant mentioned that on the previous week he went to the market inspector and aeked for permission to go into the market. The inspector mid be could go on, but not on the Saturdays—and, he trOght say, he was here some time ago, and was prohibited Zn thee ime way from spreading the living Word of God on the Saturday. He went to Superintendent Johnson and asked him if he might go down St. Mary's- street, and Mr Johnson said, "You may go' but do not cause an obsvaction ; we are against nothing of this sort." Mr. Johnsoc spoke like a gentleman. He (defendant) went to St. Mar's-street, and was there when Mr. Johnson came. lie confessed he was reading from a little book—not preach- ing—to some people. He did not know whether the Bench wimld allow him to show them the books P—The Chairman: No, no: Mr. Johnson told you you were causing an obstruc- tion.—Defendant said he did, but the. Case did not refer to that time. When the officer ordered him away he asked him if be had own Mr. Johnson. The officer replied that he

ordered him away himself, upon which he (defendant) re- plied that he expected a civil answer from an officer of the law, and further said that he would report him to Superin- tendent Johnson. The officer was not only uncivil but im- pudent, as he told him that he came there because he would not pay the toll in the market, whereas—Superintendent Johnson (interrupting) : He was turned away from the market because be would not pay; and if the Gospel is to be spread it must be spread by proper and legal means. —Defendant: We are willing to pay the toll; money is no object. You will presume (addressing the Bench) I pre- sume that as I am a servant of God, it is not a matter which—The Rev. C. Green at this juncture arose in the body of the court and said: I will speak as to my friend's character.—The Chairman: It is not a question of character at all.—Defendant asked if he was not allowed to go on the market, where must he go P—The Chairman: If they will not allow you to go on the market, you must not go.— D?lendant : Then where must I go ?—The Chairman: That is not a question for us.—P.C. Bremner was then re-called by the Bench, and said there were about 40 or 50 people around the defendant on the occasion in question, and he was preaching to them.—Defendant denied that there were so many people, and said he had not been preaching.—The Bench then intimated that they would fine defendant is and 7s 6,1 costs, or in default seven days' imprisonment.—De- fendant : I decline to pay anything.—The Chairman: It is very plain you have been ordered away, and the post-office is a place which ought to be kept clear of obstruction.— Defendant: I am willing to go to gaol, but I won't pay, for it is false what the officer said; he cannot prove that there were 40 or 50 people there.—The Chairman: You have had your say.—Superintendent Johnson: I must ask for a distress warrant. (To the defendant.) Have you any goods ?—Defendant: 1 have no goods of my own.—Super- intendent Johnson: Oh, very well; that is all I want. You must go to gaol then.—Defendant was then conducted to the cells. In passing out of the door, he turned towards the Bench and said : I will shako the dust off my feet against St. Helens.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 6, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 6, 1883.
MR. F. K. MUSPRAIT ON THE REVENUE RETURNS.

Mr. E. K. Muspratt, presiJent of the Financial Reform Association, writes as follows in the Daily News:—" In your lucid article of yesterday (Jan. 1) upon the revenue returns it appeared to me that some very considerable factors were otnitted when you came to point out the causes of recent fallings-off in the produce of taxation. lam dis- pesed to believe with you that the increase of national sobriety and the prolonged distress in agriculture, are the main causes of the diminished yield, but it is desirable to fix the public attention on at least two other factors of the position, and this I ask your leave to be allowed to attempt. The first I shall dismiss with but very few words, merely pointing out that on page 3 of your same issue, in an article on "Trade and Finance in 1882," it is stated that " the average Bank-rate for the year has been 4 per cent., being higher than for any year since 1873," and that for the last quarter of the year that rate has stood at 5 per cent., a level destructive in its effect upon the gradually returning energies of trade and commerce. The second con- sideration is the accumulated growth of our national expenditure, and its pressure on the income-tax paying classes of the country. To put this pointedly, I may cite the following figures, taking as biennial periods of corepari- elan the last two years of national prosperity, and the last two years of national depression : Profits from Trades and Pro- National fessions (Eng. and Wales). Expenditure. 1875 1876

420.2 m. 1.68.0 m. So that with £24,000,000 less coming into the pockets of the trading and professional class, we have spent £18,000,000 more. How Prostrating must be the effect upon the national prosperity ! Well may the yield of the penny per pound go down—and I have not said anything about local expenditure, which has run up to £17,000,000 more in the same interval, and a large proportion of it (if not the lion's share) comes out of the same section of the taxpayers. Is this state of things to last, or are we to see an honest and fearless remedy applied by Parliament ? The overgrown national armaments must be reduced, the tea and cocoa] of the masses must be set free from Customs in- terference, and the ring of monopolists controlling the money market by virtue of the effete Bank Act must be broken up. Any one of such reforms would be sufficient to bring back the spring tides of national prosperity, and all Them ought to be practicable with a great Liberal majority in the House of Commons."

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DISTURBANCE AT A NEW YEAR'S GATHERING NEAR EAR LESTOWN,
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DISTURBANCE AT A NEW YEAR'S GATHERING NEAR EAR LESTOWN,

A scene of a most extraordinary character occurred on New Year's Day within a hundred miles of Earlestown and Newton, and a large number of ladies and gentlemen who had assembled with the intention of enjoying themselves at one of the numerous gatherings which were held on that day were considerably alarmed at an unseemly disturbance that took place. The affair has caused a greet amount of talk in the district immediate to that in which it occurred, not only on account of its unexpectedness, but also because of ihe social position of the principal actors and prime movers connected with it. The gathering was one pro. rioted principally by a well-known clergyman and officers of a certain parish church, and to make it successful they laboured earnestly and perseveringly, the result being that a goodly number of the ladies and gentlemen of the district met at the appointed place. A substantial tea was partaken of, after which the company proceeded to en- joy and exercise themselves in a popular manner, but before they had long been doing so their pleasure was greatly marred and interfered with by an inci- dent which occurred, and it is stated that the company did not afterwards manifest the same good humour and kindly feeling which had previously been shown. Whilst all were indulging in the pleasures of the evening, the lights sud- denly went out, and the place was shrouded in perfect dark- ness. Under the impression that someone bad been playing a lark the vicar of the parish made a rush to where the meter stood, but was unable to distinguish the guilty one. In a short time numerous lights, by means of matches and candle, were procured, and a faint glimmer was thrown around, which, however, only served to make darkness visible. When the gases had been re-lit the vicar commenced an investigation into the affair, and suspicion fell upon a young man—the son of One of the wardens of the church. He wasaccordingly forcibly ej.cted by the vicar, but when the door was reached the young man turned upon the clergyman and a struggle ensued. The clergyman was the taller and stronger of the two, and suceeded in laying the young man on the ground, but the latter secured a good hold, and in a short time the vicar was rolling on the around beside him. Owing to the heavy downpour of rain which had taken place, the clothes of both were splashed and almost covered with dirt. The struggle at last came to an end, though not before there were signs of other parties engaging in it—some taking the side of the clergyman, while one, the son of another minister, took the part of the young man. The clergyman retired to his home with the object of attir- ing himself in more appropriate garments, whilst the young man 4.nd.his friend left the school and its neighbourhood.
TREAT TO THE AGED I);2OPLE OF GOLBORNE.

An annual event, which is always looked forward to with great interest by a no small portion of the inhabitants of Golborne parish, took place in Mr. Brewis'o school-room on Thursday afternoon and evening last, when all the aged people .(those over 60 years) were entertained with their annual treat for the sixth year in succession. The affair is promoted by a number of gentlemen, who formed them- selves into a committee, and solicited subscriptions towards defraying the cost of providing the old people in the district a free tea, a quantity of tobacco, &c., once a year. The appeal has always been liberally responded to, and we are pleased to learn that a balance has always been left in hand to be carried forward towards the next year's expenses. The next "treat " is provided for all those above 60 years of age, irrespective of sex or religious feelings, and thus for once a year old friends and companions are brcught face to face with each other to renew the acquaintanceship of by- gone days. As can only be surmised, the old people are immensely delighted at the " treat," and when it is stated that there are about 230 persons who have reached the stipulated three-score years, all of whom have invitations sent to, and cabs come for them, it will be readily guessed that the gathering must be a highly interesting one. The committee consists of Messrs. R. L. Pennington (the energetic and pains-taking secretary), Richard Fairhurst (treasurer), Thomas Pierpoint, J. Entwistle, H. Seddon (assistant secretary), James Collier, Thomas Hirst, Joseph Sankey. Thomas Fearns, George Pitt, John Wakefield, S. Barton, W. Walmsley, W. Jenkinson, W. Mitchell, Thomas Fairhurst, and R. Y. Woolacott ; Dr. Mapei and Dr. Dobb. These gentlemen very efficiently performed their duties, which were by no means light or easy ones. All the invited persona were brought to the schoolroom in cabs, and tea was served out almost punctually at the hour announced—three o'clock. The tables were presided over by 36 lady friends, and the old people were soon busily engaged in supplying the wants of the "inner man." Everything was of the best quality, the beef, ham, currant bread, circa being really first-class. After tea each person was gratuitously supplied with a packet of tobacco, and tea and oranges, and a miscellaneous concert was held, this portion of the " treat " being arranged principally under the superintendence of the respected and esteemed Dr. Mapei. The Rector, the Rev. C. T. Quirk, presided, and it is almost needless to add that the proceedings were greatly enjoyed by everyone present. The age of the oldest woman present was 89, and that of the eldest male 87. As the schoolroom had been previously decorated with greens, tissue papers, Jgc., it presented quite !a cheering and charming aspect to the old people. At the r conclusion of the proceedings the latter were conveyed to their respective homes in conveyences specially hired for the purpose.
THE FATAL FIGHT AT RAINFORD.

On Friday Thomas Pye was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, before Mr. J. C. Gamble, with that he feloni- ously did kill and slay Christopher Roughley, of Bicker- gaffe, at the Wheat Sheaf Inn, near Rainford, on Saturday, the 23rd December. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared on behalf of the prisoner. The facts of this case appeared at some length in our columns last week, and are, shortly, that the prisoner and the deceased were in the Wheat Sheaf Inn to- gether on the afternoon in question, and after some chaffing and disputing they commenced fighting. They closed with each other and fell. Roughley undermost. His head struck against a form, and on his being lifted up ty some other persons he was- tonna to be dead. An inquest was held on the body of deceased on the 28th ult., when a verdict of manslaughter was returned; after considerable hesitation by the jury. Prisoner was, as stated, charged as above at the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday last, when the evidence as given at the inquest was recapitulated. He was com- mitted to the assizes for trial, bail being allowed—himself in £4O and his father in £4O.

RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN : ANNUAL TEL PARTY.—On New Year's Day, the anneal tea party in con- nection with these missions was held in the Mission-room, Bottom Locks, which had been brightly adorned for the occasion. A good number sat down to tea, and the follow- ing ladies presided at the tables :—Miss Barclay, Miss Williams, Mrs. G. Howard, Miss Jarratt, and Miss Allan. The tea was followed by an entertainment, presided ove,r,'„ Mr. S. C. Beckett, who commented in appropriatmpd by the missions. The missions' band gave one ' upon the valuable work wide; was being accoir - entertainments, their program,- !heir most enjoyable by Master Ferneval, entitled "What _deluding a song ~.after.noon," which was heartily applauded; and two „itations in the Lanca- shire dialect by Master George p.unders. They were entitled "Old Fogey " and " row," and were a source of such amusement to the ..udience. Mr. Craig, Miss Toft, and Miss Taft (who reNived a well-merited encore for her rendering of "Buy my pretty flowers") also contributed to the succeed of the evening's entertainment. On Tuesday Yening. the boat children attending the Sunday school ' a.l their annual tea party and Christmas tree. About 260 sat down to tea. the ladies superintending the tables being Miss Williams, Miss Jarratt, Miss A. Owen, Miss Allan, Miss , S. Dunning, Mrs. George Howard, and Mrs. Shaw. After tea Mr. Shaw, the missionary, and Mr. Howard, missionary. Ellesmere Port, each delivered a short address. The duty of robbing the Christmas tree of its fruit of useful and orna- mental articles, devolved upon Miss Williams and Miss Jarratt. Each scholar who had been well behaved and attended school regularly during the past year received a prize. The donors of the prizes were Mrs. C. Hazlehurst, Mrs. M. Steele, Miss Martin, Miss Barclay, Mr. Meadow- croft, and several other kind friends interested in the welfare of the boat children.

div.head: TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: TREAT TO AGED PEOPLE AT RUNCORN.

For several years the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association has had to carry on its labours weighed down by a financial deficit. Its existence, therefore, has been little felt in the town, for the members content, if the association could struggle on, even as a mere newsroom and library, have introduced no new schemes, struck out no new paths for their energy. Lately, however,, the financial incubus has been removed, owing in a great measure to the persistent, energetic labours of the hon. secretary (Mr. C. Nickson). Hence a more buoyant feeling pervades the associa— tion, and the outcome was the successful accomplishment last evening of one of the most popular Christian works it has ever undertaken. We refer to the treat to the aged people of Runcorn, which took place in the Public Hall. The idea of entertaining the old folks to tea originated with Mr. John A. Smith, who had seen similar undertakings carried out at Leigh, in Lancashire. At a meeting of the committee of the association, about a month ago, he intro— duced the subject, and suggested a trial of the scheme in Runcorn. Quick to perceive that many a lonely heart might be cheered by this means, the committee decided to try the experiment. They set to work enthusiastically, but their wildest anticipations did not contemplate such a successful issue. It was• at first thought that they would' not be able to entertain more than 100 persons, bat their appeal for aid met with so ready and so generous a response from the public that with donations of £4O in hand for the object, and nnmerous gifts of beef, ham, and the other various and necessary accompaniments of a tea party, they were in a position to invite all the old people in the town over 60 years of age. The arrangements for organising the treat were very complete. The important duty of soliciting- subscriptions devolved upon Messrs. B. Kniveton, 17: J. Norman, T. Cooke, J. E. Langshaw, and the Secretary, while an effective committee consisting of Messrs. John A. Smith, Win. Shaw, W. H. Rogerson, H. Randle, T. Mil- lington, and S. Coventry were industriously employed in ebtaining the names and addresses of people who were eligible for invitation. It perhaps seems unncessary to say that the " treat " was unsectarian, or, rather, it was for all sects. Age was a sure passport, whether the person was of the Establishment, or a Dissenter, or in poor or comfortable circumstances. The treat was not given as a " dole "as many are. It was not a gift from the hard-fisted ratepayer to the pauper. It was a feast in which the members of the Young Men's Christian Association were the hosts, and the aged people the honoured guests, and all distinctions of caste or class were lost in the generality of the " hospitable board."

The Committee of the Association had issued invitations to 650 persons. a number which it way be fairly thought would include all the people in the town who had reached, 60 years of age. With very few exceptions these put in an appearance at the hall, which had been decorated for their reception. As they entered the large-room " Welcome "in large letters greeted them, and turning their gaze to what is. always the centre of attraction, the platform, they saw the wish "May the Giver of all good, bless- this meeting" expressed in illuminated capitals on a blue ground. Below was the single word "Emmanuel" and the gallery front was adorned with shields of vari- ous designs. The decorations and the arrangement of the room had been in charge of Messrs. George Howard, E. Williams, T. C. Williams, J. E. Meredith, Geo. Bellamy,e J. W. Woodland, and H. Wright. The tea meeting was fixed to start at six o'clock, but for a considerable period before that hour the guests were to be seen slowly wend-- ing their way to the rendezvous. In many instances the women travelled in couples, while in others the husband and wife, permitted to bear the joys and sorrows of life to a good old age, still jogged on together. They were received at the Hall by a band of willing young workers, who conducted them to their places, evidently -with a feeling reverence, which the aged guests seemed heartily to appre- ciate. Many of the people invited were unable to walk through physical infliction, and these Mr. S. Yarwood, who for many years had given a treat to the old people, kindly conveyed to the place of meeting in a large waggonette free of charge. As the hall became filled the sight became an impressive one. It was a sight such, we believe, as had never been witnessed in Runcorn before. Age was on every hand. There was a host of wrinkled faces, each wrinkle "a line of beauty ;" while the chastening hand of-time had turned the once dark locks of hair which crowned their, heads, into a silvery gray. Over the heads of three or four of the guests the gales of 00 winters- had passed, and, bent with age, they were still braving cold terrors of the season. One old woman, who had reached the ripe old age of 01, was compelled through an infir- mity from w hich she suffered to decline the invitation. Per those persons placed in a like position, the association has arranged to make presents of a useful kind, se that they may know that, although unable to join in the auspicious occasion, they are not forgotten, and may enjoy at their own fireside what they could not elsewhere. Many of those present had spanned the allotted time of man, and a goad number were between the ages of 60 and 70. In issuing their invitations the committee did not adhere to a hard and fast line, consequently, a few about 57 and 58 years of age, could be seen mingling with the septegenarians and octogenarians. The committee, in selecting Friday as the most convenient day for en- tertaining the old folks, overlooked one important fact. Inevitably many of their guests would be of the Catholic faith, and, therefore, from conscientious scruples, unable to partake of flesh meat, which was so plentifully pro- vided. An interview was sought with Father Fennelly in the hope that he would grant a dispensation, but that gentleman said this could not be done without the Pope's permission. A way, however, was found out of the difficu It was announced that those who could not partake dime last evening, should receive a present of same ontah much ing morning, and this arrangement was receir: Canon Bar- satisfaction. Before commencing tea, thterristian Associa- clay, M.A., on behalf of the Young m----eqr, and gave them a tion, wished all present a happy 3y would have as much hearty welcome. He hoPedee as it had given the members enjoyment in the entertanc provide it. The assembly of the association plenrk with warm applause. The responded to his,me difficulty in finding accommo- committee hall their guests, and tables were dation fos "small hall," and also on the platform, but, erected ij of the host of waiters, who cheerfully gave wi.thete/ivices, the tea passed off successfully. Afterwards r6ld people were supplied with fruit of various kinds, and a vocal and musical entertainment was given for their delectation. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, as vicar of the parish, and he was supported by the majority of the clergy and ministers in the town, and the gentry of the neighbourhood. With that geniality which is one of his chief characteristics, the vicar addressed a few cheering words to the audience, who received them with gratification. They were equally delighted with the entertainment which followed. It had been organised by Messrs. J. D. Jones, Pownall, and E. Rhodes, and it was taken part in by the Volunteer band, Parish Church hand- bell ringers, Miss Wright, Miss Jukes, Mr. Morris, and Mr. Davies. A choir, composed from the members of the various places of worship in the town, also rendered a num- ber of glees. The whole affair was a gratifying success, and must lave amply repaid the members for their heavy labours undertaken in its organisation. It is intended to- morrow (Sunday) morning to give a free breakfast to the waifs and 3trays in the town.

Gillispie, Esq., at the Newton Town Hall, on Monday last, with Leing drunk and disorderly, at Earlestown, on the 9th December, and also with failing to appear at the Town Hall, Newton, on the 3rd inst.. in answer to a summons.— P.C. div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
The floods in the Thames Valley are now rapidly ' receding.

Lord. iioston, who has been lying ill for some days at his seat, fiedsor, Maidenhead, is ittew much bettor, and hopes are entertained of his speedy recovery. His lordship is gaining strength daily. Of the 80 head of cattle belonging to the Queen at Windsor over 60 are suffering from, foot-and-mouth disease. The Home Farm has now been declared infected. Yesterday morning, at Dover,,two applications were made under the Married Women's Property Act, and in one case the court granted protection.
Matt. IVPLoughlin, who, it is alleged, struck the blow which caused the death of the man Carney. near Clare- morris, on Wednesday night, gave himself up to the police yesterday morning.

- Mr. dladstone -is expected to visit Glasgow during, hi.% forthcoming visit to Scotland to assist at a launch of a large steamer, to be named the Hawarden Castle, which is being built on the Clyde for the Sir, Donald Currie Scotch Line.

The Exchange Company's Portsmouth correspondent telegraphs that Her Majesty is expected to visit the Con- tinent in the month of March. Orders have been given to prepare the yacht Osborne to take the Queeri at that time to Cherbourg. . _ _

Tke Press Association is informed that Mr. John Given,. M.P., has been offered and has accepted the permanent Under-Secretaryship for Ireland, in succession to Me. Hamilton, who will return to the Admiralty as soma as the necessary arrangements are completed. Edward Davies, a gamekeeper, of Brymbo, was charged at Wrexham yesterday with assaulting Constable Evans. Last night prisoner created a disturbance in Hope-street, and attempted to incite some colliers to assault the police. He kicked and bit at Evans "like a mad dog," and it took four officers to get him to the lock-up. He was,sentenced to two months' imprisonment.

"An Old Whip" writes to the Pall Mall Gazette with reference to Lord Brabourne's reply to a former letter of his, pointing out that his lordship published only a short extract from Mr. Gladstone's letter to him, and adding, "I have good reason to feel assured that the full text would give a very opposite impression to that which is suggested by .scincomplete a portion of it."

A St. James's Gazette telegram, dated Berlin,,Friday, states :—Thei rumour that Prince Bismarck has renewed his- request to be allowed to retire into privats life is groundless. The Emperial Chancellor has no such cause for displeasure- as that said to exist in the supposed friction in the working of State affairs. On the contrary, he intends to fulfil the- Emperor's urgent wish that be should remain permanently in the Government's service.

At Macclesfield, yesterday, the six young men who stole two gallons of whiskey from a ball-room on New Year's Day,. were brought up and charged with the offence. The prisoners were in such a state on the last hearing that the case could not be gone on with. One of the men-0. Peter Welsh, has been in the Infirmary, and hie life is despaired of. The prisoners were each sned 5s and costs. A Birmingham money lender, named Henry Hyman, met with his death yesterday morning under extraordin- ary circumstances. On going to bed on Thursday night he left the gas lighted in his bedchamber. The servant girl subsequently turned the gas off at the meter, and yesterday morning, before her master rose, she turned it on again. On going to the room later in the molting, Mr. Hyman was found dead in bed, having been safo- cated.

At a Court of Appeal, under the Crimes Act, hell at Limerick, yesterday, three men were sentenced to three months' imprisonment. Each attackel the dwelling-house of a bailiff named Hayes, in the employment of the Earl of Sandwich. Hayes followed the attacking party, and inflicted on them several serious weunds, by means of which they were afterwards identified.— Two sheriffs' bailiffs were sent for two months' imprisonment fcr pre- senting loaded revolvers at soldiers.

THE EDUCATIONAL CONGRESS AT ABERDEEN. The Educational Congress was resumed at Aberden yes- terday, when a paper was read by Dr. Farquharsca, M.P., deprecatory of the present system of 'teaching in schools as provided by the Education Acts. After consideroble dis- cussion a motion that the present educational denunds are calculated to be prejudicial to the general health of chil- dren was passed. THE LATE EARL OF STAMFORD,

Yesterday the remains of Lord StamfordVee removed from Bridgate Park, Leicestershire, to Enville Hall, Staf- fordshire, for interment on Tuesday. At Dtadgate the coffin was placed in a hearse drawn by four horNts, and pre- ceded by the tenantry. At Groby village the tenants lined the road, as the cortege passed to, Leicester. The coffin was placed in a bier carriage, and as conveyed per rail to En- ville. A large concourse of spectators was present.

div.head: VAGRANT SWINDLER.
div.p: A VAGRANT SWINDLER.

At Bradford yesterday, Annie Watson was charged mare- mand with vagrancy. From the statement made by the Chief a Police the prisonez had been in the town nine weeks, and made distressing statements to various ladies and thus gained their sympathy. She was taken into the families of two ladies, received food and shelter, and in each case left suddenly, taking property with her. One lady was at the present time ill in bed cwing to grief arising from the false statements of the prisoner. Yesterday week she was in the streets crying, stating that she bad a brother and sister under the ruins of the mill wrecked by the fall of a chimney. She was sympathised with by a woman, and received shelter, food and money. Sbe stated to•the police that she lived in seryke at Halifax, but has Maze sa.ii that all her statements were false. She. was sentenced co three months' imprisonm2at. MYSTERIOUS DEATH AT MACCLE'SFIILD.

Considerable excitement was Qaused in Maccbsfield on Thursday by the stoppage of the interment of tie remains of an old woman, aged 72, named ElizabcAh Walker, lately residing in Black-road, a poor locality. The crcurnstances which led the police to interfere are of a somewhat extraor- dinary character, and will be laid before a coroner's jury. The deceased was a member of a local sick andburial club. On the 2Gth ult. she was taken ill, and several:lob" notes" were sent and requests made to the medical afficer of the ciub to attend her. He did not eomply wit any of th 3 requests, and on Sunday deceased's son calleeat his house, but did not see him, hiis servant, owever, said she was authorised to give him sate medicine, which she did. He took it home and gave ito his mother, and the woman died in ten minutes afterwads. On appli- cation being made to the club surgeon, b certified the cause of deatll, and as it was reported to tb police that he had not attended the woman, combined lith the fact of her dying so soon after taking the Enedicinosupplied by his servant, the cm:4%er and the pollee interpsed awl atoped

Warburton and Co., report as follows :—The holidays have continued to interfere with the course of business throughout another week, and the weather has again been muggy and unseasonable. In the retail business passing wheat and flour have been steady, but feeding stuffs, cope ially maize, generally lower. Liberal sapnlies of wheat, dour, and beans, and larger suppdes of maize than for some time past have been receivel at Liverpool. Imports of other articles have been on an, insignieciant scale. CATHOLIC SALE OF WORK AND CHRI97II4IAS TREE.-011 New Year's Day, the Catholics of Newton held a Christmas tree and sale of work in the Co-operative Hall, in aid of the enlargement fund and other expenses lesn connection with St. Mary's schools, Crow-lane. The goods consisted of use- ful and fancy articles which were left over from the late bazaar,,and the sale on Monday last was a very successful one. A prominent feature was a drawing for over 100 valuable prizes, in connection with which, a large number of tickets had been sold.

HOUSEBREAKING AT RUNCORN.--A Successful attempt at house robbery was perpetrated in Ruricorn on Sunday night last, bat the loss to the occupath-yras not great. It appears that whilst Mr. Thomas Sharrock, currier, High-stree4, Run- corn, and his wife, were at &gine service, the robbers en- tered the shop probably by ()lulling the front door with a skeleton key and ransacked th,;3 premises from roof to base- ment in search of money, foz a:(1 other articles seem to have been disregarded. Every /00t11 was visited,drawers were tumbled upside down, aud even the beds did not escape their attention. Happily the sum they could lay their bands on was not very large, but they suoaeeded in carrying off about £5. GAMBETPA. It is estimated that 15,000 persons visited the Palais Bourbon on Thursday. It has been proposed to close all the theatres and shops to-day, and make it a day of general mourning. The Paix, of Thursday declares that those persons abroad who look for a great change in the internal policy of France and who apprehend danger to the Republic owing to the death of M. Gambetta, are entirely mietaken. Another allusion which is very prevalent, especially in Germany, is the belief that the disappearance of the de- ceased statesman will not result in any great modifications in the foreign policy of the Republic, either now or in the future. " France," continues the journal, "does sot desire war nor does she fear it. If she were forced into hostilities by the action of any foreign power, she would make war without M. Gm- betta just as she would have done with him. The warlike tendencies ascribed to him would nut have led France into war, but the disappearance of the great orator will not de- prive her of the power to defend her interests and her honour should they become endangered."
